A pert lady's maid, who had not been at Petworth before, on her first arrival mistook the Earl of Egremont for one of her own servants. She met him crossing the hall as the bell was ringing for the servants' dinner, and said, "Come, old gentleman, you and I will go to dinner together, for I can't find my way in this great house." He gave her his arm and led her to the room where the other sefvanta were assembled at their table, and said, "You dine here; I don't dine till seven o'clock." European brewers recently held a Congress at Versailles. According to statistics there presented, Europe has about 40,000 breweries, producing nearly 2,500,000,000 gallons of malt liquor. Great Britain produces nearly a third, then comes Prussia, Bavaria, and Austria. Bavaria consumes 54 gallons per head; Belgium (whose beer is chiefly Made at Louvain, where, too, is her chief university), 30; England, 29. Outside of Bavaria, where the very babies lap beer, the average consumption in Germany is.l9 gallons. In Scot- land it is nine; Ireland, eight and one-half; France, four, but steadily increasing. The past 25 years, have seen tut extraordinary increase in the beer consumption of Scotland and Ireland, where formerly whiskey was the prevailing drink. Farrturnt. SERvaNT9.—The Reformation sanctifiel once more the work-a•day la° of men. It honoured the body, it consecrated marriage, it rei-Istlted the horns at the head of the human order, it blessed from God. the homeliest toils and tasks of mankind. It proclaimed afresh—and the pro- clamation rang like a battle march through Christendom stirring the Protestant peoples to a nobler life and activity, whereby they have continually grown richer and stronger, while the Latin nations are torn by intestine conflict or go down to wreck—that to prince and peasant, to master and servant, to clerk, shoptnan, ploughman, and hodman, who abides with God in his calling, the word of the King of kings will be spoken with emphasis at last—" Well done, thoa good and faithful servant: thou bast been faithful in the few things, I will make thee ruler over many things enter thou into the joy of thy Lord."—Good Words. A Menne CAUSED BY A SHOE.—A fashionable shoemaker tells a pretty little story that reads well even though it may be a cunningly devised lie. His work is exclusively in ladies' foot-wear, and to an inquisitive reporter he said:— "Last year I made a pair of shoes for a lady who had as pretty feet as were ever fasithned. It was a pleasure for me to make the shoes, and when they were finished I put them in the show window in a very conspicuous place, where I could view them at my leisure. Pretty soon a nicely.dreased gentleman stopped and began viewing them attentively. Presently he entered the s.tere arid inquired if they were for sale. I told him no that they were ready made for one of ' my Customers. lie ,looked surprised, and asked the lady's name. I would not give him this much catisfaction, but told him where she lived, however. I was considerably sur- prised to learn afterwards that he was calling at the house, and more surprised still when the lady, accompanied by the gentleman, called at the store three months later. She called him 'dear' then, so I guess they were married." VENTILATION IN TM' KITCHEN.— Good ventilation is specially necessary in the kitchen, and this is best secured by bringing the air dowa into it from above. The shaft which I described in a previous paper fur conveying air from the very top of the house to the basement is of int. mense value to a kitchen pieced under ground. This rot being practicable, the plan of bringing the air from the out- side, high up towards the ceiling, is best, and the Sherine- ton valve answers, as a general rule, very well indeed. In fact, I know of no place where this answers better than in , the basement kitchen. The air which enters at this part is rapidly diffused through the upper portion of the room, and if due provision is made to carry the air away, the place is kept free of odours from the cooking that is going on below, and at the same time cool. To convey the air away advan- tage has to be taken of the chimney shaft, and in the kitchen, where there is usually a fire at all times, there could he noticing better unless some extremely complicated apparatus of a strictly rnechanizal kind were introduced. I have seen attempts made at securing pure mechanical ven- tilation, but even when these have been tolerably successful the trouble and cost have interfered with the continued suc- cess. On the whole, therefore, the chimney shaft is the natural pull for the air that ought to be removed. If there be gas in the kitchen for the purpose of affording light, it should always, when possible, be utilised or ventilation. This serves a double purpose; it removes the products arising from the combustion of the gas itself, and it re- moves the other products of an aeriform character which require to be carried away. To make the gas serviceable as a ventilate r, it necessary to connect the burner indirectly with the chimney flue; a plan which can be carried out readily when the burners are in the centre and are suspended from the ceiling, by having them overlapped by a large funnel inverted and connectedeahe a length of connecting. pine, with the chimney shaft.—Health at Home, i,s '6 Good Words." GHOSTS AMONG Tem INDIANS.—Another occupation of the medicine-man is the allaying of ghosts and other ap- paritions, which, owing to the quantity of indigestible food which the Indians eat, they are very apt to be troubled with in the shape of nightmares. On a person seeing one he will start up with a scream. The whole lodge is alarmed, the tire is fanned up again, the dreamer snatches up feathers and eats them, and covers his head with them. His nearest relative scarifies the dreamer's limbs with a knife until blood comes, which is received into a dish and sprinkled on his face, to allay the ghostly walker of the night. If the vision still continues, the friends throw articles belonging to the dreamer into the fire, and cry," More! more!" till all his property, including clothes, mats, and even his boxes, is heaped on the fire. The greatest excitement prevails, and girls are otten sick and exhausted fur days after such an tit fortunate dream. It is very unlucky to dream about any friend, and in this case, to obviate the evil consequence, the dreamer and the dreamed about exchange names. An Indian once told me, with a very ghastly face, that he had dreamed abotet me; so instantly, like good savages and brothers in affliction, we exchanged names. aeman may thus have in a few years many names, but the relinquished name is never mentioned. Sometimes, if a higher rank in the tribe is ac- quired along with the name' the event is celebrated with feasting and present giving. As an Indian is continually troubled with fears of the malevolence of the uneeen world, the sorcerer waxes fat upon his employment and fees. People do accommodate him, they must charge extra profit to cover extra risk. Thirdly. The Law of Distress Is unfair to the general creditors of an insolvent tenant and the general public. It is a law which gives a preference to one class of creditors over-all the abets, and that

_ can only be given at extra risk to all t,he others. Money transactions connected with the cultivation of land should be put on the same footing as other commercial transactions, and it is manifestly unfair to other creditors to give the preference to one. The law encourages the landlord to allow his tenants in- dulgences at the expense of others, and not at his own risk, and this without the other creditors having a voice in the matter. Even without the law, the landlord would still*be in a better position than other creditors to assert his claim and to proceed at once, if the tenant were in arrears with the rent, while at the worst he would but lose :his rent and could
always recover his principal—the land—while other creditors- would still be liable to lose all their ad-
vances.

• It is one of the strongest objections to the present law that it is the place where the property is found, and not the persons to whom it belongs, that renders it liable to Distress. Agricultural implements, tiles, manures, and other such property, even if not paid for by the farmer, can all be distrained for the rent of the land on which they are found. Even cattle and sheep sent upon a farm for temporary-pasture, and not the property of the tenant at all, are simi- larly liable, and a ease Occurred but a few years ago In Kent, where IGO lambs where seized and sold for £360, which the landlord knew did not belong to the tenant of the farm on which they were found, and to which they had only been sent for a short time. The case of Gould v. Usher, dealt with by the High Court of .Justice quite recehtly, is a similar instance. A man left some cows at an inn for the night; paying so much a head for their standing. The owner of the premises levied on them for the tenant's rent. The owner of the cows, however, removed them, but has been ordered by the Court to pay the rent due by the tenant of the inn. That such 'legal robbery" should be possible is sufficient to show the need of a change. Of course, it would not do for the landlord to have no remedy for his rent in the case ota tenant becom- ing insolvent, say in the middle of a half-year, and for the general creditors to step limpid sweep every- thing off, and then, when the rent became due, at tae usual half-yearly rent day, the landlord to find the bare farm with nothing left wherewith to satisfy the rent then due. But this could be obviated by making the rent due froni'day to day (though payable at the usual rent days), like the interest on a loan, so that in the event of a tenant coming to grief the landlord would rank equally with any other creditor, or, in other words, would occupy the position in which the Earl of Fife has voluntarily placed himself with respect to his farm tenancies, viz., he has abandoned unconditionally his privilege, as landlord, of stepping in and paying himself in full before any other credi- tor of an insolvent tenant, putting himself in his 'proper place on a level with the other creditors. The Laud Bill of the Farmers' Alliance contains the following provisions 14. No landlord shall ley, or cause to be levied any dis- tress for rent in respect of an holding. 15. When any tenant neglects or refuses to pay any in- stalment of rent after it has become due the landlord may apply to the judge of the county court of the district where the land or the greater part thereof is situate, and such judge may order the tenant to pay such rent, and such order shall be enforced in the same manner as an order made by the judge of a county court for the payment of a debt, and thejudge may, in addition to such order, make an order that the contract of tenancy be determined, and that the tenant give up possession of his holding at such time as the judge may order. Surely that would amply protect the landlord. Undoubtedly to effect a thorough reform of the Land Laws it will be necessary to abolish what Mr. Bleu. nerhasset, M.P., has described as "an antiquated privi- lege which came into existence under social and po- litical conditions totally different from those which now prevail amongst us—a privilege which is out of harmony with the spirit of modern institutions and hostile to the fall and free• development of modern enterprise. The Law of Distress is a class privilege in the strictest sense of the term. It is a privilege which has been created by the power, and which is maintained for the benefit of one class alone, and en- joyed by it at the expense and injury of every class. In the long series of enactments from the time of Henry VIII. to our own day the dominant influence of the londlord is reflected." Its abolition is not far distant. Nearly all the Chambers of Agriculture have condemned it, while the Chamber for Essex (which county returns six Tories) not long ago passed i a resolution. That as the Law of Distress s in- jurious to the best interests of the landlord, unjust to the tenant, and deceptive to the trader, it should be forthwith repealed .r while on the 14th of May, 1881, the House 'of Commons, without a division, passed a resolution declaring it desirable to abolish he power of levying distress for the rent of an agri- cultural holding.

A man named D wyer having gone to serve writs at Youghal was attacked by men with blackened faces, who took the writs from him and made him promise not to serve them in future

A special meeting on Tuesday of the Dublin Town Coun- cil, convened to -decide on presenting the freedom of the city to Messrs. Parnell and Dillon, was postponed on account of informality of notice, after an exciting discussion. At the Cork Assizes, three men, named Foley, Shea, and Lynch, were convicted of tho manslaughter of a farmer, named Sulliyan, in November. 1880. Shea was sentenced to 20 years' and the others to 15 years' penal servitude. The Right Hon. Sir Stafford Northcote spoke at a meeting held at Exeter, on Tuesday, to raise funds for the lady pro- prietors of land in Ireland iv ho are suffering distress through the " no-rent " policy inaugurated by the Land League. In anticipation of an arrest of lady Land Leaguers and break up of their society, Miss Parnell writes to the Dublin papers to state that all correspondence relating to evictions or the-prisoners' families can be sent to the care of Miss Helen Taylor. At the Munster Winter Assizes, Joseph Southwick, manager, Kelfinane • branch of the Munster Bank, was sentenced to penal servitude for five yearefor etnbezzlement and forgery. Thomas Netterfield, accountant, Mallow branch Provincial Bank, Ireland, was sentenced to two years' im- prisonment for embezzlement. Mr. Donough O'Brien went on Tuesday to Glandure, a mountain district near Tulla, to value farms on Sir Robert Keene's estates. Sir Robert is a very liberal landlord, and Mr. O'Brien, as the son of Smith O'Brien, was well received. On returning to Ennis, an armed party on the hillside fired at him, fortunately without injury. It has been rumoured for some time past that the Irish Executive contemplated taking action against the Lady Land Leaguers. An official circular has just been issued to the constabulary declaring that the proclamation pronouncing the League an illegal and criminal association extends to females. The police are instructed to see that the law is enforced, and that the meetirgs of the ladies' branches are broken up. Preparations have been made for the incarceration of a number of lady suspects. News reached Dublin on Monday night that Patrick Down, a tenarit farmer, had been murdered atßoley, Queen's County, it is supposed by a returned American, with whom he had bad a dispute about his farm. In County Limerick a farmer, who was sitting at his fireside, was shot at on Sun- day night and dangerously wounded. The two men Timothy O'Keefe and James Jeseph Hennessy, who were convicted at Cork, on Saturday, of " whiteboyism," were sentenced to eighteen months each. His Lordship intimated that but for the recommendation to mercy by the jury, he would have sent the prisoners into penal servitude. The Dublin police made an important seizure last Satur- day night in a district notorious for its Fenian proclivities. They forced an entrance into a house in Brabazon-street, and there after arrestingfour men they seized a regular magazine and a number of Fenian documents. The seizure in this house included the following, found in the front room i-22 breechloading rifles, one carbine, two sword bayonets, 400 rounds of revolver cartridges in a bag, 6,000 rounds of re- volver cartridges under the bed, 100 rounds of cartridges, three flasks of gunpowder, one cannister of ehot, and a pike. In another room the police found a six-barrelled revolver, three rifle bayonets, some muzzle-loading cartridges, 12 band grenades, a ladle, a gun handle, and a box containing sus- picious documents. At a. house in Cross Kevin-street the police seized 17 sword bayonets, 1,500 ball cartridges, two pistols, two small packages with the inscriptfon " explosives " upon them, which, it is believed, contain dynamite, a second six-chambered revolver in a case, and several cart- ridges. In a box, the lid of which was nailed down was found a package containing 381 b. of powdel and a large quantity of blank cartridges. In a desk were 90 rounds of rifle cartridges and also 1,500 bullets. On Monday the four prisoners were charged before the newly a ppointed•magistrate (Mr. Curran) with conspiracy. After the evidence of the police the case was remanded until to-day (Saturday), and an application for bail was refused.

Cosr ow ELECTRIC LIGHTING receives 7,400 dols. per annum for lighting Four. American paper states that the Brush Electric Light atufrenws Cteoerautphalyreet, in New York, from Fourth to Fifth Avenue, Fifth Avenue, and Broadway from Fourteenth to Thirty- fourth•street, and the latter street from Fifth Avenue to Broadway. In addition, the company, under their contract, also furnishes two groups, of six lights each, in Union and Madison-equal-es respectively. The street lamps have been lighted for several months; those in tee squares have been In operation for a shorter period. The illumination is said to be fairly Satisfactory. The tower lights, however, are effective only upon a small area, and it is also thought that their effect will be still further impaired by the heavy foliage in summer. The total number of gas lamps which it his been possible to extinguish by the substitution of elec- tric lamps is 430. The municipality of New York formerly paid 17.50 dols, per lamp per annum, which is estimated to have been at the rate of 1 dol. per thousand cubic feet net; but it is stated that that rate was so low that the gas com- panies did not care about lighting the streets. The gas lights, therefore, cost the city (and probably the producer) 7,525 dole, per annum, and are replaced by the electric light at a cost of 7,400 dole. It is a doubtful point, however, whether the Brush Company, as in London, makes or loses money at this rate. The advertisement alone, in either city, is worth something, and it is just possible that this was taken into account in making the contract. At all events, there seems to be very little margin of difference where gas is supplied at 1 dol. per thousand cubic feet. This, how- ever, it should he clearly understood, is mach less than the charae made to private consumers of gas in New York.—

Large quantities of English potatoes and cauliflowers are being shipped weekly to New York for consumption in that, city. The cauliflowers are fetching Bs. a dozen ; potatoes, after paying freightage, leave a handsome profit; and such is the scarcity of celery, that a quartepdollar (Is.) a stick is paid for it. Dr. Delbrook has established a factory in Germany for the manufacture of yeast from potatoes, which it is thought wilt be a goad and cheap substitute for yeast made from corn. Two million cwts. of con, at the cost of 18 million marks, is yearly made into yeast, whereas three million , cwts. of potatoes would only cost four and a quarter million

_ marks. _ FACTORY CHEESE It.l Cansna.—Cheese making on the factory system is about te be undertaken on a large scale in Canada by Mr. Geo. Morton, who is stated to have appor- tioned out 224 farms Into holdings of 169 acres each, each of which he will stock with 30 cows. IL narrow-gauge rail- way will run through the entire estate. A station will be built on each farm. By these means the whole of the milk will be carried to one central factory twice in each day. This it the largest undertaking of the kind which has ever, been projected. MALT AS FOOD FOR CATTLE.—With young animals, both lambs arid calves, I consider malt to be an excellent addi- tion to the other artificial foods usually given to them. During the winter of 1880-81 malt and linseed were ground together in the proportion of 2 bush. of malt to 1 Of linseed, and half a gallon of this mixture per cow was mashed in cold water and'poured over a bushel of "chop" and given at two feeds ter dairy cows. During last spring, wnen the couples were folding off turnips, the lambs, as soon as they would pick from the troughs placed in front of the hurdles, bad a small quantity of malt mixed with the linseed cake, and that mixture was continued until weaning time (June 5). The malt was discontinued during the hot dry weather, but again given in the autumn, when the lambs were put upon rape, the mixture then being linseed and cotton cake, with 2 gals. malt to 6 gals. cake. The result has been very satisfactory. I have also given a mixture of malt and lin- seed 1 bush, per week (in addition to the allowance of 1 cwt. of crushed oats) to an old horse that was out of condition, and the result in about four weeks has been an evident Im- provement in the general appearance of the animal. My experience in feeding with malt confirms the opinion I have always held that, being easily digested and containing, so little moisture, it would be an excellent food for all young animals, particularly for lambs when eating very succulent green food, as turnip tops or young rape.

DIRECT AND INDIRECT AGRICULTURE. VACANT FARMS. " J. W." writes to us as follows :—There is one aspect ol affairs that landowners and farmers should seriously con- eider. It vitally affects their interests, and should lead them to understand their position and to concert the best means of meeting it. The remedy for their distress is not In a return of rent, nor in Acts of Parliament to give them Protection, nor in any temporary means by which they may meet the effects of wet seasons. They have not now the monopoly of producing food for the people of this country, nor will they ever have as long as the sun and moon en- dure. They have to meet the markets of the world,land to sell at the same prices, and their prosperity does now, and will in the future, depend more on the quantity produced than the price at which it sells. This being their position, Is it either wise or manly to look to any source for help but to their own skill and industry, to just and wise arrange- ments between landlord and tenant, to improved modes ef cultivation, to secure to each Party their respective rights to draw capital to their business by making it a safe and profitable investment, and to go hand in hand to make the land as productive as possible. Their prosperity depends on themselves, and if they be wise they will be up,and doing, they will put their shoulders to the wheel and make the best of their position. In the latter part of the last century and the beginning of this, seasons were frequently cold and wet, and the crops of grain small in quantity and bad in quality. Sometimes flnr was sinence a penal, and barley meal so scarce that It could not be bought for money. The roads were bad, canals few, and the conveyance of goods both slow and costly. Each part of the country had to depend in a great measure on its local supply. A ve.,:sel was then thirteen weeks in going from England to America, and did not pro- bably take at one time more than a fourth of what a vessel now takes. Under these circumstances there was little or no foreign supply, and consequently, when the crop was deficient, prices were high, and the farmer made as much money, if not more, in a bad as a good season. But it is not-so now. A great and lasting change has taken place. We are not fed only by the harvests of the United Kingdom, but of the world, and the result is we have a plentiful supply in all kinds of seasons at moderate prices. The effects of had harvests, therefore, in a great measure fall on the farmers of this country, and not on the consumers of their produce. We have in Lancashire and other parts of the kingdom a large and continually increasing amount of indirect agri- culture. We are producing every year a large amount of all kinds of grain, cf beef and mutton, of bacon and cheese, of all sorts of fruit, and of every kind of food that man consumes. A mill is built, furnished, and started. The engine works the machinery, and cloth is produced in large quantities. Pecple in all parts of the world are in want of clothing, and must and will have it to the extent of their purchasing power. We take the produce of the mill to the neutral markets of the world, and sell it cheaper than other nations. We exchange our goods for their produce, and ' bring home an abundance of food. In this way we produce ' an enormous quantity of grain and other provisions, and the people are well and cheaply fed. It is impossible for man to imagine the extent to which this kind of agriculture may be carried. The high andl hilly parts of Lancashire have room for more mills and a climate in which cotton can be manufactured 20 per cent. cheaper than in America and at`a much cheaper rate than it can be in other parts of the world. By the means of quick ard cheap carriage the whole world is open to us, and every wind from every shore is sending us of its stores. Popula- tions are rapidly increasing, the resources of the earth are everywhere being daily more and more developed, and our supply of food and other ale gs will only be limited by our ability to purchase them. That ability is great at the pre- sent, and will be still greater as machinery is multiplied. Improved machinery has been in the past, is at the present, and will be in the future a mighty factor in the world, and greatly benefit mankind. Engines will work machinery, run shuttles, and the produce of our mills be such that indirect agriculture will procure us an abundance of food and amply supply all our wants. In Canada and the States of America there are millions of acres of gocd land, which can be had at a cheap rate, wait- ing to be occupied. Roads are being made and every means adopted to develop it. Men are looking at the prospect for farmers here and there, and concluding that farming across the Atlantic will do better for them than in England, and are going in considerable numbers to employ their capital and energies in the far West. This is a serious blow to our agriculture. The money and energy that should have been expended in our country are taken to another and laid out there to produce grain and other thine. The people of India, New Zealand, Australia, and the whole world are increasing and will continue to increase their produce for the English market. Who can say they are not to do it? Wto can stop our trade and cut off our supplies? Who will stand in the way of our prosperity? Whoever may try to do itgaill be swept away with the irresistible tide of public opinioirlTld utterly fail in the attempt. The wants of the world and the good of mankind will certainly ensure it. It is therefore very evident from the position of our nlanufactories and the producing powers ofthe world that we have at present, and shall have in the future, emwetille, etllnetrhee almost an ewalimt htherefore, pro- be that i tee (l agriculturists supply of f food. this Tire country rsult u de. eßutc eanatd t hmeo smt a erkffiect iepnr tic ewoafytsheowf ovirlodr,kaongd at dhoe p the irt fa rmcsh and making them as productive as possible. Another adopts "The Cradlejthe Dungeon, and the Tomb." A third, "Bad, Orange Blossom, and Cypress." But "Hatches, Matcher, and Dispatches" still carry off the palm. THE LAST OF THE WAS CHlEFS.—Another most re. markable man Was Tsosieten, war chief of Taitka, now—if not dead—a very aged man. In old times his prowess in war was sung along the coast for many a league, and still lives in the memory of the neighbouring tribes, whose terror he was. War after war he waged with them, until the whole coast paid tribute to him, and he really did not know his wealth in slaves end blankets. Sometimes he would buy slaves—if captives from the distant tribes, so mach the better—give them canoes and provisions, and set them off to their homes. Than everybody would gather round and eagerly ask, "01 who bought you and set you free?" "Tsosieten bought me and set me free." Then great was the name of Tsosieten. In "piping times of peace" he lived on "Indian Island," in a stockaded fort armed with cannon Which he had bought from the Imperial Fur Com- I patty in Russian America, and inside its pickets was the village of his chosen warriors. Alas !—sic transit gloria mundi—blind and helpless, last of his name, when I last saw him he still lived in his ruined fort, with only the recollections of his former deeds to console him. "They all call themselves chiefs nowadays," he said bitterly to me. "I am the only chief l"—The Peoples of the World. EFFECT OF Dun UPON HEALTH.—We shall probably never know the real effect of dust upon health. It is by no means improbable that many ailments, which are now as- cribed to other and more remote causes, are really due to it. Professional and business men would perhaps be more hale and hearty if they worked under more cleanly conditions ; but any housewife, even the most careless, would be horri- fied if she saw the state of dirt in which by far the greater number of Offices are left from one year's end to another. In many of the busiest parts of London, and other cities it is an almost universal custom to have the windows cleaned only once a year, and their grimy and sooty appearance during the other eleven months must be familiar to every one. In many offices the dusting operations are wholly limited to the desks in use, and to the removal of the surface dirt and scattered scraps of paper from the carpet- Books endpapers, which notoriously accumulate more dust than anything else, are very rarely dusted at all. It is true that now-a-days professional and business duties are performed upon a 'thigh pressure" system, but it is to be regretted that more care is not taken to minimise the dangers to health to which an enforced sedentary and indoor life ex- poses the great majority of men; and a great change for the better may reasonably be expected if the charwoman or care-taker is required to do something more than the present quantity of work, and periodical and thorough cleaning of -offices is insisted upon.—Cassell's Family Magazine. A SAD CASE.—The Free Press has received and placed •in the refrigerator a poem from a young girl at Ann Arbor, who is groping through one of the blackest clouds of opaque grief that ever rolled athwart the horizon of youthful love. The sheet upon which the poem is written is covered with discoloured spots that experts in the office pronounce to to traces of grief-laden tears, but they may be simply drops of juice which flew out from an apple she was muching as she wrote. The poem opens— The tale of woe I fain ilvould tell Would crush all hearts with sorrow, And call to mind the pangs of—well. Eternity's tcemorrow. The skill displayed by the presumably fair writer is getting around the pronounciation of a real bad work will commend itself to every despiser of profanity in the land, The poem =tains about sixteen verses, which are, with one or two exceptions, it a fair stare of preservation. The heart- piercing streak of gilded grief runs through each verse, and gives evidence that the writer had it pretty bad. She may have been a little bilious when the sad lines oozed from her pen, and yet it is seldom that an attack of the most acute biliousness will cause such morbid grief. As the reading of the lines progresses, however, the cause of her terrible tussle with sorrow becomes apparent, and in the last stanza the whole truth stands out like a bay-window. It runs in this limpid shape:— No more will I see John Mc.Coy, He's left his loving Harriet; . He's wrecked my every earthly joy, He's false as J. Iscariot. He's left me for another, who, Her wiles exerted o'er hit*. And who erelong will shake him, too— Ah, cruel fate before him! The poem has been very carefully placed on ice, and will be forwarded to the next World's Fair for public exhibition.— Detroit Free Press. , THE EDUCATION OF CRILDREN.—The education of chil- dren is another very serious item of expense when it has to be deducted from a small income,,but it is one which all wise parents will strain every nerve to meet fully and without stint. It is better worth while to spend money over the education of children than it is to save the money in order to bequeath it to the children for use in the future. An in- dividual who is well educated is :more likely to make bis way than is one who, lacking education, can boast only of the possession of a small yearly income which is his apart from work. Let parents who feel inclined to mourn because , they can never leave their children a fortune take comfort in a fact which, though we may find difficulty in accepting it, is in accordance with the teaching of experience. Chil- dren who are healthy, energetic, and sensible, are never really the worse for having to make their own way. Private means would be more likely to hinder their progress than to advance it. The consciousness of possession might make them self-indulgent or conceited but it would not tend to increase that energy and determination which distinguish the men who have made their mark. Real progress affects character as well as position, and good education is one of the best means of enabling young people to gain it. It is the eimple fact that, with scarcely an exception, the most successful men we see around us, and those most distin- guished for energy and ability in any marked form (we are , speaking here of social, not political life), have been " self- made " men; that is, they began life with nothing but their own brains and their own hands. , BY A. SOUTHWEST L—ANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. _ [SPECIAL.] XXX. . DAMASCUS (Continued.) rette the highest of the minarets we had an exceedingly find view of the city in all its length and braedth. Smoke- less and shining in the blaze of noon it presented a picture 41 wnuderful beauty. Rising up in every direction from a !ea of white terraced houses, crowned with an endless mass of cupolas, were lofty domes and tapering minarets, whose goldeli finials were glittering in the rays of the sun; while aroundihe city for miles was theencircling border of the meet `Mated and brilliant green,—a fairer scene or a fresher findscape'ne eye need wish to rest upon. The" street called ghaight," is perhaps the busiest, as it is the longest, thorough- tare in Drn aaicus. It runs from east to west directly through the city in a straight line, with the exception of one short angle. Mark Twain's description that it is "straighter than a corkscrew. and not as straight as a rainbow," I one is"m simply , a t of those thousand and one departures from strict truth, the cost of which his eternal straining after jokes and smart , sayings is purchased. Instead of seeing in the words "called straight " a bitter irony, I see in the fact that the street has really been preserved " straight" through all the changes that must have fallen upon this oldest of all cities, one of the most remarkable things intistory,and a grand corrobora- tion of the Divine records. We mush have stood with.ln.a Sew yards of the great Apostle's spiritual birthplace; rinif)yn a few yards, also, of the place in which he was enabled Divine grace to struggle from death unto life; a his .yards from the place too, on which he first lifted ultt , 00, on theratitude, proclaim M tense, thrilling with love and g had come to alorY and the power of that Saviour whom he•n his voice to Damascus to persecute and blaspheme. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 24, .1881.
"HE'S GONE YONDER."

1 "And what's 'going yonder'?"• asked Jamie Dunlop, in itstonishment. "Ah, that is hard for you to understand, roy poor boy," said the minister; but it is my real self—the real Henry Dundee who lives inside this body. When you go to bed at night you take off your clothes, and when I go yonder I shall not want my body, so I shall just put it off." And Sandy will put it in the box and the hole," said the boy, ruefully. "Yes, Sandy can lay the bones and what- ever flesh is left, in the grave, but Sandy will not lay me. I shall have gone yonder,' and no one knows that better than Sandy himself. Sandy knows I should not like to take yonder with me a poor weak sickly body like this, and so when I have done with it he will take it and lay it in the ground; but as to me, my real self, I am away." "And will ye no' take nothing with ye ?" asked the boy. "I've sent everything on before," said the minister. "Eh, by the coach ?" "Nay, Jamie, the coach does not run there, or take anything there, but you can send a deal there for all that. All that we give here to the King of that place, we shall find before us there, and a great deal more too. Jamie, Jamie," said the minister—shaking his head some- what sadly, for he was in despair as to. ever making him en- tirely understand—" you cannot make out how all this is, and indeed, I only know a part about it mystlf, but you may know enough to do as I am doing, and just to think that when you die you are not being put an end to as you think. You are not going to be shut up for ever in the grave by Sandy, as you fear; you may know, my poor boy, that you are only going Fonder, and all fear of death and the grave may be taken away from you."—The Rev. P. B. Power in The Steadfast Aim," bang the extra Christmas Part of "The Quiver," .tor 1881.

A Curtis-vans RHYUE.—Christmig comes but once a year, nights are very dark and drear, children eat trio much, I fear, ghosts are fancied to appear, meat is always very dear, cynics at the season sneer, lots of people feel most queer. Perhaps its best, from what I hear, that Christmas comes but once a year.—Moonshine:

, Theseeds of mistletoe ripen late, between February and April. If the ripe berries are rubbed upon the branches of trees, between February and April, they may be readily cultivated; and mistletoe has thus been found to germinate on the oak, several of the pine tribe, cherry, common laurel, Portugal laurel, holly, lime, elm, hornbeam, birch, syca more ash, chestnut, hazel, and acacia; as well as the apple, pear, and vrhitethorn tribe; but on all except the apple and'pear, the seeds soon sicken and die. - A Paw DELusrorrs.—That anybody likes Christmas. That nursery books are published for children. That panto- mimes Make you laugh. That the clown is duller at home than he is on the stage. That all stage fairies belong to the Church and State Guild. That anybody but the singers themselves care to listen to a glee. That a good Gorgonza cheese equals a good Stilton. That it is possible to get a good Stilton. That it is better to go without wine alto- gether, if you can only afford middling good wine. That, as a rule, anybody knows the differance.

LIVERPOOL CORN, THIIRSDAY.—There was a quiet tone per- ceptible throughout to-day's market. Wheat met with a limited inquiry at about last Tuesday's quotations. Flour was firm, but not in much demand. Indian corn was steady at 5s 10d per cental for pew mixed American, but not much busi- ness was concluded. Beans were rather firmer in tone. Peas, oats, and oatmeal experienced a slow sale at the prices of last market to-day. MANCHESTER CORN, THIIRSDAT.—The trade has continued to exhibit signs of weakness as reported for some time past: Buyers have limited their operations to the merest retail tran- sactions, at prices tending in their favour for all articles except flour, for which there has been a healthy inquiry at full price". There was somewhat of a holiday attendance at this morning's market and a limited business. English wheat was fully as dear; foreign Id to 2d per rental lower. Flour firm. Oats and oatmeal were dull, if not lower. Beans and peas steady. Maize, notwithstanding small supplies, must be quoted Id per cental under the currencies of last market day. LIVERPOOL COTTON, Thursday.—The market to-day on the spot has been very s'eady throughout. ' The market 'is poorly supplied with stapled American, which commands extreme prices. Above 6 15-16 d. there is a good supply of staple offer- ing, but below that price th 3 supply is unsatisfactory. The trade demand has been moderate, and holders have offered rather freely, but always at full rats. Good middling Orl.•age are advanced 1-16 d. THEFT BY • HAYDOCK POLICE CONSTABLE. Joshua Welfenden was charged with having, on the 24th Septem- ber, whilst baile, of a certain sum of Ll 10s., belonging to Superintendent VVelr, of Wigan, stolen and carried away the same. He was also charged with absenting himself from duty as a police officer without proper notice. Superin- tendent Weir, of Wigan, said the prisoner had been a police constable stationed at Maydock. On the 19th September he received the sum of 6s. from the clerk at the Occasional Court House, and on the 24th of the same month he received two other sums, £1 33. ed. and ss. 6d., making a total of .21 459. The money was entrusted to prisoner to keep until the end of the month when he should have paid it over to witness. He, however, absconded the same evening and fad not been seen until be was apprehended at Huddersfield.— Prisoner said he went to see his cousin, and got "muddled in beer." Since his wife died he had taken to drinking.— Mr. Artingstall : Drunkenness does not make the crime less. —Superintendent Weir said the prisoner got into the police foroe under false pretences, as he represented he had never served in any police force, whereas he had been in the Hud- dersfield police force. Prisoner had only been a few months in the Lancashire county police force.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined £5, or in default one month, for leaving the force, and for the embezzlement was committed, for three calendar months' hard labour. James Hankinson was summoned by the Warrington Rural Sani- tary Authority for permitting a nuisance to exist on his premises at Hollins Green, in consequence of the yard drainage being turned into an opeb ditch.—Mr. J. C. Sutton appeared on behalf of the Authority, and Mr. Rawlings, in- spector, proved the. case.—Defendant was ordered to abate the nuisance in a month.—James Berry was summoned for having on his premises, in Hollins Green, a pig-stye kept in an offensive condition, and he was ordered to abate the nuisance.

div.p: ANNUAL REUNION.

The twehty-first annual re-union took place on Thursday evening, in the Town Hall, St. Helens. Mr. Arthur Sinclair presided, and there was a good attendance, including many old scholars who manifested considerable interest In the pro- ceedings. In one of the ante-rooms were arranged a number of maps, drawings in pencil, crayon, and water colours. The specimens exhibited were very beautiful, and the folloiving exhibitors deserve special mention :—J. T. Roberts, Herbert Bamford, George Spencer, NV. C. Tayler, W. Morris. T. 11. Grey, Fred Hague, W. G. Smith, and John Warne. There were also specimens of writing, and ornamental penmanship by an old scholar. Praise is due to Mr. Dutton and his staff of teachers, for the way in which the School is conducted. An interesting programme:was gone through, a novel fea- ture being the performance of Molieres French comedy "Bourgeois Gentilbomme," by Masters Beckett, R. Bennett, E. Bennett, Dutton, Guy, Jordan, T. Roberts, J. Roberts, R. Roberts, and Skaife. The first act commences with th e• e- meetin of the music and drawing masters at the house of Mons. meeting "bourgeois gentilhomme " to give him lessons. While M. Jourdain is dressing they enter upon a discussion as to the merits of their respective professions. M. Jourdain enters, and the masters endeavour to impress him with the importance of their hearts. Musical composi- tion was illustrated, and a lesson in dancing is given. The fencing master enters and demonstrates the importance of his heart. A quarrel ensues, and the master of philosophy entering tries to restore peace, but only exasperates them more. A general sqnabble ensues, and the performance ends. The fairy scene of Shakespeare's English comedy" Midsum- mer night's dream," by Masters Allsebrook, Bamford, F. Hague, J. A. Hague, Harvey, Johnson, Leather, Taylor, and ISkaife. Glees and part songs were given by the scholars under the conductorship of Mr. Dutton.

Why does a duck go under water 7—For divers reasons. When has a man four hands 2—When he doubles his fists. Where is happiness always to be found 7—ln the dic- tionary. Why does a duck cross the road 2—To get to the other ide. s4')What is that which can often be found where it is not?— Fault. Why is a cow's tail like swan's breast ?—Because it grows down. What day in the year do women talk the least 2—The shortest day. • What length ought a lady's crinoline to be 2—A. little above two feet. Why is a dog's tail a very great novelty ?--Becauss no one ever saw it before. What is that which is a cat, is like a cat, and yet is not a cat P—A kitten. What is worse than raining cats and dogs 2—Hailing cabs. and omnibuses. What trade would you recommend to a short man ? Grow, sir ,(grocer). What fruit dors a newly married couple most resemble 2 —A green pear. How many dog-days are there 2—As many as dogs, for i‘ every dor has his day."' Which has most legs, a horse or no horse 7—No horse, because no horse has five. Why do ducks put their heads under water ?—To liquidate their little bills. What sort of cookery does a young lady prefer 2—DresSing her hair (hare). Why do ladies like a north-east wind 7—Because it brine chaps to their lips. • In what circumstances is a woman that wears stays ? Straitened circumstances.

When is " Mary " not a dissyllable P—When you change it into Polly-syllable. What is better than presence of mind in a railway acci- dent ?—Absence of body. When did Ruth behave ill to Boaz P—When she pulled his ears and trod on his corn. Why are children like jellies r—Becluse as they: are moulded so they will turn out. If you were to ride upon a doakey, what fruit would you resemble ?—A rear (pair). What ought a skipper to do after weathering a gale ? Why, thank his (s) tars. How can a boy make his jacket last 7—By making his waist-coat and trousers first.

Why is a cab-stand like a lawyer's desk P—Because con- veyances are drawn up upon it. Why should a favourite hen be called Macduff 7—Because , we wish her to "say on." 1 Which is the strongest day in the week 7—Sunday, because all the rest are week-days. Why do little birds in their nests agree 7—Because if they I did not they wouldfa// out. What relation is that child to its father who is not. the father's, own son ?—His daughter. When does a man shave with a silver razor 2—When he cuts off his heirs with a shilling. Why is sympathy like blind-man's-buff?--Because it is a fellow feeling for a fellow-creature. Why are you very unlikely to catch the 12-50 train?— Because it's ten to one if you catch it. Why are ladies like telegrams P—Because they are beforel the males (mails) in intelligence. Why are cowardly soldiers like butter 7—Because when they are exposed to fire, they run. Why are fowls the most profitable things to keep P—Be- cause for every grain they give a peck. Why should people marry in what& P—Because ladies want niufs and gentlemen want comforters. What is that which every one can divide, but no one can see where it has been divided P—Water. What language does an Arabian child speak before it cuts its teeth?—Gum-Arabic, unquestionably. Why is the Emperor of Russia like a workhouse boy?— He feels Hungary, and wants a slice of Turkey. Why do the birds feel depressed early in a summer morn- ing 2—Because their little bills are all over dew. Why is a coal charity the best of all charities P—Because it makes the receiver's grate full (grateful). What two counties in Ireland would you suppose to be lighter in weight than the rest 7—Cork and Down. When was beef-tea introduced into England on a large scale ?—When Henry VIII. dissolved the Pope's bull. Why is a horse the most humane of all animals P—He gives the bit out of his mouth and listens to every woe. What is the difference between a Catholic priest and a Baptist ?=One uses wax candles and the other dips. Why is a doctor better taken care of than his patients ? —Because, when hb goes to bed, somebody is sure to rap him up. Why is a tired cat -like the main attraction of the Brighton Aquarium P—Because it is a knocked-up puss (an octopus). Why is a lawyer's profession not only legal, but religions 7—lt involves a knowledge of the law and love of the profits. If two men fight and one bite off the other's ear, what would the magistrates require him to do?—Keep. the piece (peace.) What is the difference between a D.D. and an M.D.?— One preaches and does not practise, the :other practises and does not preach. What is that which everyone wishes to have, and which everyone wishes to get rid of directly he obtains it 7—A good appetitd. Why are wheat and potatoes like the idols of old 2-- Because the former have ears and hear not, and the latter eyes but see not. What proof have we that there was sewing in the time of David 7—We read that the Philistines were hemmed in on every side. At what hour did the serpent make his appearance in the garden of Eden P—Some time during the night. He certainly came after Eve. Why is a young lady who does not mean what she says likely to fall into the hands of the police P—Because she is liable to be Miss-apprehended. - If you are gding up for the Civil Service examination which ought you to mind most, your p's or your q's ? Your p's, because p will make any ass p-ass. Why is Gillot, the penmaker, the most wicked of men ? Because he makeemen steel (steal) pens, and then persuades them that they do right (write). When a girl is kissed by her lover what newspapers would she mention P—No "Guardian," no "Spectator," no "Ob- server," but as many" 'limes" as you please. Why are sheep the most dissireted animals in creation ? Because they gambol in their youth, spend most of their days on the turf; the best of them are blacklegs, and they. are sure to be fleeced at last,. .
Why is a roguish lawyer like a man who cannot sleep?— Because he lies first on one side and then turns round and lies on the other, and is wide awake the whole time, and even when dead he lies still.

GENTLEMEN'S Ammar, (London: Chatto and Windus.)— Under this title we have two capital tales : " Madamoiselle Angile," by Alice Corkran," and "A double Bond," by Linda Vinod, well calculated to have a large sale amongst the lovers of fiction.

FINANCIAL REFORM Aratixac (Liverpool: Financial Reform Asseciation).—The excellent collection of statistics contained in this valuable annual ought to have a place in every housebord and be read by every taxpayer. It is one of the most useful works that a politician can study, and as snch we heartily commend it to the notice of our readers. There are in the issue for 1882 three classes of tables that deserve to be widely read and carefully considered by all who take an interest in the welfare of this country. The first demonstrates by extraordinary figures the necessity for a re- distribution of seats; the second relates to the details of tqe wonderful progress made by the' country since the adoption of Free Trade principles; and the third gives invaluable information about the landowners of the United Kingdom.

It is published by the above well-known firm and occupies the first rank amongst the Christmas annuals, being issued in its old quarto size with a wealth of coloured and black and white illustrations, well calculated to enable it to retain all its old popularity. This year Old Peter professes to hen met a party of peculiar people, to turn old, to be the origi- nal tinker, tailor, soldier, sailor, rich man, poor man, plough- ' boy, and thief celebrated in primitive nursery fortune telling. Each of these relates his own adventures, and some of the stories told are capital. • WARD, LOCK, dz CO.'S PIIBLICATIONS.—This month's issue of the Universal Instructor com.nences the second volume, and is replete with carefully written articles on botany, zoology, electricity, magnetism, and 'a number of other use- ful subjects. It is an excellent work and deserves a wide circulation. The part now before us of DP. Athens' Clark's Commentary on the Bible brings the work up to the end of the first book of Samuel, and as the work is well printed on good paper and beautifully illustrated, we com- meend it to the notice of our readers. A WOMAN'S SPITE.

Towards evening, Cosway's arrangements for the elope- ment were completed. He was eating his solitary dinner when a note was brought to him. It had been left at the door by a commissioner. The man had gone away without waiting for an answer. The note ran thus :—" Miss Ben- show presents her compliments to Mr. Cosway, and will be obliged if he can call on her at nine o'clock this evening, on business which concerns himself." This invitation was evi- dently the result of Adela'a visit earlier in the day. Cosway presented himself at the house, troubled by natural emotions of anxiety and suspense. His reception was not of a nature to compose him. He was shown into a darkened room. The one lamp on the table was turned down low, and the little light thus given was still further obscured by a shade.. The corners of the room were in almost absolute darkness. A voice out of one of the corners addressed him in a whisper: "1 must. beg you to excuse the darkened room. I am suffer- ing from a severe coll. My eyes are inflamed, and my throat is so bad that I can only speak in a whisper. Sit down, sir. I have got news for you."—" Not bad news, I hope ma'am?" Cosway ventured to inquire.—" The worst possible news," said the .whispering voice. "You have an enemy striking at you in the dark."—Cosway asked who it was, and received no answer. He varied the form of inquiry, andsaked why the unnamed person struck at him in the dark. The experiment succeeded; be obtained a reply.—"lt Is reported to me," said Miss Benshaw, "that. the person thinks it necessary to give yon a lesson, and takes a spiteful pleasure in doing it as mischievously as possible. The person, as I happen to know, sent you your invitation to the party, and made the appointment which took you to the door In the lane. Wait a little, sir; I have not done yet. The person has put it into Mr. Restall's head to send his daugh- ter abroad to-morrow."—Cosway attempted to make her speak more plainly. "Is the person a man or a woman?" he said.—Miss Renshaw proceeded without noticing the in- terruption. "You needn't be afraid, Mr. Cosway; Miss Restall will not leave England. Your enemy is all-powerful. Your enemy's object could only be to provoke you into planning an elopement—and, your arrangements once com- pleted, to part you and Miss Regall quite as effectually as if you were at opposite ends of the world. Spiteful, isn't it? And, what is worse, the mischief is as good as done already." —Cosway rose from his chair.—" Do you wish for any further explanal,o?" asked Miss Benshaw.—" One thing more," he replied. "Does Adela know of this ?"—"No," said Miss Bensbaw; "it is left to you to tell her."—There was a moment of silence. Cosway looked at the lamp. Once roused, as usual with men of his character, his temper was not to be trifled with. "Miss Renshaw," he said, "I dare say you think me a fool ; but I can, draw my own con- clusion, for all that. You are my enemy."—The only reply waa a low chuckling laugh. All voices can be more or less effectually disguised by a whisper—but a laugh carries the revelation of. its own identity with it. Cosway suddenly threw off the shade over the lamp, and turned up the wick. The light flooded the room, and showed him—His Wife.— From "Your Money or Your Life," in Belgravia Annual.

MR. GLADSTONE AND THE REFORM OF PARLIAMENTiEt PROCEDURE.--Mr. Gladetone's secretary, in reply to a reso- lution from the Bath Young Men's Liberal "Association urging a referm in parliamentary procedure, writes that the Premier observes that the need of reforming the procedure in the House of Commons and of supporting some measure of reform in it wee fully admitted. He is glad to receive such expressions of sentiment, and trusts that when Govern- ment comeslo deal with the matter they will receive the requisite's:ippon from the country at large. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE LAND LAWS AND PARMA- MENTAIIY PROCEDURE. The following letter from Mr. Gladstone has been received by the hon. secretaries of the London and Counties Liberal Union, in acknowledgment of a resolution passed at a recent meeting of the General Council of that body, urging upon the attention of the Government the necessity of a thorough roform of the Land Lawa of England and Scotland :—"10, Downing- street, Whitehall, Mb Dec., 11131.—Sir,—I em directed by Mr. Gladstone to thank you for communicating to hint a copy of the resolution, which was adopted at the recent meeting of the General Council of the London and Counties Liberal Union, in favour of reforming the Land Laws of Great Britain. In reply, I am to assure you that her Majesty's Government are very sensible of the importance of the subject; but, regarding this and other legislation, I am to observe that as to time much must depend on the re- form which it may be possible to effect in Parliamentary procedure. I am, sir, your obedient servant, E. W. HAMILTON.

The Liberal members for Manchester (Messrs. Bright and Slagg) and Mr. R. Leake, M.P., attended the opening on Saturday of a Reform Club in Cheetham. Mr. Leake, who presided, discussed the merits of Political clubs, dwelling especially on the social and educational advantages which they afford. Mr. Stagg condemned the obstruction prac- tised ia Parliament during last session by certain members of the Tory party and the consequent waste of valuable time, and ridiculed their pretensions to pose as the " moral " party in the State. Mr. Bright :observe d that he was not sure whether the temptation of our time—owing to the fact that we had veteran statesmen in the Cabinet who had con- ferred such enormous benefits on the country—was not to repose a too great allegiance in the Government, without questioning sufficiently the acts and public conduct of the Government. Nevertheless he considered the only occasion during the past session when any portion of the Liberal party displayed any great independence was an occasion on which the Government was wholly right. The hon. mem- ber said it had been his Misfortune now and then—he hoped not often—to take a course which had not been approved by the whole of his political friends, but amengst all sec- tions of the party be had received even on these occasions a a kindly sympathy which to him was very dear.

The Marquis of Hartington, speaking at a great Liberal meeting at Nelson' on Saturday, referred at length to Irish affairs. He said that whilst the Government would welcome temperate and suggestive criticism, the reckless and heated accusations of their opponents were to be deprecated. They would continue to use the power they possessed, whether under the ordinary or the exceptional law, for continuing the conflict in which they were engaged against the great evil of disorder In Ireland and the accumulated evils which former misgovernment had bequeathed to them. The end was net yet accomplished. In some respects the prospect was as dark as it had ever been, but there was no reason for despair, nor even for despondency. The power of the Land League had been broken; and Irish juries, notwithstanding, all the influence that was brought to bear upon them, were giving fair and impartial verdicts, even in agrarian cases. No doubt a guerilla warfare of outrage and intimidation was still going on. He did not, however, know of any case in which when an organised body—which in the present instance was represented by the Land Leagua,—had been driven from the field, a victory had been finally gained by those bands who carried on a guerilla warfare after the main body had been dispersed. Speaking of the necessity for re- form in parliamentary procedure, Lord Hartington said that the subject was one in which the country, as well as the House of Commons, was deeply interested. It involved the question whether or not the country cared to have any of those great legislative reforms for which it voted at the last general election carried into execution during the existence of the present Parliament. It was of cardinal and vital importance to the interests of the countiy that the House of Commons should not lose any part of the fame and dignify which it had enjnyeil for so many centuries; but he feared that, under present circumstances, it was rapidly losing some part of that fame and dignity; and it was for the country to say that it would badk. up and earnestly support any mea.ures that might be necessary for the restoration of the efficiency of Parliament.
