Derby, Plank-lane, slightly injured; WilliamSeaton, 46, Wigan-road, West Leigh, slightly injured ; James Bagshaw, Wigan-road, West Leigh, seriously injured Buckley, Brick-street, West Leigh, slightly injured; Themes Smith, Abram; John Steam, Cook-street, Leigh; William Taylor, Wigan-road, West Leigh; Peter Speakman Gas- street, Leigh; Hugh Gillian, Dukenfield Terrace, Leigh; John Lewis, Talbot-road, Plank-lane; James Lynn, Plank- lane; all badly injured. Several of the explorers were over- come with the after•damp, and had to be brought to bank, and at one time the search was seriously interrupted by the fact that the lights of the party were extinguished. Mr. Hall, government inspector for the district, who had been telegraphed for to Reinhill, arrived at four o'clock, and at once went down the pit. Up to the hour of writing the fate of the great bulk of the men bad not been determined. The two mines are, however, supplied by independent air courses, and the belief of the engineers is that those in the Arley Mine, though imprisoned, will be perfectly safe. The loss of life is still uncertain, but it is not expected that it will be less than 50, and May be many more. The work of rescuing is progressing slowly, owing to the numerous fails of roof blocking the roadway. The recovered, besides those already sent, are Edward Cox, Co-operative- street, West Leigh, seriously burnt; William Wood, Kirk- hall-lane, West Leigh, injuries serious; Peter Walker, Stout's Houses, West Leigh, injuries serious; William Pass, Plant- lane, injuries serious. Altogether the injured recovered number 2s, and there were known to be 75 in the Orrell Mine. Fortunately all the men in the Arley have been brought out in safety, one only being at all injured. One of the missing ones is a young man named Richard Cren- shaw, son of the Rev. James Crenshaw, vicar of St. Thomas's, Wigan, who wait learning mining engineering. The father of Pass states that he has another son down the pit, and that he was only prevented from going owing to his feeling un- well this morning. A man, unknown, who was fearfully injured, was taken at once to the Wigan Infirmary. John Brimelow, who was brought out alive, died soofi afterwards. It is expected that some others will yet be brought. out, but the explorers have found numerous dead bodies, and the deaths will doubtless be somewhere about forty. The ex- plosion has happened at the pit where the first serious riot took place in January in connection with tile great strike of colliers. All the killed are associated with the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Permanent Relief Society. The cause of the explosion can only he surmised. Safety lamps were used in the pie, and a blown-out shot may possibly have .been the cause of the mischief. The explorers have taken down a large number of fire extincteure,part of the workings baying taken fire. Up to the present 28 dead bodies have been recovered, and 36 cases of serious injury have been attended by the doctors. No correct estimate can be given of the number of bodle.s still unrecovered, as the only record of the number of men Lis the pit was kept by an underman at the bottom of the shaft, who has been killed, and whese books are buried amongst the debris at the bottom of the mine. Seventy, however, is the full complement of miners to this pit, and, 36 having been brought out alive, the number killed may be estimated at 34. Several cases now under treatment are not likely to recover. No clue has been obtained as to the cause of the accident, and, indeed, it seems hardly likely that there will be. The colliery was always regarded as one of the safest in the Wigan district, inasmuch as there was no blasting whatever done in the pit. The ventilation was effected by means of a fan instead of the ordinary furnace at the bottom of the shaft, and the most perfect safety lamps were in use. The only explanation which the most prac- tical V the miners can give as te the cause of the catas- trophe is that either some man must have opened his lamp, or have struck his pick accidentally through the gauze of his lamp. The pit caught fire in no less than five places after the explosion, but the fires were rapidly got under. The operations under ground have been conducted through- out the night by Messrs. Hall and Hedley, the Government inspectors. The pit is stated to be in a terrible state of wreck, there being enormous falls of coal, extending in some cases for upwards of 200 yards. Great difficulty has con- sequently been experienced in getting out the dead, and in some cases it has taken hours. Most of the corpses show conclusively that death has resulted from the explosion itself rather than from the effects of the after-damp. Many people watched at the pit mouth all night, hoping against hope that their missing relatives might yet be recovered alive. About two o'clock on Tuesday morning a most affecting scene was witnessed at the pit head, when James Johnson and John Jackson, who had been given up for dead, were brought to the surface without having received any appreciable injury, and were enabled to proceed, un- attended, to their home!, where piournip for their loss had I been already commenced. Both men looked remarkably I well, considering that they had been in the pit for upwards of 13 hours since the accident, and had seen several of their fellow-workmen dying around them from after-clamp. Their escape if regarded as almost miraculous. The total number of lives lost by the explosion may now be put down with some certainty at 46. The bodies of 30 of those killed in this seam have been brsught up, and 32 have been rescued alike from the ill-fated seam. Three of tbese have since died—two in the cabins of the pit bank, from whence the doctors did not consider it advisable to remove them, and the third in the Wigan Infirmary, where he had been taken. The total number of dead is thus 33, and there are 13 persons still to be accounted for. Possibly one or two may have ascended the pit before the explosion occurred, but should this prove not to have been the case— and there is a considerable. doubt about it—the total number of lives lost will have to be put down at the figures stated. The number of deaths from the explosion at the Abram Colliery now reaches 38, and it is believed that eleven bodies are still in the workings. The Coroner's inquest opens to-day (Saturday), but only formal evidence of identification will be given, and the in- quiry adjourned to allow of the recovery of the other bodies and a careful examination of the whole of the work- ings. Mr. Edge, coroner for the Bolton county district, has received a letter from the Home Office, which has been forwarded to Mr. Driffield, in whose division the collieries are situated, stating that the Secretary of State had thought it right that counsel should be employed to attend on behalf of the Government and watch the proceedings at the in- tined. Mr. Hall, inspector of mines for the district, will also be present at the inquiry. „ With reference to the two deaths at the Wigan Infirmary another inquest will have to held by the Wigan coroners. It was thought that the county jury might view the bodies, and so present a dual inquiry, but it appears that this cannot be done, the deaths having occurred in the borough. LATER DETAILS.

The inquest on the bodies of the men and boys who lost their lives in the colliery explosion at Abram, was opened on Thursday, before Mr. Barker, the deputy coroner. Mr. Barker said he was sure the sufferers had the entire sympathy of the whole country. The inquiry was one that must occupy a considerable time and therefore he did not pro- pose to do more then than take formal evidence of identifica- tion. They would then adjourn for a month to enable the Home Office to instruct counsel to attend. The jury pro- ceeded to view • the bodies. Formal evidence of identifica- tion followed, and the inquiry was adjourned. It may be mentioned that the survivors of the killed who held policies in the Prudential Assurance Company received their money on identification. The district Superintendent re. ceived an early intimation of the accident, and, as there are a large number of insurers in the company in that district, at once went to the scene of the explosion. On telegraphing to headquarters, he received instructions to pay all claims without waiting for the usual formalities—an act of great consideration to those deprived of their bread-winners. We are informed that claims were made on 14 policies, which number may be increased by the death of some of the in- jured or the finding of more bodies. The company paid in compensation for lives lost in the gale,at sea on Oct. 14th, £1,831; on the occasion of the Princess Alice disaster, £521; and on similar disasters to the above, as follows: —Swarth Main Collery explosion December, 1875, £136; High Blantyre, October, 1877, £24i; Kersley, March,l 878, £173; Haydock, June, 1878, £312; Abercarne, Sept., 1878, £665; Dinas, January, 1879, £289; Rism, July, 1880, £399; Seaham, September, 1880, £620; Pen-y-Craig, December, 880, £3OO.
WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
IVIONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Major Ca.rtrigi.it, Alderman

Chandley, and bonncillor Fairclotigh.. DESERTELLS.--JAMeS Connor was charged with making a false answer on attestation, on the 6th December, at Liver- pool, by stating that be had never been in the army before. He had, it appeared, been discharged from the army for felony. The prisoner's proper name was Michael McGrail. Sergeant Byrne said these cases were becoming very com- mon, and the Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for three months.—Martin Lawler pleaded guilty to being an ab- sentee or deserter,. from the 103rd Regiment, stationed at Manchester, and he was remanded to Kirkdale. NEGLIGENT PARENTS.—The School Attendance Officer (Mr. G. Riley) appeared on behalf of the &tool Attendance Committee to prosecute the following persons for neglecting to send their children to school :—Elizabetli Marsh, Litton's- row; Joseph Clare, Eldon-street; John Maloney, 29, Sowcock-street.—A floe of ss. was imposed in each case. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks. Vioramr ASSAULT ON TRE POLICE.—James Gallaghan and _James Shields, privates of the Bth Regiment, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street and Rose and Crown-street, and violently assaulting P.C.'s Crickett and Powell.—Margaret Fleming, a bad character, Was charged with a similar offence, and with attempting to rescue the male prisoners.—About five minutes to ten o'clock ' on Monday night P.C. Crickett was in Bridge-street, when he saw the prisoners, who were drunk and very disordtriS• He obtained the assistance of P.C. Powell, and then ap- proached them and tried to persuade them to go home. Prisoners became exceedingly violent, and Shields called out, "Man for man; here's a -- knife." P.C. Crickett used kis stick, and knocked the prisoners down. He then ran to the end of Rose and Crown-street and blew his whistle, but in the meantime the prisoners had attacked P.C. Powell, and be knocked them down again. A severe struggle ensued until further assistance arrived. The male prisoners kicked P.C. Crickett on the jaw and breast, and he was similarly treated by the girl Fleming, who also got hold of him by the hair of the head, and dashed his head against the wall. A witness named Houghton, who went to the assistance of the police, said Crickett was scarcely able to move, owing to the ill-treatment he had received. P.C. Powell was knocked down by Shields, and had his bead badly cut by its coming in contact with the kerbstone. The female prisoner also kicked him about the legs.—Shields denied that be had a knife in his possession, but Mrs. Mather, landlady of the Rose and Crown, said she distinctly saw the blade glisten in the gaslight. She believed had it , not been for the girl Fleming, the row would not have oc- I curred.—Lieut. S. H. Harrison said he could not say any- thing in favour of the male prisoners.—Gallagher, who had previously suffered four months' imprisonment, was again - committed for that term, and Shield for six minths • a similar sentence being passed on Fleming, whom the Bench described as an intolerable nuisance.

COURTED BY A MARRIED MAN.—Edward McElroy, a filecutter, was charged with having made use of malicious threats towards Ann Swindles, whereby she was afraid he would do her bodily harm.—Prosecutrix said the prisoner had "been her young man," and under promise of marriages she had borne him a child, which, however, had died. On Saturday evening prisoner sent for her, and she saw him near the railway arch in Winwick-road, where he threatened to take her life with a piece of steel. She screamed, and her sister and mother and two young men came up, and one of the latter told her prisoner was a married man. She did not know tefore that night that be was a married man; he had courted her under the name of "Fred Jones."—Prisoner denied be was -the father of prosftutrix's child, and said he had a wife "a dozen times better than her." Prosecutrix's "real" young man worked with him, and had "gone with" her three years. He maintained the case was a "made tip thing against a married man to crush him down." He had a wife of his own present. It was a made thing, and he hoped they would give him the benefit of it.—Mr. Hunt: You deserve a benefit. (Laughter.)—Prisoner was ordered to be bound over, himself in £2O, and two sureties of £lO i each, to keep the peace for twelve months, or go to gaol three months.

BREAKING INTO A Siarray.—Patrick Foy was charged with feloniously attempting to enter the lock-up spirit ware- house of Mr. James Jolley, Bewsey-street, between Saturday and Monday; and with breaking and entering the smithy of Mr. J. C. Sutton and Co., and stealing therefrom 15 steel pick-locks and three door keys, value 12s.—Remanded. THEFT BY BOYS.—Edward Allen, William Kirkham, and Samuel Cartwright, boys, were charged with stealing from the shop of George Marsh, tobacconist, Irlam-street, on Mon- day, a quantity of cigarettes and wax matches, value Is. Gd. —Allen and Kirkham were discharged with a caution, and Cartwright was ordered to be birched.

• WEDNESDAY—Before Aldermen Davies and Chandley. I A LAWLESS CirertAcrFn.—A young man, named Thomas Farrell, was charged with wilfully damaging the furniture and fixtures of the house of Maria Waiting, an eating-house keeper.—The prosecutriX said the prisoner entered her house, on Saturday night, and demanded food, but as he was drunk she refused to serve him. Prisoner seized the plate of another customer, and ate a portion of the food. He I then commenced to fight another man, and in the scuffle the mantel shelf, an arm chair, and other furniture was broken. , When he was ejected from the house he broke in the door: —James Osborne, a joiner, deposed to seeing him break open the door.—Prisoner denied breaking the furniture, and said some men in the house would kave killed him if another man had not helped him.—Mr. Hunt remarked that prisoner was a very lawless character, and that he had a very black sheet against him. He had served four months for assault- ing the police.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month With hard labour.

- - THUBSDAY.—Before Captain Litton (chairman), Alderman Webster, and Councillor Milner. A GANG OF YOUNG ROBBERS.—Patrick Foy, Edward Scaile (10), and Thomas Day (10),were charged, on remand, with feloniously breaking into thaspirit stores of Thomas Jolley, Bewsey-street, between Saturday, the 3rd instant, and Monday, the sth instant, and stealing 11 receipt stamps. —Mr. Hunt, the chief constable, said an entrance to the shop was effected by the back door with the aid of a dupli- cate key. The prisoners had used great violence in break- ing into Mr. Jolley's private office, and had also broken a piece of brass of a- Milner's safe in attempting to open it. When information was given to the police, on the sth Dec., P.C. Cokely and Sergeant Spinks took the matter in band, but could obtain no clue. • On Monday last, however, the officers munched the house of Foy's parents, in Sugar House- yard, and secreted in the roof df the water closet they found a poker, 15 skeleton keys, a jemmy; and several other articles. Foy was arrested, and he made a statement which led to the apprehension of the prisoners.—The prisoners wePe remanded.—Patrick Foy was then further charged, with a lad naraed John Edward Kearney, with attempting to break into the spirit stores of Mr. Jolley, between the 17th and 19th inst.; and also with entering the smithy of J. C. Sutton rk Co., Market-street, and stealing 15 picklocks, three door .1!1, ttc.! of the value of le.—oh n ?tfferson; workman for .Mr. Sutton, went to the nlrh on Sunday at noon, and discovered that the place was in great disorder. A further examination showed that an entrance had been effected by the back door, and the articles found at Toy's home, stolen. The prisoners bad made statements impli- cating each other.—Mr. Hunt said Foy Yeas liberated from the reformatory school, where he had served five years, in July last. A month ago Kearney ran away to Liverpool with £9, and secured a passage to New York. He was, however, apprehended, and the money recovered.—The prisoners were remanded.

1 TRITESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. L this case Peter Robinson, horse slaughterer, sued the Cor- poration of Warrington for the sum of £2 —Mr. G. T. Moore appeared for plaintiff, and. 1,,.. J. L. Whittle (deputy tat (depute- town through do nu only M ly clerk) r for otrh ethCeorps loaruatgi, hoten .r7h.o ars. e. MooreTb saidec oirnpot rhaet ifoani r, of November, 1880, two horses were found to be glandered fit f .Norman inspector, went to the plaintiff's slaughter-house in Arpley, and while he was away they slaughtered the animals. The following day Norman and plaintiff met. and walked down to the slaughter-house together, in company with a person named Wall, a veterin- au surgeon. Norman asked the plaintiff to prepare the horses for post mortem examination to see what was the matter with them. Plaintiff took the entrails out of the two horses, for which he charged the sum of 10s. He did some- thing else to another horse for which he charged ss. There was a 04rd horse in the stables of Mr. Wall, veterinary surgeon, Which was also glandered, and he took that to the slaughter-boost and slaughtered it. For that the plaintiff charged the sum of ss. A grave eight or ten feet was dug for the horses, and the Corporation put about five tons of lime on the carcases after they were buried. A mound was thus created, and the sum of 10s. was charged for level- ling the ground. Plaintiff further charged 10s. for the use of the land occupied by the Corporation, making a total of £2, which he (Mr. Moore) thought was dot unreasonable considering the nature of the work.—Plaintiff cosfirmed the statement of his solicitor, and added that Mr. Norman told him whatever he charged the Corporation would pay. This was plaintiff's case, as Mr. Wall, who was subpcened, did not app.ar.—Mr. Whittle, for the defendants, said the me arose in consequence of the execution of the Contagious Diseases Animals Act. Mr. Norman was the inspector under the Act, and it was his duty to visit the fairs, seize any horses suffering from any contagious disease, to have them slaughtered, and to bury them, after reporting the matter to the local authority, in six feet of earth. In addition to that, he was required te slash the hide. At the fair in November last year Mr. Norman found two horses suffering from glanders. He called the attention of the veterinary surgeon to the animals, who inspected them, and found they were suffering from glandera. Mr. Norman seized the horses and immediately took them to the field belonging to plaintiff, and there slaughtered them or had them slaughtered. On the following day he met the plaintiff at Market Gate, and said "Oh, I have taken two horses down to your place at Arpley and slaughtered them. I want you to give me your permission to bury them." Plaintiff said .40h, yea;" and they Bent down several men to bury the animals. The horses were not disembowelled, and plain- tiff did nothing whatever to the horses.—Mr. Norman gave confirmatory evidence, and emphatically stated that the horses were not disembowelled. Plaintiff appeared to agree with what had been done, and he (witness) said nothing to him about payment. A horse belonging to the Corporation died, but witness would not let plaintiff have the carcase for the sum he offered, and plaintiff said, "If I can't have the horse, I will be paid for what you did in Arpley."—Leonard Bawling said when they were bnrying the horses plaintiff said he would want paying.—After hearing two other wit- nesses for the defence, his Honour, in summing up, said the items appeared to be trumped up, and gave judgment for 103. for the use of the land. •

__- -- ---... CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON BUTCRER.—Mr. HUH% solicitor of Altrincham, appeared for the plaintiffs in this claim, Messrs. Balshaw and Hancock, auctioneers, Man- chester and Altrtncham, and the defendant, Richard Ho'. croft, butcher, Warrington, was represented by Mr. G. F. Moo re.—Mr. Harris said the action was in respect to certain stock sold by plaintiffs on October 6th, at [Watley. Defen- dant was present at that sale, and bought four heifers, a calf, and a barren cow. In regard to two of the animals, one worth £B, and a calf worth lie., these defendant had had, and he had paid an amount into court, be supposed in respect to these. Mr. Moore told him the main contention would be in regard to a barren cow, bought for £l2 17s. 6c1., which had died. He, however, thought the bargain would be proved. The conditions of sale said that the parties might, if they pleased, leave the animals on the premises of Mr. Simpson, where the sale took place, for days, bu', if 'hey did it would be at the risk of the pur- chaser. After the sale the animal was taken to Mr. Daw- son's, who was tho owner of the animal, and afterwards in accordance with the defendant's wish it was taken by a man named Warren to the Railway Inn, Heatley, but defendant was not there to receive it. Warren therefore took the cow to Simpson's field, where it died. Plaintiff said the animal had not died within the sdven days allowed, and that they had done everything necessary for the purpose of completing the bargain. Mr. Balahav, and other witnesses corroborated the above statement, and his Honour, who said what took place between Warren and defendant was an acceptance, gave a verdict for plaintiff. Disrum Brravutor FARDIRRS.—WiIIiam Percival, farmer. Appleton, brought an action against William Tickle, farmer, Keckwick, to recover the sum of £8 Bs., for potatoes supplied.—Mr. Moore appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. T. J. Ridgway for defendant—Mr. Moore said the parties were respectable well to-do farmers, and he believed there must be some misunderstanding between them. In September last defendant went to plaintiff's farm, where he had some magnum bonum potatoes growing in a field. Defendant said he wanted some sets, and it was ultimately arranged that he should have 15 loads and that the price should be 11s, per load. The defence would be that the price was 7s. per load and not lie. Defendant had paid into court £5 125., ibut even if he admitted the price to be 7s. per load he had not paid sufficient by 103.—Plaintiff said he sold the pota- toes at Hs, per load.—Defendant said the price was 75. per load, which was a fair price at the time. He called Messrs. P. Percival, W. Whit/ow, William Kinsey, farmers, who also stated that 7s. per load was a fair price for such pota- toes last September.—Judgment was given for plaintiff.

ST. HELENS LITERARY AND SCIEN- TIFIC ASSOCIATION. Mr. Fletcher, alkali works inspector for this district, Olt Tuesday evening gave a lectur*on "Electricity," before the members of this association. Dr. Twyford, in the absence of the president (Mr. R. Pilkington, the Mayor), presided, and the attendance was better than it has been this session. The L.Berrnrn commenced his lecture by giving some elementary experiments in the science such as the charging and discharging of the Leyden jar. The storage of electricity' or electric energy was occupying the attention of scientists of the present day, but how it could be effectually and com- pletely stored remained an unsolved question. In the case of the Leyden jar, the storage was only momentary. Wind could not be stored, but we could store up wind power by means of the windmill. He then made several other experiments ehowina the power of electricity, amongst which was the exhibition of a small swan light, which was very brilliant, and the magnetising by electricity a large horse shoe mag- ner, which wa doable of holding several fifty-six pound weights. He next show 4 ).?.7 means of tbo lime lght, the lighting of mines, electric ploughs, and by thii C! gramme machine turned a sewing machine. That, he said, might be very interesting as a toy, but he hoped the day would not be far distant when we might be able to drive machines in the same manner. People, in a rough way, spoke of electricity doing a great many things, that all kinds of machinery were driven by electricity. But the electri. apparatus in some cases had to be movei by steam engines The advantage of electricity was obvious in some cases when distance made it necessary. If a person had an engine at work seine distance from his house, and wanted to work a sewing machine, it would be far cheaper to connect the two places with a copper wire than with a steam pipe. Ho showed by experiment how an explosion could be made a long distance from the necessary apparatus, and showed the arrangement of iron filings when scattered over a piece of , paper under which were magnets placed parallel to each other, showed that under the influence of magnets each filing became a complete magnet, with its positive and nega- tive poles. In conclusion, he said there was a power more or less of storing electricity. Electricity had now got into com- mercial fields, and having done that, they might reasonably suppose that immense strides would be made by it. Mr. J. C. GAMBLE proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer. lie had showed them some of the results to be produced by electricity, in which they were all interested. They had seen the swan or signet light, and for the lacties there had been the turning of tke sewing machine. He could like to see the Radical storage of electricity or elec- tric energy. There had been great improvements daring the last two or three years, and no doubt they would be pushed forward to greater extent. Although he for one did not think thesgas would be extinguished altogether, there wouli no doubt be a great deal of lighting done by electricity. He had been watching the progress of lighting by electricity during the last four years, and he thought it would be cheaper than gas in time. Dr. Mcncorz seconded the motion, and in doing so remarked that the splendid attendance at the lecture in the Town Hall, and the good attendance that night showed that if science war presented to St. Helens by able and scientific expositors they would prove as magnets, and draw respectable audiences. Mr. FLETCHER, in thanking them, referred to the cost of lighting by electricity, and gave Sean instance the lighting of Messrs. Crossley's works in Halifax, which had been to lighted two years. The apparatus in the first place cost £650. The coat was greater than that of gas, because it was only used a few hours in the evening. lithe hours of light- ing were longer it would pay. It depended a great deal on how much was used. The tendency of the electric light was to increase the consumption of gas by inducing better light, and as horses were not diminished in value by the spread of railways, so it would be with gas.

Scailes, and Thomas Dacy, were charged, OR remand, with feloniously entering the spirit warehouse of Mr. James Jolley, Bewsey.streot, and stealing therefrom 11 receipt , stamps.—The charge was reduced to simple larceny, and Foy pleaded guilty.—Mr. Hunt did not press the charge against Scaile and Dacy, and they were discharged.—Foy was further charged, with John Edward Kearney, with stealing 15 picklocks, 3 door keys, tbc., value 123., from the smithy of Messrs. J. C. Sutton and Co., Market-street.— Both prisoners pleaded guilty.—Foy was sentenoed to six months' imprisonment with hard labour—threa months on each charge; and Kearney was sent to gaol three months with harlabour. CRUELTY TO AstuaLs.—William Rothery, who did not appear, was charged with causing two cows to be cruelly ill-treated by allowing them to be overstocked with milk on the 29th November. Mr. James Allen, inspector for the Royal Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, did Mr. Robinson, proved the case, and defendant, who had been previously convicted, was fined 40s. and costs.—Geo. Beeson, of Bury, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by travellirftz it from Bury to Warrington. Inspector Harper, R.S.P.C.K., said he WAS attending Warrington horse fair on the 30th November, and at four o'clock be went into the Old Bell public-house yard. There he saw an old brown mare, little better than a skeleton, and which appeared in great pain. Its near shoulder WS completely dislocated and was greatly swollen. It I appeared ES if it had travelled a long distance, and the sweat was drying upon the horse. The owner of the horse was not to be found, and Mr. Harper waited at 'the house until six o'clock, when the defendant and another man entered the yard, and commenced whipping the horse, he supposed, to enliven it, and the defendant offered to sell it to Mr. Mason, veterinary surgeon, of Sale, for £.3. The defendant and his companion adjourned to the public house, and Mr. Harper followed and revealed his identity. The men then attempted to escape, and Mr. Harper, in guarding the door, received a blow ore the face. The defen- dant he managed to detain, and get his address, but his com- panion escaped through the window. It transpired that the horse, which was not fit to walk 40 yards, had travelled from Bury.—The defendant was fined £5 and costs, or in default, a month's imprisonment. POTATO ENGINES AND ORSTRUCTION.—JOIui Murray, a young man, was charged with having on the 16th December, obstructed the free passage of Horsemarket-street, by allow- ing a donkey and potato engine to remain there a long and unreasonable length of tirne.—P.C. Clyne said the defendan stayed opposite the Rams Head for twenty-five minutes. His shouting and prowling about the street was a greut nuisance to the inhabitants.—Captain Reynolda thought would be for the public convenience to be able to get a hot potato.—Mr. l'White (the magistrates' clerk) said if they wished to suppress the thing the Corporation should not exact toll.—Captain Reynolds said the defendant would only be fined in the costs ou this occasion, but he must conduct his business in future without flaking it a nuisance. past, ani by reason of that slip to be afflicted with ei poignant remorse and sense of shame for a long time thereafter! Oar readers will not condemn Our moralising tone, we hope, if we venture to interpose a friendly admonition on this point in any case where it might be requisite or timely. It would be more agreeable to the public writer, when otriving to indite words which shall be in harmony with the associations and anticipations of Christmas, to drop out of his cognizance the circumstances which detraot from the benefits and comforts of the great mid-winter holiday. Bat the celebration has in real experience its shady side, and nothing is gainedby turning one's blind eye towards it. . Just in proportion as we rejoice that Christmas for our deserving toilers is a universal resting place on the rough highway of life; and a season for most of ample good fare, and of glad meetings of separated kindred and friends, and of happy romps and games for the youngsters, do we grieve that it should be so often abused, to the utter neutralising of its healthful effects upon over- wrought body and mind. Bat we have no more to say on that score;—" a word to the wise is enitigh.i' There is great consolation for us in the belief that the present Christmas will not find the great majority of the industrial class in this part of Lancashire unpro- viad with the means of making the holiday an occa- sion for bright festivity and agreeable relaxation. A csrtain number of unfortunate poor will, indeed, be met with in populous communities in the busiest timo, whose dependence upon the bounty of the good- hearted for a full Christmas mealis a fact not to be for- gotten. These, however, are the exceptions to the general rule of comparative prosperity amongst our working-class neighbours at the present time. We are truly glad that most of those who work the hardest with their hands, are as able to command a savoury Christmas dinner with dessert to follow, as that limited number who work chiefly with their brains, or that still more select (we don't say fortu- nate) few who don't work much with either hand or brain. The salutation "A Merry Christmas!" will eours9 round amongst the working folk in their cot- tages where the kitchen fires blaze cheerfully, as well as in more stylish homes, and will not sound a more impracticable wish in the one case than in the other. Will our friends and readers graciously allow oar written greeting, "A Happy Christmas I " to mingle with the spoken greetings of their nearest and dearest, as that of a weekly visitant who on this week's-end,jef all in the year, desires to be honoured with the privilege of a friend P

LOCAL NOTES. I hear a report to the effect.that Mr. Robert Shaw is dis- inclined to render pecuniary help to the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association, to the extent which he has done in previous years. He considers that other friends of young men in the town ought to take their fair share of the burden; and that if, after another special efbrt, the requisite amount to clear expenses cannot be raised, the place ought to be closed. Well, the Literary Institute is on its last legs; and if the young men's building be closed there is the com- fort left for all those who have the welfare of the future citizens of Runcorn at heart, that there are still open the "pubs" and beershops; and in the case of a difficulty they might visit one of the penny theatres. The Runcorn Parliamentary Debating Society has come to a sudden stoppage. I inapt admit that there bad been strong symptoms of a week state of the internal machinery, so to speak, of this body politic, for some time past, but it was not generally supposed the committee would discontinue to call the members together at so early a date. Shakespeare says that there is a tide in the affairs of men, which, when taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; and those young men in the town who have disregarded the splendid opportunity which has been offered them for some time past, of ;improv- ing their speaking talent, will probably not have such an opportunity for some time to come. The Widnes Local Board had a special meeting yesterday morning, at which they unanimously decided to let the tender for the sewerage works to a Chester gentleman, for the sum of £11,878 Os. 2d., which will amount to an extra rate of twopence in the pound. -

• I am sure that all your readers will be gratified to see that the Widnes Local Beard, under the advice of their able chairman, Major Cross, are determined that the busy town whose local affairs are in their hands, shall not quietly sub- mit to the cool style in which the workmen of the London and North-Western Railway Company conduct the business of the principal level crossings. Complaints—loud and deep—have for a long time been made about the obstruction caused to the public passenger and vehicular traffic in Waterloo-road, through this cause; but from the last com- munication received from Euston by the Board, it appears that the company are gradually making advances which may, if permitted, lead to still further encroachments, as they now take the stand that having provided a bridge by which the foot passengers may cross the line, they are not obliged to keep the gates open to enable them to cross! This is tantamount to saying that the people of Widnes are to sell their just rights in the matter of public traffic, and the price is to be a ricketty, dirty-looking bridge which is an offence to the eye, and ought to be pulled down and sup- planted by another which has some claims to a little beauty. The Local Board, as the guardians of the interests of the ratcplyers, do not, I feel sure, intend to part with their rights for such a mess of pottage. The report of the pro- ceedings of that body, at their last monthly meeting, clearly shows that they were justly indignant at the phlegmatic treatment which all their appeals meet at the hands of the directors in London. It seems very likely that no material change will take place in the working of the crossing until a Government enquiry is demanded. Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., made a very pleasant an- nouncement at the list Widnes Board meeting, to th• effect that it was highly probable when the new contracts were entered into by the Gas Committee, at the end of the financial year, a recommendation would be made that the price of gas should be reduced. For some time past, it is stated that the rights of free- holders of nuncio& have been interfered with by certain gentlemen who appear to act upon the motto that possession is nine points of the law. The Commissioners have hod their attention drawn to the matter, and a meeting of free- holders was held last week, at which it was decided that the conduct of these land freebooters should be no longer quietly tolerated. A committee was appointed to consider the question, with Mr. Win. Handley as secretary, and steps are to be at once taken for asserting the rights of the free- holders. PLACCUS.

WIDNES PARISH CHLIRCIL—The special Aclve.nt services were continued at this Church on Sunday, when the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, Vicar of Widnes, preached from the text, Litt up a standard for the people," on the subject "Th. King proclaimed." There was a good congregation. The some evening, the Advent services for workingmen were continued in the National Schoolroom, Waterloo-road, the Rev. W. 11. Duggan officiating.

RTINCORN PARLIIMENTAIL-Y DEBITING SOCIETY : IMPORTANT MEETING.—At the meeting of this society ot Tuesday evening, the final debate on the Parliamentary Disabilities Bill was commenced and supported by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The member for Cheltenham subsequently opposed it, and after the Home Secretary had replied, a division was called, the result being that 14 mem- bers voted against the Bill, and 13 for it, which created much laughter and great cheering on the Opposition side. The House then resolved itself into Commiitee for the pur- pose of hearing the result of the financial position of the society. The Chairman of the Council read the resolution which had been arrived at on the Saturday evening previous which was as follows :—" That after considering the financial position of the society, and it being found that there is only a sufficient amount to pay the liability at present incurred, it is deemed inadvisable to continue the meetings of the society for the present session after the 20th inst." This announcement apparently caused much dismay and astonish- ment, notwithstanding the anticipations which some mem- bers appeared to have respecting the uustability of the association as regards itb pecuniary position.—The Chan- cellor of the Exchequer, at the conclusion of a somewhat jocular speech, in which be congratulated the members Opposite upon the hard hits which they bad given to the members on the Government side of the House, proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be given to the Speaker and-also to the Clerk of the House, for the services rendered ! by them in conducting the affairs of the society, which were ! eldtably acknowledged, and the meeting terminated.

would have to say, upon the evidence put before the what was the cause of death,' and with regard to that they would be guided entirely by the medical evidence, which showed clearly that death resulted from apoplexy. And now came the important question: How did that apoplexy arise? Apoplexy could be caused by violence, but it must be violence in the true sense of the term—something very severe to cause such an effect as that they were investigating. It was not similar to the apoplexy caused by the rupture of a small blood vessel, where the man might become insen- sible but live for days. This was a case where there had been a sudden rush of blood front the brain and the ques- tion for them to consider was WU it brought about by violence.; and, if so, was that violence attributable to the prisoner; or, was it the result of another cause, namely, excitement. The facts of the case were perfectly clear It was alleged by one witness that the prisoner struck the deceased, but it was very singular the act was seen by no other person. The witness could not say the deceased fell from the effects of the blow, or on what part of the body the deceased was struck. That was the only evidence which practically affected the prisoner. Ile WaS much impressed by the evidence of Mrs. Higginson, who said she saw the deceased reel and ; and that was exactly in accordance with the medical testimony. Prisoner might or might not have struck the blow, but even if he did, the jury must con- sider whether it was of such violence as to cause the results the doctor had described. The only question was, Did they think the apoplexy was the result of violence, and was it the violence of the prisoner? The jury retired to consider their verdict. After about one minute's absence, they returnecVand the foreman said: lam happy to tell you, Mr. Coroner,we have considered the ques- tion, and we are unanimously of opinion the man ha died of apoplexy brought on by excitement. A verdict to this effect was returned accordingly.

The prisoner, William Wright, was again brought up at the police court on Thursday, charged with causing the death of William liassall, loy striking him with his fist.— The magistrates on the bench were Captain Litton, Aid. I Webster, and Councillor Milner.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the prisoner, and pleaded not guilty. Dr. Bride was the first witness called and he repeated the evidence given at the inquest—that the deceased died from apoplexy, caused by excessive excitement. There was no evidence external or internal of the deceased having received a blow.

Aid. Webster: Could the clot of blood found on the brain have been caused by a blow? Oh yes. Cant. Litton: There would have been an external mark if it had been caused by a blow? Certainly. I should have found extravasation beneath the skull. Mr. Hunt: After the evidence you have heard and what I heard the other day, I cannot carry the case any further., Capt. Litton: If that is the case I don't know why we should try it. (To prisoner). You have been brought upon a serious charge, and I should recommend you to mend your manner in future. It would be much better for you to be a steady sober man, and go regularly home after finishing your work. You have narrowly escaped beisg tried for a most serious offence, but after hearing all the evidence we can get we don't think you could have done anything to cause the death of the deceased, and, therefore, you will be discharged.

Yesterday the two men who were fighting, James Hassan and Edward Cartwright, were brought before Captain Reynolds, Mr. John White, and Mr. Ziba Armitage, at the Borough Court, charged with committing a breach of the peace. The defendants pleaded guilty. Mr. Hunt, in stating the details of the case, said fighting amongst the ironworkers at Bewsey was very prevalent, and he did not hesitate to say that the Staffordshire men seemed to have "no sort of control or discipline—had no behaviour whatever." Fighting was constantly taking place, if not on the main road in:some adjoining field as they seemedto think the police could not interfere with them there. He wished to show them differently, and should be glad if the magis- trates would more rightly enforce the law with regard to disorder and fighting in Bewsey. In answer to Captain Reynolds, Hassan said it was cos- tomery.amongst the ironworkers to play "shove penny" for beer. Worrell was in the room whilst the games were being played, and he (Hassall) thought two half gallons were played for, Defendant was not drunk when he went out to fight, which Worrell tried to prevent. Mr. Hunt: How much drink had you P—l don't know. Captain Reynolds: I suppose you got beyond reckoning after you had two gallons. (Laughter.) • Mr. Hunt: Had you any bets on ?—No. Captain Reynolds remarked that the playing for liquor ought to be suppressed, and said to the defendants :Yon will have to give over fighting. We shall make it heavy for you If you don't.—The defendants were each bound over in £lO, and two sureties of £5 each, to keep the peace for six months.

CHEISTMAS AT ST. HELENS. 1 The whirligig of time has brought us round to the festive season of the year known to old and young as the Merry Christmas Time, which comes but once in a twelvemonth, and which brings with it abundance of good cheer and friendly greetings. A walk through the towa on Thursday showed that active preparations were being made by the tradesmen to look their best and encourage trade by a tempt- ing display of goods in their shop windows. Mary Challoran, sentenced so dea-th—a-t Cork for the murder of a child at Odomey, has been reprieved. Yesterday, a suspect named Moore arrived in Queenstorrr in custody of two policemen. He has been liberated CM condition that he will emigrate, and the police accompanfed Rim from Limerick to see that his promise was carried out.. In the firsttlivision of the Session at Edinburgh, yester. day, decision was given in a claim by the liquidators of the city of Glasgow Bank against Wm. MacKinnon for £311,000 paid as dividend while he wasAirector. The court decided against the liquidators. Yesterday evening a bailiff seized a horse and cart tinder the civil bill at Mobile. The owner struggled to keep pos. session, and a large crowd gathered. The police fixed bayonets to keep the crowd hack, and took the owner, bailiff, and horse and cart to Banacks.

By the direction of Captain Templar four of the Por4. land lenets, which are capital sea boats, left Portland yesterday afternoon for the purpose of cruising over the 211 miles of water about West Bay for the lost balloon, which it is thought will be found about six feat below the surface. Mr. Cozar, ex-mayor of St. Ives, Cornwall, was charged before the magistrates yesterday with obt lining from the Corporation certain sums under false pretences. Evident, was given to show that he had not accounted for carte' sums received as rate collector, and the case was adjourned in order that the Government auditor might attend.

A meeting of operative potters held at Hanley definite brought the strike to an end, and all the operatives will be at work after this week. A good feeling exists betweea masters and men on the whole, and several of the manufac- turers have advanced their workpeople a week's wages to enable them to have a good Christmas.

At a meeting of the representatiyes of the Cleveland miners and 'their employers, yesterday, the men reported that they were instructed to accept the proposed two years sliding scale with the gumanteed minimum wages offered for the past six months, tlAis minimum being equal to one penny per ton to miners, te'n per cent, to underground, and eight per cent, to surface natal men.

Miss Reynolds, of the Dublin Ladies Land League, was charged at the Petty Sessions, Castletown, Bere, county Cork,-yesterday afternoon, with. inciting a tenant named Catherrre Murphy not to pay rent to her landlord, the Earl of Bantry. Mr. Warburton, R.M., was the only maes- trate present, and ordered her to find bail to keep the peace for six momhs, or, in default, to undergo a month's impri- sonment. She refused to give bill, and was therefore cow-. mitted to prison.

The public examination in connection with these schools took place on Wednesday in the schoolroom, Waterloo- street. In the afternoon the infants were put through a variety of exercises in reading, geography, mental arithmetic, dm., varied with recitations, and singing. There was a number of parents present, and the answers of the children reflected great credit on Miss Parr, the mistress. The Rev 3. M. Wainsley occupied the chair. In the evening about 300 children were seated upon a temporary platform erected at the entrance end of the room, and including the children there were about 700 present, who manifested the utmost interest in the proceedings. Mr. Brearley presided, and after a few remarks the scholars in standards 3 and 4 were put through exercises in reading, and subsequently literature and grammar A's ere taken. Scott's " Marmion ' was the subject test in literature, each scholar being required to commence at a given point and proceed until stopped by the teacher. The answers in grammar were readily given to Mr. Brown's questions and merited the applause of the audience. Mental arithmetic formed the next testly Mr. Brown and Mr. Sales, the assistant teacher, and the correct- ness and readiness with which the answers were given was really astonishing, and would have taxed the mental i faculties of many older persons. An interesting , "spelling competition" followed. The scholar who made ! a blunder, was debarred from taking any further part in the ! competition. THE NORTHERN CIRCEIT.—The following dates have been fixed by Baron Pollock and Mr. Justice Chitty for holding the winter assizes on the Northern erenit—viz.,

- WINSFORD AND SANDBACH /NEE METHODIST CIROTIT. —The quarterly meeting of this circuit was held on Mon- day, when a full representative assembly of preachers, stewards, and leaders were present at Middlewich. The financial matters were in such a healthy state that the funds I were able to increase the salary of the second premher, the Rev. J. Wright, as well as to give him a hearty invitation ta remain another year, which was accepted. There was every prospect of a similar invitation to the very esteemed superintendent, the Rev. W. J. Hopper, whose term of three year's labour will soon be up, but he declined the honour of a fourth year, having resolved to go to another circuit. This Is much regretted by his numerous friends and admirers it? 11l parts of the circuit. 1113Aziert AT OVER. A I azaar in aid of the Marshall Memorial Schools, Over (Independent), was held on Wed. nesday, in the above schools, which were a long-felt want, in the time of the late esteemed pastor of this church, the Rev. Jno. Marshall, who was actively for 54 years, and less Bo for 0 years, the chief of the above church. The schools have been built at a cost of nearly £l,OOO, of which a considerable sum has yet to be raised. Much of nits sum is hoped. for in connection with this bazaar, which Mi. Verden, of tbe Breckhurst, Northwich, opened, and the following ladies patronized :—Mesdames Turner, of Over Hall ; Tomkinson, Willington Hall ; Mossy Rwenscroft , Hall; Mayoress of Over, Woodford Hall; Leak, Dingle House; Okell, Over Lodge. There was a good attendance. ,

rENKE:III WOLKIDES'S CLUB.—On Sattuday evening: the members and friends of the above club, to the number of about 70, spent a pleasant evening in the hrge room of the club, where supper had been prepared by Mr. Pete' Johnson, the manager. After dinner Mr. James Watson was called to the chair. Re spoke of the advantages to be de- rived from that and similar institutions, and referred to cer- tain suggestions contained in a letter he had received from Mr. Hobson, who was unable to attend owing to indisposition. The writer stated he was very anxious that the young Men of the village should avail, themselves of the privileges and benefits to be gained by jolting the Improvement Class, but it should be distinctly understood that the club was neutral in politics, as its title indicated. It was an institution for the use of workingmen. An interesting programme was afterwards gone through, in which Messrs. Mainley, White, Cross, Watson, Peter Johnson, IL Campbell, Mrs Soderland and Miss Plumpton took part. THE MISTLETOE AT CIIIIISTISIAS.—The name of this

plant is derived by Johnson from mystelan, Saxon; rnistel, Danish, birdlime; and tan, a twig. It is a parasitic plant, found wild in England, very rarely in Scotland, and nowhere in Ireland; and is a production of great interest to,the pby. tologist. The seeds in germination offer an exception to a general law, that the rad ic' s of the embryo shoots downwarer, and the plumula upwards. Thus, if a cannon ban, to which mistletoe seeds are glued °nail sides, be suspended by a cord some distance from the earth, both the upper and under I seeds as well as those at the sides, all direct their radiclB. to the surface of the ball. This property ensures their growing upon the branches of trees to whatever side they happen to ,wtick.

INSTITUTION OF TUN NRW VICAR OF FARNWORTII.— On Friday evening week, the Rev. George Bond, MA., of Lincoln College, Oxford, late rector of Sutton, Norfolk, was instituted to the perpetual curacy of Farnworth. The Venerable Archdeacon Bardsley acted as his commissary, and preached an eloquent sermon from Titus B. 13-14. The prayers were read by the Rev. Joseph Holden, and the les- sons by the Rev. S. A. Spooner, M.A ~ curate. At the close of the service, the vicar-designate knelt down at the altar rails whilst Archdeacon Bardsley read the institation deed and performed the laying on of hands' thus signifying the appointment of the new vicar to the charge of the parish of Farnvrorth. MR. BANTOCE NERPOINT'S COMM CONCERT, A.T RIIN • cons.—Our Runcorn readers will be pleased to know that Mr. Pierpoint has already engaged artistes for his coming concert in Runcorn. There will take part Miss Clara Semen (soprrano), Miss Emilie Lloyd (contralto), Mr. Henry Dunman (tenor), Mr. Pierpoint (baritone), Mr. Frank Arnold (solo violin and solo harmonium). Miss Samuell has already made her name as one of our most successful ballad singers, both in London and the provinces. This Is her first visit to Runcorn; and we feel sure she uill receive an enthusiastic welcome. Miss Lloyd is too well known to re- quire comment from Us. Mr. Dunman has already dis- tinguished himself at the Royal Academy of Music, where he has gained a bronze medal sod other rewards. Mr. Frank i Arnold s acknowledged to be one of the most promising young violinists in the country. He has galt4 both a bronze and a silver medal at the Loyal Academy of Music, and has been further honoured by being made a sub-pro- fessor. He is a favourite pupil of M. Sainton, the celebrated French violinist. Mr. Argent will, of course, act as con- ductor.

PEF-SCOT UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.— A. meeting of this committee was.held on Thursday at the Board-room. Whiston. There were present the Rev. T. Chambers (in the chair), Messrs. J.T . Hall, J. Leatherbar- row, J. Ranson, T. Dobell, and G. J. Paris; Mr. H. S. Hall, J.P., and Mr. H. R. d'A. Willis, J.P., (ex-did o mem- ber) ; Mr. Hartley (clerk), and Mr. H. S. Welch (attendance and enquiry pfficer).—Mr. Welsh reported that of the 20 cases ordered to be prosecuted at the last meeting, twelve had been fined, with costa ss. • one dismissed; one parent left the district; one recommended to be held over, and five held over on account of sickness of children. As directed at the last meeting he had made a house to house visitation of the township of Ithyton, and found as follows :—Houses occupied 419; empty 9; number of children under five years of age? 298; number of children between five and fourteen years of age, 4sl; total 779; of which 391 were boys and 388 girls. The cases of the children not attending any school had been reported to the Huyton Local Commit- tee, and the complete census and\returns would be submitted to the January meeting of that ommittee. RUNCORN rm,,ISEE CHURCH DIVIDING CLUB AND MurcAL ASSURANCE SOCIETT.—OR Monday evening the annual meeting of the members was held in the National Schoolroom, the Rev. Canon Barclay, the president of the soctety, in the chair. The financial statement was read by the secretary (Mr. James Littler), from which it appeared that upwards of £l5O bad been paid as subscriptions during the year by 104 members. Only 18 members had been in retwipt ).f sick pay, none of them, with two exceplions, hay- log been on the books more than three successive weeks. Hence the amount expended for sick allowance had been £26 10s.; and £6 for levies for death. After deducting working expenses, amounting to a little over £7, it appeared that £lll Sc. was available for dividend, being at the rate of £1 2s. 3d. each to 100 members. Mr. Edward Imison was unanimously re-appointed treasurer, Mr. James Littler secretary, and Mr. James Moores and Mr. William Shaw stewards. Nine members were elected by a show of hands to serve on the committee. , _

- - €ST, ogle 13 gmanr Elswg Clam I lON OWN:, MANA oitzmi MiSsiotene—On Monday evening, the annual meeting, in connection with these missions, was held in the above place of worship. The chair Was taken by the Rev. Evan Williams, who briefly introduced the deputation, the Rev. Josiah Thomas, M.A., of Liverpool, secretary to the Foreign Missionary Society. This gentleman gave a very interesting account of the work in India. He stated that the denomination bad a normal college in India, and 100 schools which were Supplied with teachers from that institution. Most of the teachers .were also engaged in evangelical work. There were seven paid native preachers, and a like number of Eutopean preachers, and one medical missionary connected with the work on that continent. The members numbered 2,000; and 3,000 of the persons Who had been brought into connection with the society's labours had given up their heathen practices. In India it was found a very difficult matter to get the girls to go to a Christian school, but in this particular the society had been very suc- cessful, and had about 850 under instruction. The Rajah of Nonyswalia, in the district of Siam, had recently joined the church; and at a public meeting recently, the Bajth delivered an address, in which he spoke at length on the great good which had been done by the missionaries. In former years it bad horn the practice for his deputy to bring him a large number of rupees every 12 months, which were made up by fines for intemperance and theft; but for some time, such had been the great improvement in the habits of the people, that not a single rupee had been received.—The Rev. John Thomas, BA., of Liverpool, gave an account of the Home Mission work. From his statement, it appeared that though this department was in a fairly prosperous con- dition, the improvement which had been made in it was not at all in proportion to the advance which the society's agents had made in the Foreign Mission *ork, in connection with which 500 members had been added during the year. It was stated that the contributions from St. John's Chapel, during the year had been between £37 and £3B. CONCERT la FARNWORTIL—On Monday evening, a miscellaneous concert was held in the boys' schoolroom, Farnworth, on behalf of the local reading-room, which is in want of funds. A special interest was attached to the con- cert by the fact of the chair being occupied by tl;..a Rev. George Bond, the new vic tr of Farnworth, who thus in a sense made his first public appearance out of the pulpit be- fore his parishioners. The concert-room was filled almost to overflowing, among those present being a fair sprinkling of local notabilities and Widnesians. The Chairman, at the commencement of the concert, said evening they were met together in support of a. charitable object—their con- cert was in aid of the funds of the reading-room, which was a most desirnble thing to have in their midst, and he for one would like to see it flourish. Still it was only right that the first task to which they set themselves should be the clearing off of the debt on their room. They must be just before they were generous. (Applause.) He hoped they would be able to clear off the debt and pay Mr. Henry Lea the money due to him. (Hear, hear.> He hoped that some time in the future their wishes in regard to the ,reading-room would be realised, and their aims accomplished. If he could do anything to promote its success he should be very glad to do it, and to lend it a helping hand in every way he could. (Hear, hear.)— The Farnworth glee party, which comprised Messrs. Bate, Large, Mounfield, and Lea, rendered their first piece, "The Forester's Sound," with taste and harmony. Mr. Schofield gave "A holy friar" and on being encored gave "Mary of Argyle." This was followed by the difficult duet, "The Elphin Call,* sung by Miss Davies, a singer well known and gener- ally appreciated in local circles, and Miss Bond, daughter of the new vicar, a young lady who possesses a soprano voice of considerable sweetness and compass. Miss Bond followed with the song," Carissima," and was recalled. Later on in the evening she sang "Good night, sweet mother," with correctness and sweetness. Mr. Lea gave "The monarch of the woods." He was followed by Miss Davies; who sang Mrs. Heman's popular song "The Better land," and she had is hearty encore. She was also on the programme for another song," The last chord," which she rendered in her usual felicitous manner. In the course of the evening Mr. Schofield also sang "The outlaw ;" the glee party, "lireathe soft, ye winds ;" Mr. Lea," Old Adam ;" and the glee party, "Good night." The comic element was furnished by Mr. J. W. Davies, who appealed very successfully to the risible susceptibilities of his audience in the "Irish schoolmaster." CoxcEne IN THE PERM) HALTJ, WARRINGTON.— A concert was given in the Public Hall, on Monday evening, in aid of local charities. There was a good programme, but notwithstanding this fact, and that the artistes included the names of Madame Edith Wynne, Mr. Frank Weston (violoncellist), and those of several local amateurs of well- known ability, the attendance was very discouraging, and we fear that little, if anything, will be added to the funds of the institutions in aid of which the concert was held. Madame Edith Wynne sang two new songs, " Heaven and earth" (Ciro Pineuti), and "The rustic wedding" (Ander- ton), and both were ably interpreted, the latter, a pleasing composition, resulting in an encore, to which she responded with "Trove has eyes." Madame Wynne also took part with Mr. P. C. Price in the duet, "The manly heart" (Mozart), and sang "A bird in hand," for which she was warmly applauded. The pathetic song "For ever and for ever " (Testi) was given with much expression by Miss Lambert, who, in response to a hearty recall, bowed her acknowledgments. She was also very successful in Behren's song, "Auntie," and in the duet "Home to our mountains," with Mr. G. Cropper; but her best effort was undoubtedly in the melodious song, "lid he ever love me" (Bond), for which she secured an enthusiastic encore. Mr. P.C. Price acquitted himself with his accustomed ability in "The bugler" (Pinsuti), and "Blow high, blow low" (Dibdin). "When the shadows of even fall" received a fitting interpretation at the hands of Mr. George Cropper, for which he was recalled. He was equally successful in "The maiden's story" (Sullivan), and for his excellent rendition of "Good bye, Sweetheart" (J. L. Hatton), Mr. Cropper received a deserved encore, to which he responded with "The anchor's weighed," and was warmly applauded. Mr. Frank Weston's two violoncello solos were played in a masterly manner and were listened to with deep interest, he bring recalled with considerable enthusiasm. CONCERT AT Wnsxmr,—Towards the redaction of the debt on the Weston Wesleyan Day-school, the bead-master of which is now Mr. Medley Fitton, late of Warrington, a concert was held in the schoolroom on Wednesday night: There was only a moderate attendance. The chair was taken by the Rev. John Nowell. The programme contained the names of sense of our best local amateurs, and was a choice arrangement of taste. The glee party sang, by way of opening, " 0, who will o'er the Downs so free?" being followed by Miss Wright, who gave " Barney °llea." Miss Jones tastefully rendered the "Kerry Dance," followed by Miss Tomlinson, who was encored for a piano-forte solo. Miss Pieipoint sang with her accustomed freshness the popular" Minstrel boy." Mr. R. W. Pierpoint was encorcd in the cornet solo, "The hurricane polka." Mr. Fitton read with great ability a selection from "David Copper- field" in a manner that won well-deserved applause. Miss Clarke was very successful in the'song "Children's voices r Mr. Morris was in,excellent voice, and was encored for his first-rate rendering of " Goodwin sands." Mr. G. S. Hazle- hurst is no every-day elocutionist, and he was loudly ap- plauded for the recitation "The northern cobbler.' Miss Pierpoint's sweet contralto voice was heard to advantage in "The lost chord," and she reeieved an encore. An instru- mental trio from Hadyn'a " Creation " was rendered with a correctness and expression that won hearty applause. Aliss Wrtght threw much pathos into the favourite song "In the gloaming," and was encored. Miss Jones sung with effect "She wore a wreath of roses." Mr. R. Morris received an encore in the "Midshipmite," and Miss Clarke sung very effectively "Punchinello." A cornet solo from the opera, "La flue du Regiment "brought a concert which had been of sustained interest, to a close. Mr. S. S. Hazlehurst was the accompanist. RENT AUDITS IN CHESHIRE.—The Duke of Westminster has returned to all his tenantry on the Eaton estate 20 per cent, of their rentals. A reduction of 10s. per acre has also been made on all meadow lands for five years, to campensate for flooding. Earl Shrewsbury has postponed the rent audit on his Cheshire estate for a month, from December to January, in consequence of the lateness of the harvest and the difficulties of the past season.

Mr. G. W. Latham addressed a Liberal meeting held on Tuesday atllnutsford under the auspices of the Mid-Ch sshi re Liberal Association. In the course of his speech he urged upon the Liberals of the district to perfect their organization as far as possible, in order to be prepared for the next geheral election. He also pointed out the advantages which the tenant far.ner would possess were the proposals contained in the Farmers' Alliance Land Bill given effect to. A Sr. HELENS SCHOOLMISTRESS PRESENTED WITH A MEDAL.-It is announced in the London Gazette that the Queen has conferred the Albert Medal of the second dais on Miss Hannah Rosbotham, 23 years of age, assist ant school- mistress of the Sutton National Schools, for having, at the imminent risk of her life, rescued four infants from among the debris caused bv the fall of a stone belfry through the roof of the schools on October 14th, during a heavy gale, an account of which appeared in The Examiner at the time. PRESENTATION TO A ST. HELENS DAY SCHOU TEACEIEII.—An interesting presentation took place at the Parish Church Schools, on Friday. The mistress of the gills' school (Miss Furniss) is about to leave the schools soon after Christmas, and as a mark of the respect and esteem in which she is held, by the scholais and pupil teachers, she was presented with a beautiful mounted cabinet album, a neatly wrought silver, brooch, and an umbrella. The pre- sentation was made, in the name of the donors by Miss Houghton, Baldwin-street, senior pupil teacher, who, in a few brief remarks explained the motives which bad prompted the movement, of which she was the promoter. Miss Furniss, in a few well chosen words, expressed her appreciation of their kind recognition of her services. . .
