Banner, M.A. The following werh the artistes :—Miss Fanny Gardner (soprano), Miss Kate Parry (contralto), Mr. George Barton (tenor), Mr. Edward Grime (la isso), Mr. G. Bernard and Mr. C. C. Vickery, Mr. T. A. Barrett, solo pianoforte (of the principlil Manchester c-mccrts), the Excelsior Glee Party (male voices); conductor, Mr. Edward Gt ime ; accompanist, Mr. T. A. Barrett. There was only a very meagre attendance, probably owing to the inclement state of the weather, and it is not too much to say that those who were absent missed a treat, as the concert in every respect as regards the performances of the artistes was of a superior character. SUOCICING DEATHS FROM V.A.:CINA.TION.—Mt. E. Here- ford, the Manchester Coroner, held'an inquest on Monday, on the body of William H. Carpenter, ten weeks old. The medical gentleman who gave evidence in the case said the deceased was brought to him on the 7th inst. There were five distinct Vaccination marks upon its arm. Eryalpelas had then begun and had extended to the body. He visited the child every 'day until Ls death. HA had made a post- mortem examination, and found the organs healthy, with the 'exception that there was congestion of the lung, which be expected followed the erysipelas. Vaccination was sometimes followed by "breaking out." He saw nothing to lead him to think that vaccination had not been properly performed. He considered that as legislation made vacci- nation compulsory some compensation should be made when there were results as in, the present case: The father of the child said be had now lost two children from vaccination. He had objected to this one being vaccinated. The jury returned a verdict that death resulted from erysipelas, caused by vaccination. • Dream rnox Seems AT WenatiNetrox.•=3lr. Barker, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Bowling Green Inn. Bank Quay, on Saturday, touching the death of Eliza Hill The evidence showed that the mother of deceased, who Hied in Bostock-street, was preparirrg breakfast on the morning of the 3rd inst., brad having poured out a cup of tea, turned to place the teapot on the fireplace. As she did so, the deceased overturned the tea upon herself, scalding her right shoulder and breast. She did not seem to be dangerously scalded at the time, and the mother dressed the wounded parts with flour, as she was then unable to get oil. Subsequently she went to Dr. Bride's for medical assistance, and got some ointment for the wounds, and the deceased seemed .to be getting better. On the morning of the 15th inst she was put in her cradle between eleven and twelve o'clock, and one of her boys rocked it. The mother went to a shop for a few minutes, and on returning, saw the deceased's hand was thrust out from the clothes, and that she looked rather strange. She I died almost immediately after. Tne jury returned verdict of "Accidental death." - .

DEATH FROM HEAVY DRINKING AT ST. HELY i.—An inquest NM: held on Monday before Mr. Barker, de?uty coroner, on the body of John Hagan, (35), who died sud- denly in the street on Saturday evening. Deceased was stated to have enjoyed good health when sober, but after a drinking bout he was troubled invariably with a severe headache. He had been in the habit of leaving his work and going on the spree for days and even weeks together, and at the time of his pleath he had not been working for seven weeks. Erysipelas appeared in one of his arms, and he saw Mr. Maclean, chemist an druggist, Higher Parr- street, who gave him a lotion with which to rub the parts afflicted. On Saturday deceased left home informing his wife that he was going into the town and would soon re- turn. While in Church-street deceased fell and died almost instantaneously.—Evilence was given by deceased's wife and Mr. Maclean, who was of opinion that the deceased had died from disease of the heart, or apoplexy.—The jury re- turned a verdict of "Died from natural causes, death being accelerated by excessive drinking." ECCLESTON HILL MISSION BOOM BAND OF HOPE, ST. EaLENs.—On Wednesday evening an entertainment in con- nection with the above, was given in the School-room. The roam was nicely filled. Mr. Edward Pennington, of Thatto Heath. who presided, commented upon the degradation brought upon the workingman's home and family by the drink curse. He urged upon those present the necessity for taking the pledge. Miss Janet Lyon gave a recitation en. titled' Little Jim," doing herself credit,on her first ap- pearance. Mr. Brockbank rendered a song "Teetotal car,', after which Mr. J. C. Westworth gave a recitation on prayer. A trio by Messrs. Jones, Prgscott, and Westworth, accom- panied by Mr. Porter on his accordion followed, And Mr. Brocklebank, of St. Helens, gave a stirring address on the temperance question, showing the importance and necessity for Christians and others to work in the cause. A recitation followed by Mr. John Lawrinson, Master Gervase Green rendered a song, and was followed by Miss Well, who ac- quitted herself well. A trio "Social glass," having been given by Messrs. Jones, Westworth, and Prescott, another song was given by Master Gervase Green, and a recitation by Miss Wells. An interesting stretch was given "Wanted a confidential clerk," the parta being well sustained by Messrs. J. C. Westworth, R. Foulkes, J. Lawrinson, jour., .1. Hill, Jos. Forber, and R. M. Prescott. Mr. Westworth took the part of Jonathan Dobbs, a shipping agent, in want of a con- fidential, while in the applicants appeared Mr. Forbee, his character showing be was too fond of beer; Mr. Lawrineon's character that he was too fond of attending halls and parties, and neglecting business; Mr. Prescott as a loquacious indi- vidual, and Mr. Foulkes as a young man, temperate, in- dustrious, and persevering, he being selected for the appoint- ment. Mr. Hall took the part of John, the servant of Jonathan Dobbe, with credit. Votes of thanks to the chairman, Mr. Broca-melt', and all taking Part, closed the meeting.

div.head: SHOCKING TERMINATION OF A FIGHT AT WARRINGTON. CHARGE OF MANSLAUGHTER.
div.p: SHOCKING TERMINATION OF A FIGHT AT WARRINGTON. CHARGE OF MANSLAUGHTER.

A scene of a most shocking description, and one which gives an insight into the manner of life of a certain section of the inhabitants of Warrington, occurred in a field off Beweey-road, on Saturday. At six o'clock on thia morning of that day, a number of men employed at Bewsey Forge during the night, left their work, and shortly afterwards I went to "Werrall's beerhouse." They here had beer sup- plied to them, and engaged in a game of chance called by the name of "shove penny;" and occasionally in lots of three or four adjourned to a private house in the neighbour- hood to play dominoes. One man risked as much as sovereign on a game, and the others half a crown. Several pints and half-gallons of ale were consumed in that house, and the debasing pastime of drinking and gambling was continued until about half-past twelve—a period of about six hours! The men, numbering about 26, were at that time in the beerhouse, where a dispute arose between a man named Edward Cartwright and James Hasaall, the former accusing the latter of having taken 2d. from the table. Cart- wright challenged James Hassell to fight in a field near the house, but the latter manifested great reluctance to do so. His brother William, however, threatened to strike him if he did not, and dragged him out of the house in a most violent and excited manner. They went to the field aCcom- panied by about six other men from the beerhouse, and they were all in drink." Wm. Hassan acted as second for his brother, and a man named Wm. Wright acted in the same capacity for Cartwright. When about six rounds had been fought, Wm. Hassell accused Wright of unfairness, and, in the altercation which ensued, it is alleged that Wright struck William on the face or neck with his fist. However that may be, he fell down, and when Francis Harrison went to him to raise him up he was dead. He called out that the man was dead, but the combatants, with a most disgusting callousness, continued fighting three more rounds. Wright was taken into custody on the charge of manslaughter, and his companions were taken to the police station to be ex- amined. The Chief Constable, Mr. Hunt, informed the Bends on Monday morning, when the prisoner was brought epee be formally remaaded, that the prisoner was the only sober man amongst the lot. The inquest was held by Mr. Barker, the deputy-coroner, at the Three Pigeons, Hallam-lane, on Tuesday. Mr. John Hough was the foreman of the jury, and Mr. Percy Davies watched the procceedings on behalf of the prisoner. The Coroner, in opening the inquiry, said it was very sad that these men should be so foolish as to quarrel in this way. A most lamentable feature in the case was that after the brother was told the deceased was d.ad they bad several rounds, and seemed to take no notice. It was disgraceful to think that no feelings of kin-ship prompted James to attend to the deceased when he was kis own brother. The first witness examined was Martha Hassell who said:l am the wife of the deceased, and live at 41, Gladstone-street. My husband was a mill-man at the Forge. He was on a night shift last week, and on Friday evening he left home at ten minutes to six to go to his work. He was a strong, healthy man, and was in good health when he went to his work. He was sober. On Sattfrday morning he came home between six and seven, but only stayed to change his clothing. He had a little bread and butter, but no drink. He said he was going to Worrall'e beerhouse to play a match, but of what kind hedid not say. I asked him to stay at home, and he said he would be at home for breakfast. I never saw him alive again. His body was brought home about one o'clock on Saturday. He was 39 years of age. He never, took beer at any time until the week ends. He was a steady man, passionate at times, but his passion soon passed away. I know the prisoner Wright. They have been on good terms up to a fortnight ago, when they "made" a dog race, which aid_ not," come off." I heard some wild talk at that time, and Wright has threatened "to do for him." Mr. Percy Davies: Did you ever hear Wright use any threat to your husband? No, sir. Francis Harrison, of 23, Powys-street, said: I sal a forge labourer. I went to Worrell' beerhouse between six and , seven on Saturday morning. I wont Mime. Deceased and his brother came directly afterwards. A great many men came in, amongst them the- prisoner, William Wright, and Edward Cartwright. We had pints of beer to ourselves at first, and then we drank together. We stayed there all morning. Deceased had not many pints. We had all had drink at noon, when a quarrel began between Cartwright and James Hassan about 2d. The twopence was what they played at shuffle penny with, and Cartwright- said James Hassell had taken the money. Cartwright challenged Has- sell to fight. James Hassell was not willing to fight, and the deceased said he would make him fight. So they went out to fight, the deceased saying if James Hassell did not go out and fight he would hit him hitnself. Deceased was very excited at the time. He did not make such a great noise. He encouraged the fight, and I don't suppose they would have fought but for him. I went with them into the field across the road. We had all had drink. The deceased acted as second to his brother, and William Wright, the prisoner, for Cartwright. The fight proceeded, and after several rounds had been • fought, the prisoner got hold of the deceased's brother and gave him a chuck off Cartwright. lat oid "Os Woll, Let things be fair." Deceased and the prisoner then had words, and the prisoner struck the deceased. I cannot say where. lam sure he struck him. I was not above a yard or two off. He struck deceased with his clenched fist and knocked him dowo. I cannot say whether be fell from the blow. I said "For God's sake come and help me, the man's. dying," but nobody would come near me. I raised him up. but he could not stand, end I shouted "Oh, for God's seke drop off fighting, for the man's dyin a" but they would not stop, and they had two or three meetings after that. Deceased died in my arms whilst they were fighting. I said " Will, get up and auswer me." but all he did was just to turn his eyes up. Bye the Coroner: The blow given by Wright was not a violent one. It was just an ordinary knock. There was no obstruction near to trip the deceased up. By Mr. Percy Davies; Being seconds, the deceased and the prisoner would be behind the fighters. Wright left his man to go to Haman. There were six of us together. I did not see the deceased strike Wright.—By a Juryman: I cannot tell where the deceased was struck. lam sure the blow landed home, but I cannot tell where. The Juryman: That's very strange. e By inspector Singleton: We were drinking at tVorrall's lall forenoon. We left and went into Bradford's., We were playing dominoes. I had a game for half-a-crown. Wit- Bradford and Hassell played for a sovereign. We had no drink ia Bradford's house. I think we had a quart now I recollect. I only left Worrall's and went to Bradford's 'that once. rwo or three times they went out and played for money. William Bradford said: I live at 11, Albert-street. I am a millmlfn, and left work at six o'clock on Saturday morn- ing. I went home.and changed my clothing and it would be about 6-30 when I got to Worrell's. Deceased, his brother, and the prisoner all came afterwards. We were drinking together until about one o'clock. They played eight games at "shove penny." for half gallons of beer. I did not play. There were above twenty drinking beer. How the quarrel corn- menced I-don't know, but I saw the deceased pulling his brother James out of the house. Deceased was in drink, and a little wild, but he could walk pretty straight. He "egged" his brother on to fight. Six of us left the house to see the fight and when we got into the field, deceased wanted to pull offlis brother's shirt. His brother would not allow him. I saw eight or nine rounds fought. When they had fought about six rounds Francis Harrison called to me, and said " Braddie, come here; William Hassan Is dying." I went as sharp as I could, and put my ear to his month, but I could not hear or feel him breathe. I then said "Re's dead; he's gone right I think." The Coroner: Gone right! I am afraid he went wrong enough. Witness: The men were still fighting. I saw no one strike tke deceased, nor did I see him fall. When I first saw him his head was on Harrison's knee. Deceased made more noise I should think than any one else about the fight. I have known deceased for many years. He was not what you may call a regular drunkard. He might get drunk now and amain. He soinetimes stopped in the beerhouse five or six hours, and sometimes longer than that. By Mr. Davies: The deceased was "raving" and shout- ing a great deal on the field and dragged his brother out of , the house in a very excited manner. If the prisoner had struck the deceased I should have seen him. By Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) : I have heard that the primmer And the deceased were not good friends. Ann Higginson said she was going down Bewsey-road a little before one otelock on Saturday when she saw two men fight- ing in a field. As she approached she beard deceased shout,' "All keep away," and then say to his brother, "Hit him under, and you will kill him." He ran towards his brother and reeled and fell. She did not know why he fell. The only man who went to the deceased was Harrison, and the fight continued. Deceased seemed very excited before he fell. She saw no one strike him, and the prisoner was a distance away from the-place were he fell. By Mr. Davies: If the prisoner bad rstruck the deceased she should have seen him. She simply saw him reel and fall. By Mr. Hunt: The prisoner has lived,with-me since my husband left me. The Coroner: Have you cohabited together? No, sir. He has been with the militia. The Coroner said the two men who were fighting were in attendance, but he thought their evidence would be imma- terial to the inquiry. It was quite clear no act of theirs con- tributed to the death a the deceased. The jury decided not to examine those witnesses, and Dr. Bride was called. He said he had made a post mortem examination of the deceased, and found there were no marks of violence externally or internally. He removed the skull cap, and underneath the membrane of the brain was a large quantity of effused blood, which would cause a compression of the brain and death. All the organs of the body were in a healthy condition. He attributed death to sanguinons apoplexy. The apoplexy might have been caused by a blow or by the deceased jumping from a great height, but there were no evidences that such had been the case, and he was of opinion that it was brought on by excitement. The Coroner': Can you form any opinion whether he might have received a fairly strong blow, and yet received no mark? Suppose he had had a blow from a fist, would you hive expected to find a meth ? - There would have been some mark or discolouration after death. To the best of mew belief death resulted from excitement and not from violence. The Coroner then addressed the • jury. He said the jury

I dare not i attempt in the limits of a letter to enter into details, but, if' YOU will permit me, I am willing to supply the requisite information as to the methods which are adopted, or the recipes which are employed, to accomplish all that I have indicated to any person who will communicate to me his or her name and address.—Yours truly, R. He plumped himself into a chair directly, to take one on each knee. Then Sage and I busied ourselves in taking off pelisses and woollen leggings, and reducing the little things into a less rounded shape, while John at as stolid and serious as a judge, evidently being very proud of his two little ones, as he was of his handsome young wife, who bad quite lost her old pallor and dejected look, and settled down into a happy young mother. I then went up with Sage to her room, and she began to tease me about Frank, but ended with an affectionate embrace. e. I'd marry him any time, Rue dear," she said, "for I think he's a good fellow, and if you are as happy as I am with dear old John you will be satisfied." I smiled, but I could not help thinking about seven years ago, when Sage was only eighteen, and was in such trouble about aunt's nephew, Tom Latchley, who used to live with us to learn farming, and behaved so ill that uncle was thinking of sending him to Australia when•he got into trouble by nearly killing one of old Sir Edward's keepers, and had to get out of the country as fast as he could. Poor Sage was nearly heart-broken, and used to tell me that she would go after him if he sent for her; but he never even wrote to her in spite of all his professions; and then we learned how badly he had behaved about two poor girls in the village; and after that Sage never mentioned his name but in a quiet subdued way, and a good deal at uncle's wish accepted John Berry—a man of sterling qualities—and she had grown brighter and happier ever since she had been his

THE CONSERVATIVES AND THE WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to say a few words in reply to the letter of "Anti-Sham," which appeared in your issue of Saturday last, respecting the Conservative mem- bers of the Parliamentary Debating Society. As might be supposed, he wishes to lead people to the belief that the letter sent to the Speaker by the Conservative Whips did not give thereat reason why the members withdrew from the society. Of course he does; it is the only way of getting out of the difficulty by accusing the Conservative members of concocting a lie. Perhaps " Anti-Sham " is not aware that many persons outside the society consider the course taken by the Conservatives was justifiable; and let him say whatever. he likes the fact still remains that the "tone " (I hardly like to use the word considering certain late members object to it)—of the society was not improvtd by the personalities Indulged in aid the unveiled insults offered in many instances by certain members of the party in office to the oppposition. Will " Anti-Sham " say If it is not a fact, that a debating society formed some time ago at the Liberal Club was broken up simply because certain members of it could not keep from remarks of a personal character? And when Liberals cannot keep from insulting each other' how can it be expected that the element which existed in that society would refrain from insulting persons holding different opinions from themselves in our mimic Parliament? I will only add that, from what I can learn, the Leader of, the Opposition, whose retreat into oblivion "Anti-Sham" so devoutly wishes for, was not in any way responsible for the course taken by the Conservatives, although he quite agreed with the declaim arrived at; and had some members behaved themselves in the gentlemanly manner which has always characterised the Leader of the .Opposition, I feel sure the society would not have died a premature death.--Yours, Sze., A SPECTATOR,

CHAPTER L—Rox. " Toms may say what they like," said Uncle Joseph, giving his scrubby grey hair a rub, looking fiercely at nobody with one eye, and giving me one of his merry, comical looks with the other; "but Christmas is Christmas, and it always Wm Christmas. and it always will be Christ- mas, and as for those folks who talk about its being a thing at the past, why I'd hang 'em all up in a row." "Now don't exaggerate so, Joseph, my dear," said nay awe, Nan*. "You know you would do nothing of the kind." "Wouldn't I though, but I would, and then starve NOM tO death, and make 'ens mad to see me eating my rnaSt beef and plum pudden before 'em." "But Christmas has only been in existence u foleratlignhgtethene centuries and a-half, Joseph," said my of falnkaintugre bottom of her apron, a habit of her's whenamshiste:a:'kaes "Oh, ain't it? Well, then it was a for not having it sooner, and I'm sorry for them as lived before." o always like "Weil, Joseph," said my aunt, about keeping LJaristmas, and lett to have your own way Rue and I will cla; our best. "Of course you will, Ins" " dear," he said. "And now, old woman, if you want any lunch, have it, and then go and pop on your black silk and bonnet, while I order round the libelee, and I'll drive Tou to town." "No, Joseph nu; exclaimed my aunt, who had now gathered the whole of the bottom of her apron into pleats and let them go. ' "I said last night that I would not go pith you any more unless you left the whip at home. I cannot bear to it in that chaise and see you beat poor apple as you do." "But I must have a whip, old girl, or I can't drive." "I'm sure the poor horse goes very well without," said my aunt; and her sweet, placid old face looked so full of tenderness and gentle love towards everything that I felt as if I must go to her and kiss her. "Bat not through the snow, my dear," said my uncle, giving me another of his droll looks. "Really, Polly, I Wouldn't answer for our not being upset without a whip." , "But you wouldn't use it without you were absolutely I obliged, Joseph?" said my aunt. "On my honour as a gentleman," said my uncle; and aunt smiled and weut upstairs to get dressed; and uncle walked to the door, crunched through the snow, and I heard him shouting his orders to Dicky Dykes to harness Dapple and bring him round to the door. I stood in our low-celled old-fashioned parlour, waiting for unble to tome in, and somehow that morning I felt as if iny heart was full of joy. There was a smile spread upon my lip, and as I listened now to my uncle's load, hearty voice shouting orders to the different men about the yard, and now to my dear aunt's heavy toddling footsteps over- head, I was gazing straight into the great glowing wood fire, whose ruddy dames flickered and danced in the broad, blue- tiled chimney; and thengt it was so cold that the frost was making silver filigree upon the window panes, I felt all aglow, and kept on picturing in the embers the happy Christmas scenes that were to come. "By George!" roared my uncle coming in. " Hallo ! didn't kick all the snow off. Here let's melt it before the tyrant comes down ; " and he shone all over his broad face, and his eyes twinged with mirth, as he held first one boot and then tke other to the blaze. "Give's a kiss, ducky." He hugged me to his side, and gave me a smack upon the lips, holding one close to him as he smiled do min nay eyes. "And I used to grumble my pet, because I had no chil- dren," he said, tenderly, "little thinking I should have Sage and Rue to take care of till—Oh! I say. Ha-ha-ha! Look at the colour. Poor little woman then. Was he coming to- day ? " "Please don't tease me, uncle," I whispered, as I laid my head upon his shoulder, and hid my burning face. "I won't then," be said; but I could fen him chuckling as he went on. "I say though, Rue. I've hien thinking One ought hardly to ask him to come and stay here for Christmas, though. Very hospitable, eh? But hardly con- ventual. No, no, I mean conventional. No you don't. I've got you tight," for I had trierto run away. "Then please don't tease me, uncle." "But what will old Vinnicombe say ?" "Uncle dear," I whispered, appealingly. "There then my pet, I won't,' he said. yen expect Jack and Sage ?" • "By about four o'clock, uncle," I said. "That's right, my pet, and now you must bustle. See that there's plenty of jolly good fires, for I hate people to come and fin l the place chilly. Let's give 'em a warm re- ception, and I'll see if I can't till up some of old Vinni- combe's wrinkles out of his face this Christmas." "I want Rue," said my aunt, calling down the stairs. " Yts, aunt." "Hold that wrapper to the fire, my dear, ready for your I uncle," and she threw down a great white cashmere belcher for me to air. "Here! Roil I say, old girl, Fin not going to wear that thing," roared my uncle. "Yes, dear, it's a very long drive," said my aunt, " and the air is very cold." My uncle sank into a chair and said "Tyranny, tyranny, tyranny! Oh! why did I ever marry such a woman as this ?" "Now deb't talk nonsense, Joseph," cried my aunt, *rust- ing down into the room so wrapped up that she looked double her natural size, what with cloak, and boa, and-a large muff. "Put it round your uncle's neck, Rue, the frost is very severe." The old gentleman threw his head back ready for me to tie on the wrapper, uttering a low moan the while, and then sighed as he stood up and walked—at first slowly and than with alacrity—into the hall to pat on his hat. "I can't get into my coat with this thing on," roared my uncle. "Here, Rue, come and give us a lift." I ran laughingly into the hall to help the great coat on I to his broad shoulders just as the four-wheeled chaise came crunching through the snow to the front door, Dapple giving a snort or two, and stamping upon the frozen gravel. Just then soy uncle gave me a comical look, rushed to the corner by the eight-day clock, and made a great deal of rattling as he took up the whip and gave it a sharp lash :through the air, and another on the broad balustrade. I heard my aunt start, and my-uncle chuckled. ' Now, old lady." he said. " That's right, Rue, plenty of rugs, or we shall have her frozen. I have told Dicky to I cut plenty of green stuff for you to arrange. Hold his head still, Dicky. There you are; tuck that rug round you. There, that's better," he cried, taking his seat and fasten- ing the apron. "Let him go, Dicky. Tck." My uncle started Dapple, and thee rose up in the chaise with a quick motion, raising the whip as he set his teeth, and seemed about to strike the cob a tremendous blow, making my aunt jump and seize his arm, when be subsided, looking round at me with a comical expression in his eyes, but pulled up short in the snow. " fiere. Hi! I say. Yab ! artful. Here you, Frank, you're three hours before your time," he cried. "Yes, sir. I thought I might help a little, and—" "You thought you might help a little, and—G'on., ,with you—get out. Glong !" and my uncle flicked and lashed at Frank Romney, as he stepped to the side of tbe chaise and shook hands, while I, with my heart beating fast, drew back into the porch, seeing my uncle begin poking at the new arrival with the butt of the whip handle. Then the cob was started again with age:Aber pretended ftwious cut, which made my aunt catch at uncle's arm; and and then as, frightened, fluttering, and yet so happy, I saw Frank coming towards me, my uncle's voice came roaring through the wintry air— "l say if those rooms ain't evergreened before we come back—' "Rue, my dear girl." Those were the words I heard next as one of my hands was taken, and a great strong arm went round my waist, to lead me back into the ball.

We had a busy time of it decorating the rooms so as to g 6 done; but we all eorked so well that the litter was cleared away, and the table spread for high tea, long before uncle and aunt came back with the chaise loaded up, and aunt protesting that she would never go out again with uncle if be took a whip. The old man chuckled as I helped him with his overcoat, shouting orders all the while to Frank and John Berry, who were busy bringing in the load of parcels fill it seemed wonderful how they could all have been got into the chaise. At last the final packet was in, and the cold night air shut out; but hardly had the door been closed, and we were standing laughing at Sage's little girls, who were staggering in and out of the great parlour with packets which they carried by the string, than the bell rang. "Here's Vinnicombe," cried my uncle, and our old doctor, in a fur cap tied down over his ears, blue spectacles over his eyes, and his tall lean form muffled in a long thick great coat, came in, stamping his feet. "Merry Christmas to you, doctor," cried my uncle heartily. 'Glad to see you." "Bah! 'Taint Christmas yet," said the doctor sourly. "Isn't it, by George! " cried my uncle, slapping him on the back and hauling him to the parlour door, where the glowing fire lit up the abundant evergreens, and the bright looking table spread, as my uncle loved to see his board, with plenty. of the good things of life. "There, don't that look like Christmas ? " "Here, help me off with this coat somebody," growled the doctor. "How do, girls? Take away those children or I shall tread on 'em. Hate youngsters ranning about under one's feet like black beetles. What have you got there ?" he added, pointing to to the parcels. "Pal-Ida and kickshaws. The old woman's been pretty well emptying the grocer's shop." "Now, Joseph, that is really too bad," said my aunt, full of mild indignation. "Now you know you would persist in buying three-parts of what is there." "Humph! thought you fancied you were going to be snowed up," growled the doctor, shaking himself free of his coat, and holding out first one leg and then the other for Frank to pull off his goloshes. "There, look sharp, girls," cried my uncle. "Come, old lady, take off your things. Rue, put the doctor in the chimney corner to thaw. He'll soon come round." • Dr. Vinnicombe shook his fist at my uncle, and let me lead him to the glowing fire, while the next moment the lat- ter was having what he called a glorious cuddle, four little chubby arms being fast about his great neck and a couple of pairs of little red lips kissing him all over his rugged, ruddy ace.

C EIAPTER IL—SAGE. "I hardly hoped for such good fortune, Rue," he cried as I gently disengaged myself from his arm, and stood gazing rather sadly in his face; "but oh! pray, pray don't look at me like that, darling. It's Christmas time, and I've come to go Ltwn on my knees to you, Rue. There," he cried, "I will, to bog pardon—to tell you I was a weak, jealous fool—that I know you could not help Sir rdward coming and admiring you (he'd have been a fool if be hadn't !)—that you're the best, and dearest, and truest, and sweetest, and most innocent-hearted of girls—that I love you more dearly than ever, and that I've been a miserable wretch ever since that day." " Don't do that, Frank," I said, as he literally went upon hia knees to me; "it hurts me." "And I'd suffer anything sooner than give you a mo- meat's pain," he cried, springing to his feet; and we stood new in the middle of the old parlour. "But you haven't ftttrgiven me,Rue," he raid, piteously. "Yes, Frank, I've forgiven you," I said; " but I want you to know and trust me bitter. Your words seemed so cruel to me, and if you knew me better you would not have said them. I did not know that Sir Edward when he called did so that he might see me, and we hardly exchanged a dozen words." "And if yon bad exchanged a thousand, sweet, what then?" he cried, I.roudly. "I was a jealous idiot, and ought to have known better; but it has been a lesson to me my weakness, and you may trust me that it shall never oecur again." I was silent, for I was thinking it was my duty to tell him that, after the sad little trouble that had come between us, it would be better for us to separate for a time; but I could not say it with his eyes looking so appealingly at me. I was very weak, for Frank Romney had somehow won my heart, and I had 'felt so proud of him for his handsome face, his manly bearing, and straightforward honesty of purpose. The words would not come, and somehow the next minute I was sobbing in his arms as he whispered those two words, but in such a tone—" My darling'!" I started from him guiltily the next moment and ran up- stairs, for there was a tresh crunching of wheels through the snow, and the trampling of a horse's hoofs. I came down again though, directly, to welcome my sister Sage and her husband, John Berry—a bluff, middle-aged hop-grower, to whom she had been married five years now; and they had eo ne, with their two little girls to spend Christmas. "Al], Frank, my lad, how are you? Rue, give us a kiss. Bless you, how well you look. How am I? Hearty, and so's Sage." I was kissing dear Sage affectionately the next moment,

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock. SERIOUS CASS OF ALLEGED UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING. —David Hatton as charged with unlawfully and mali- ciously wounding William McNamara.—Prosecutor said he was a labourer, living at the Old Marsh. On the 12th inst. he-went into the Sportman's Arms public house, at about eight o'clock at night, and saw the prisoner there with two other men, named John Brawley and Michael Mannion. Hatton paid for two pints of beer for the two men and him- self, (witness). Prosecutor came out of the house shortly before eleven o'clock, accompanied by Brawley and Mannion, leaving the prisoner inside. Brawley and himself stayed on the canal bank, talking together, when they observed the prisoner come out of the house at eleven o'clock. He went across the Iron Bridge, and in about five minutes returned for some more beer, but he did not get any. Mannion went up to him and said "Coma home, and we will see you right." Prisoner was drunk. Witness and Brawley went to help Mannion, who took hold of prisoner's arm. They had walked about 300 yards, and had arrived at the Soap Waste Walk, when the prisoner turned round on Mannion, and said " Who are you ? "and began to struggle. A fight ensued, snit he tried to get the prisoner off Mannion, who was under him. Whilst he was doing so, he felt that he was stabbed in the left hand, and in the right arm. He saw a knife in the prisoner's hand, and called out to his compan- ions to get away, owing to prisoner having the instrnment in his hand. Prisoner then ran away, and witness went home, and found that he had received three wounds. He caused information to be given to the police, and the wounds were dressed by Dr. Cooper's assistant. He was still in con- siderable pain. He never gave the prisoner any provoca- tion. He was well acquainted with him, having known him for a long time. They were both on friendly terms whilst in the public house: Prosecutor produced his coat, in which were cats corresponding to those he described to the Bench. —Michael Mannion, who is a private in the 40th regiment of foot, now stationed at Warrington, gave corroborative evidence. The reason why they took the prisoner under their care was that McNamara said that if he got into the -canal they would be blamed for it, as they had been with him: Prisoner knocked him (witness) down near the bridge when they were going home, and he saw the knife in his hand. —John Brawley, who belongs to the 3rd South Staffordshire Militia, stationed at Warrington, was also called, and said he saw the complainant bleeding and the prisoner running away.—P.C. Pitt said he was on duty in Waterloo-road, about midnight on the 12th inst., when he saw the prisoner pass. His coat and hat were covered with mud, and he was under the influence of drink and very excited. Hatton told him he had been attacked by three men as he went along the Soap Waste Walk, and knocked down and kicked. Pri- soner pulled out his purse and remarked that the robbers had IlOt taken everything away from him at any rate. Ile en- quired of the man if he knew anything of the persons who had set upon him, and he replied "No." In answer to another question, he said he had just come from a flat which was lying in the river. Prisoner never mentioned a knife.— Dr. Cooper said he had examined the prosecutor, who had two wounds on his left hand, and one on the inner side of the upper part of the right arm. There were also several smaller wounds upon him. The chief one was upon the palm of the hand, which had nearly cut the whole of the soft part of the flesh away. It would be six weeks before the man could return to his work.—Sergeant Robinson gave evidence as to apprehending the prisoner on the 13th inst. He made a fierce resistance, and .was only taken to the police station with the aid of another constable. On being charged, the prisoner replied "I cannot help it," and never made any reference to having been robbed.—On being formally charged by the Bench, the prisoner said "I am guilty of defending myself." Ile was committtd to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. WEDNESDAY.—Before E. K. Muspratt (chairman), and

_ Mr. George Pilkington. RISING To LEAVE A Promic-notrsn.—Peter O'Grady and John Manning were proved to have been drunk and re- fused to quit the Barn's Head public-house, Caroline—street, at three o'clock on the afternoon of the 12th inst.—O'Grady, who was represented by his wife, was fined 7s. 6d. and costs; and Manning, who did not appear, 10s. And costs.

A COLLIER'S COURTSHIP. EXTRAORDINARY REVELATIONS. John Atherton, •a collier, was brought up on remand at the Borough Court, on Monday, before the Mayor, Major Cartwright, Aldermen Davies and Chandley, and Councillor Fairclough, charged with stealing a quantity of furniture valued at £2O, the property of Ellen Dixon.—Mr. Moore appeared for the prisoner. The details of the case as related by Mr. Worsley, the pro- secutrix's solicitor, showed that Mrs. Dixon was a widow with three children, residing at Haydock. Her husband ' had left her four houses and a houseful of furniture; and as he died intestate, letters ef administration were taken out on behalf of herself and her children. Some time since she made the acquaintance of the prisoner, who paid his addresses to her, and she agreed to marry him. Her furni- ture, which up to that time had been at her father's house, she removed to a house she had taken at Blackbrook. This was on the 15th October, and a few days afterwards the prosecutrix received a communication from a woman who was in the family way by the prisoner. The marriage was in consequence broken off, bat unfortunately the prisoner had succeeded in seducing the prosecntrix, and she was also enciente. The prisoner, however, by expressirg much sorrow and contrition for his past conduct, prevailed upon the prosecutrix to again promise to marry him. The banns were put up at St. Catherine's Church, Wigan, and the mar- riage was to have taken place on the 7th November. Immt- dlitely on the banns being put up, the furniture at the pri- soner's request, was removed from Blaekbrook to the home of the prisoner's brother at 73, Knntsford-road, Latchford, 0 where prisoner at that time was living. The prosecutrix, on the 25th October, went to the house at Latchford, and there lived with the prisoner as his wife for over a week. Now the prisoner's real object in wishing for the marriage ap- peared. He frequently made enquiries as to the four houses at Haydock, and on the 30th October he asked prosecutrix if she had the deeds in her possession. She said no, and asked why he wanted the deeds. "Because if you die first I shall have the first chance," was the answer; and he added, "If there's no deeds there's no marriage." When told the pro- secutrix's father had the deeds locked up in a box at home, prisoner said he must have them some way, even if she had to break open the box. She Went to Haydock to try and obtain the deeds, but her father would not allow her to have them, and she returned to Latchford. On the 3rd November she again broke off the "match," and was at Bank Quay Station waiting for the train to Haydock, when the prisoner, who was with her, became very violent, and said "Tell your father his life is nOt as long as he expects it to be, and tell your Tom; and sooner than you shall go home and live with your father 1 would dash you in the river." She told him she intended Lo fetch the furniture the following day. "Don't fetch it for a week," he pleaded, "and I will help you to take it, and we will live with the old folks and get married." Prosecutrix's father and brother, however, went to Latchford on the following day, and found that the pri- soner had absconded, and sold the furniture. A warrant was taken out on the 4th November, but a month elapsed before he was apprehended. Prosecutrix Was called, and corroborated Mr. Worsley's stateinent. She stated that in addition to the furniture, a large quantity of wearing apparel had also been disposed of. The value would be about £27 10s. Cross-examined: The banns were first put up at St. James's Church, Latchford, but her father stopped them. Mr. Moore: When he parted from you didn't he kiss you? He took hold of my hand and kissed me, and told me "Don't let your heart down." (Laughter.) Mr. Moore: Didn't you like that? (Laughter.) Didn't you kiss him again? (Laughter.) No. Cross-examination continued: She bad never consented for the prisoner to sell the furniture, and use the money to go to America. Prisoner lived at the house at Blackbrook, and she cooked his meals daily. Mr. Moore: If it were not for your goyernor you would marry him now? No I should nee—never. Not if he were made of solid gold. (Laughter.) Mr. Moore: Well, lam afraid that's impossible. Joseph Crocker, furniture dealer, deposed to baying a large quantity of furniture. The prisoner had stated to him that the reason he was selling the gebels was that he and his " missus " were going to America. Elizabeth Wainwriglat said her husband was a hair dresser, and had bought a hair-seated sofa and other articles from the prisoner. P.C. Bowen stated the prisoner, when charged, replied, "Oh there's fin mistake about it ; I sold them. They were her's." Mr. 11166 re, in addressing the Bench, said if it had not been for the interference of the father the parties would have been married. He considered the prosecutrix had behaved very hard in certain respects to the prisoner, and it was more a case for a County Court than for criminal pro- ceedings. The prisoner Was committed to take Ws trial at Knutsford Quarter Sessions.--Major Cartwright said he considered it a hard case; the woman had been very cruelly treated. Mr. Moore applied for the prisoner's release on bail but this the Bench refused.

div.p: POTTERS' STRIKE.

am directed by the Staffoydshire Potteries Manu- facturers' Association to say that they will be glad if you can find room in your valuable paper for an account of the strike in the Staffordshire Potteries, which has now assumed a ' very serious aspect. I send you herewith a copy of the Sunday Times of December 11th. This paper, you are aware, circulates almost exclusively amongst the working classes. The account given therein is correctly given, and was sup- plied by an independent correspondent. lam also directed to forward you a statement of the real earnings of the work- men in the potting trade in this district. The earnings of 13 branches, employed at 15 manufactories impartially selected, are taken. I mention this because the gentleman who wrote the article in the paper herewith seems to have been misin- formed on this point. Manufacturers understand that appeals for help are being sent to your town, and think it only right that the public should know the real facts of the case. The workmen in the potteries are on strike for the purpose Of obtaining a rate of wages ruling in 1872, when the earnings of all operatives were exceptionally high. Manufacturers submit that inasmuch as almost all other classes of workmen have since had their earnings reduced, there is no reason why they should assist the potters in ob- taining what they themselves do not enjoy. I give you be- low the statement of earnings above referred to, and remain, yours truly, HENRY WM. ACKRILL, Secretary to the Manufacturers' Association. THE .GUARDIANS AND THE TREATMENT OF PAUPER PATIENTS. Sir,—The question of the treatment of out-door paupers is one which, we believe, will interest the public in being fully discussed. • By this we mean sliscusaed in a spirit of fairness, honesty, and impartiality, and not in the mere barren love of argument, public notoriety, or personal motive. We have diversity of opinions in most public matters, amongst professional men as well as layman, and generally it is well there should bet but unfortunately we have amongst us a certain class of individuals, who, when they take up a ques- tion, impart to it aew phases of light and reason which really are sometimes wonderful; they talk about every- thing but the right thing, and seem to believe that *ey change black to white and every other colour to its widest contrast the moment they open their mouths ; they fly off at a tangent the moment thempeak, and run dway from the main points. The main point and the only one of principle is "Who is bound to provide for the out-door Paupers in vase of sickness," and upon this everybody seems agreed. Lumley, the editor of the Local Government Chronicle, and even Glen (all, of whom, we believe, are barristers) are of one mind now, although the latter gentleman was formerly of a different opinion. Of course, even such a great man as Mr. Glen may sometimes be wrong. Other lawyers have been wrong, as the decisions of the -Chancery and other courts have proved. Mr. Glen answers Mr. Jeans's question in a way we think he little expected, and which shows as clearly as words can put it whose duty it is to provide for out-door paupers in case of sickness. "If any destitute per." sons (he says) whether in health or sickness require relief, medical or otherwise, for themselves or any member of their families, lam of opinion that it is the duty of the Guardians to provide the required relief either in the Workhouse or out of it. In some way or other they are bound themselves to provide proper and adequate relief for all destitute persons applying to them for assistance, and cannot shift the re- sponsibility of doing so upon any other public authority or other persons." This lb the only question in it—the only question of principle and honesty. If it is the duty of the t Guardians then let them perform it. If they will not, are we to understand that they are trying to shirk their duty in endea- vouring to compel the Corporation to de it ? If that is so, the position the Guardians are taking is a false one, and it leads to this, that the Guardians are attempting, by their t own neglect in making proper arrangements for the treat- ment of paupers, to foist them upon the Corporation, who, to be consistent in carrying out the Aet in preventing the spread of the disease, will have to provide for them. It oozed out the other day that a neighbouring body, having the privilege of *fending their patients to our hospital, con- -trary to the understanding and arrangement with them, very quietly sent one -of their pauper patients to our hospital, and never "let on to anybody," as the saying goes. We cannot say, but in all probability if it had not been found out, that body would have attempted the thing again and we are informed that the resolution passed by the Sanitary Committee was to prevent the repetition of any such unfair advantage being again taken of them. That Committee have had a hard battle to fight of late, a battle against dis- ease in the first place; but a harder and fiercer battle against the prejudices of a certain class of gentlemen who appear to be blinded with the rEd rag of their popularity, gentlemen from whom the Committee have received nothing but insult and interference; gentlemen who appeared to take a delight in pestering. the Committee in evorything they undertook, never on a single occasion showing any desire to see what good there was in anything that Committee did If the resolution the Council has passed will only prevent attempts being made which may in any way destroy or injure the usefulness of the institution which has done so much good, and prevent its being turned, as it is proposed, into a place where paupers may be sent, in fact to make it into a second workhouse, it is a good thing dime. The Guardians cry out " fle cannot compel them to come to our hospital, we have tie compulsory power to remove them here, and we are helpleSs if they refuse." Helpless they are it is true, and helpless they will remain unless they help themselves. Is there no way out of the difficulty? Supposing the law gives them no power to compel removal, the whole thing is reduced to one of arrangement. If they admit their duty in this question, their liability to provide for destitute per- sons in case of sickness, then let them approach the Cor- poration in a straightforward and honest manner, and admit their duty in a proper spirit, and say, "If you will make provision at your, hospital by separate wards or otherwise for our paupers, we will pay you for it," and we believe the Corporation would, seeing their position, make arrangements with them, or, as we believe could be done, the Corporation would remove their paupers to their own hospital. Under the Public Health Act the Corporation have power to remove all persons within the borough suffering from disease and without proper accommodation' to any hospital within their district, which in the work we have on the subject, is ex- plained by Lumley to include a hospital at a workhouse. The whole difficulty is a mere myth. There is a way out of it if the Guardians will only go that way, and not stand afar off be- wailing their position with a long face, and with a Peck- sniffian snuffle pray Heaven provide for the poor. Aboye everything else in the world there ought to be in public bodies a high standing of public virtue and honesty, and the goodness of intention should actuate them in everything they they do. Let us have fair dealing in this matter.— ours JOSEPH. truly,

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA'

CHAPTER lll.—WEwns. The warm fire and the pleasant social meal did make the doctor come round, and very joyous everything seemed as we afterwards sat about the blazing fire., I cannot describe my feelings, only that it seemed to me happi- ness even to exist, as I returned the proud glances of Frank, and saw how happy and contented Sage was, with her pretty young matronly face, as she sat by her husband's side and seemed to glow with content, as first one little golden-haired cherub and then the other was seated on Dr. Vinnicombe's knee, the old cynic telling them tales to which we all listened with almost childish delight. It was a happy Christmas Eve indeed.--a time of simple and sweetest joy; and how well I remember the colour flushing into my cheeks when I went up with Sage to put the little ones to bed, as she half mockingly said—" How long will it be, Rue, before I am helping you to put a little Frank and a little Rue to sleep?" We were very silent directly after, and I felt a kind of wondering awe as, in obedience to a word from their mother, the two little white-robed things, with their fair hair like golden glories round their head, knelt at Aunty Rue's knee to lisp each a little simple prayer to God to send his angels to watch round their couch that night; and as I listened I seemed to dream of another little child born nearly two thousand years ago ; and then back came Sage's merry words and with them wondering awe, almost dread, at the possibility of such as these at my feet ever calling me mother, and looking to me for help. We stayed for a few minutes to see them sleep, with their ro 7 little faces on the same pillow, and then, with our arms around each other, Sage and I, happy girls at heart, ence more descended to the dining-room, where dear aunt was telling Doctor Vinnicombe about her troubles With her gar- den, while my uncle's face was full of good-humoured crinkles as she spoke. "Here girls," he said, putting down his pipe and spreading his knees, "come a,td Se little ones again and comfort me while I'm being flogged." "I'm not flogging yon, Joseph," said my aunt, in a dear old serious, half-plaintive way; "but I do say that it is a shame that in my own garden you will be always planting seeds and things that have no business there." "Never put in anything that isn't useful," chuckled my uncle, with his arms round our waists as we sat upon his knees. "Useful, yes; but you ought not to sow carrot-seed amongst my mignonette, and plant potato-cuttings in amongst my tulips and heartsease. I declare, doctor, if my verbena-bed was not full of cabbage plants one day, and 1 when I pulled them up he had them planted again and often and often I've allowed swedes, and mangolds, and rape .to get ever so big in the garden before I've known what they were." "He's a wicked old rascal, Mrs. Hurst, that be is; and if I were you I'd have a divorce," said the doctor. " Ab, do, old lady, I'll find tha money," chuckled my uncle, when the tears rose to my eyes as I saw the sweet, loving smile with which the beautiful old lady rose from her chair, came behind us, and stood with her hands resting upon his shoulders. "Forty-six Christmas Eye's we've passed together, Joseph," she said, simply; and he leaned back his head, and said softly— "Ay, dear, it is, and, please God, we'll have six-and-forty more—here or in the better world !" There was a dead silence then in the room for a few minutes, during which both Sage and I left uncle and re- turned to our places, just as Dr. Vinnicornbo turned his head slightly aside, blew his nose loudly, and then exclaimed— " Now, squire, how about that game at whist?" "To be sure. Now, girls," cried my uncle,.cheerily, "aide. tables out while Maggie and Cook set the supper. My word what a night! It's a nipper indeed. Let's have another log on, old lady, and—What the dickens is the matter with those thms ?" I For just then as the flames and sparks were roaring up the chimney, the two dogs in the yard set up a furious barking, growing so excited, and tearing so at their chains, that my uncle went out to the door, opened it, and a rush of cold, searching wind reared into the room as he shouted— " Down Don! Quiet, Rover! Who's there?" "Uncle Hurst, ahoy-y-y!" came in reply, in a rough voice, that made me start and then turn, for I heard a faint cry behind me, and there stood Sage, with her hands clasped, gazing at the open door, and looking as pale as death." "Why, it's Tom Latchley!" cried my aunt, rising, from her seat, and then sinking back trembling as she heard the door close; and-directly after a tall, dark man,' with his clothes and board Whitened with snow, entered the room with ray uncle, who seemed too much surprised to speak. "How are you all 2" he said quietly. "Didn't expect to see me at#A, elt ? Thought I'd come to the old place and see if you'd give me a bed and a bit of Christmas dinner in remembrance of old times. It wasn't far to come." "Why, Torn—Tom," said my aunt, trembling. "Tom it is, aunty," he cried. "110 w well you look. Give's a kiss, old lady." My aunt embraced him, her sweet old face looking very careworn and troubled. Then be turned to me. "Why, is this Rue? How you have improved. Grown quite a handsome woman, instead of being a little wisp, as you were seven years ago." •noly at my trembling voice, as she kept gazing deprecatingly "Were you close by then, Tom ?" said my aunt, in a uncle. I'd come and see you all again. By6on uncle ?" "Oh yes, aunty, only fourteen thou,sanedsmarileebsy! gTonheosu,gehht, "Yes, yes, "Glad to see you again,c "and how is Sage, eh? How are you, sir—how are you p" way at John Berry as he shook hands, and then turned to Frank. "And is this Rue's husband?" he said, laughingly, but conTtoemm'patulus in a sarcastic way that turned me cold. "Well, no; I am not Miss Ilurst's husband, Mr. Latch- ley." said Frank, smiling, and taking the extended hand, his tone saying plainly enough that he hoped soon to be.

" Ah, well, we all get married some time or other," said Tern, in a careless, unpleasant way. "Have you got married then, my lad ?" said uncle. "No, not yet. I've come over to fetch myself a wife, perhaps. flab! how cosy this room is after the bitter night." "Yes, of course," said Aunt Hurst; "and we are giving you a _cold welcome, my boy. Rue, my dear, hurry in the supper, of which, of course, you'll partake." "That I will," said Tom, "and glad of it. I'll dry my boots a bit. And how's Dr. Vinnicombe, eh?" "Doctor Vinnicombe is as well as can be expected," said our old visitor, gruffly ; and, after glancing once at Sage, I left the room, feeling as if Tom Latcliley hal brought the bitter winter time into our hearts with him, and as if his coming had cast a chill upon the cheery home. I was right—it had, for, as the night wore on, he seemed to be trying to pique Sage by his strange bantering ways, while all the time he was so persevering in his free attentions to me that I saw Frank's face grow red, and a frown gather upon his forehead. Tom La.tchley saw it too, and as be found that his conduct annoyed both Sage and Frank be increased his attentions, and still kept on chatting about himself. How had he got on in Australia? Oh!' splendidly. He had had a good time at the gold diggings, and got enough there to buy and stock a sheep farm. "And now I'm as warm as some of your men about here, uncle' and I only want a wife to take back with me, and I shall be all right." 'Then you are not going to stay ?" said my uncle. " Stay ! what here? No, thanky ; I had enough of England when I was here. Other side oLthe wand, for me." He had the ,greater part of the conversation, and was still al king at one o'clock, when Sage and I rose, with aunt, to o to rest, leaving the gentlemen to finish their grog,-and wishin them "A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year ""for it was the first hour of the Christmas morning; but alas! it was to be neither merry nor happy, though we knew it not.

CHAPTER.—FALLING LEAVES. I was not surprised, when I was alone with Sage in her room, that she should burst into a hysterical fit of weep- ing; but she soon cheered up, wished me good night, and I left her bending over the little bedstead where her children

slept. It was not a happy Christmas day for us: Uncle was as jovial and genial as ever, but our unexpected visitor seemed to have come upon us like a blight. Sage was pale and excited, and Frank was so angry that he would hardly speak to me, and again and again when I met is eyes they were full of reproach; and in spite of all I could do short of being rude, I could not keep Tom Latchley from being ex- ceedingly attentive. "You are not married yet," he said, laughingly; "and I consider you fair game. All's fair in love or war.' It was a sad and a painful time. The days succeeded one another till a week had passed, and:then Frank had to go, which he did almost in anger; but Tom still stayed, and I was in such trouble that I did not know what to do. For a horrible suspicion had come upon me, and fight against it hard as I Would, I could not drive it away. A great change had come over Sage, and it seemed to me, though, so horrible, that I reproached myself for harbouring the idea, that my sister's affection had come back for her old lover; that he was trying all he could to win her from her duty as a wife and mother; and that I was being used as a blind to hide the real state of the case from my mint and uncle. As for John Berry, there was no need to try and tbrulinedt ihnimhiefowrifien;haisusdimitpalue,v one had hinted to him that she honest fashion he had the fondest hwea swfoaul ilidn gh aavwea A fortnight had passed, and the frost still lasted. people said that it was a glorious Christmas, but to me it was a time of the most intense mental pain. For I was alone. Frank sytrfurcoltmhhiminitio l down. believe, if it had been a man, seemed to have forsaken me, though he kept coming back to spend an evening, but only, so it seemed te me, to watch me with jealous eyes, to Tom Latchley's great delight, for he was doubly attentive when Tom was there. At last, from little things I saw, I felt convinced that Tom had gained, from old associations, an influence over Sage that she could not resist; and, to my horror, I was nearly certain that they had had a stolen interview. I prayed that John Berry would make up his mind to go, but he announced his intention of leaving his wife and children for another week, and then coming to fetch them back home. The news prostrated me almost, for in a quiet, resigned way, Sage said it would be best, and I saw Tom Latchley's eyes flash. - I could not speak to my uncle and stint; I dared not accuse my sister, for I mitt not sure, and hour after hour I was praying that I might have been deceived; but all the same I felt bound to act, and I deternained that I Would never leave Sage alone while Tom Latcbley was in the house. Mvplan was good, but I could not keep to it; and one day, as I was about to enter the dining-room, where I had left Sage alone for a few moments, I heard her say, in a piteous voice, "Oh, Tom, spare me! I cannot—l dare not I " "It is too late now," he said. "All is arranged. You must ! " I did not enter the room, but stood there trembling I heard my aunt go in by the farther door, and begin chattering to them both; but, with my blood seeming to run cold, I hurried up to my own room and threw myself on my knees to pray for strength and wisdom at this terrible time. If I told my uncle or my aunt, the consequences seemed to me terrible. If I spoke to Sage, I foresaw that she would deny all. I now determined what to do. I would attack my cousin himself, and insist upon his leaving the house at once, never to return; but on going dawn to put my plan into effect, I found that he was gone out, and he did not return. To my surprise, Sage seemed to have grown calmer now, and as the evening wore on she was almost cheerful as if a load was off her mind. Her equanimity almost disarmed me; and about eight o'clock, as we were sitting with my aunt and uncle, listening to the roaring of the wind, the precursor of a snow storm, I sat quite still as she rose and said that she wanted to go up and see if the children were asleep. she lit it, and left the room, while my Frank Romney's brains are in the right place, he'll stay at unTclaekisnaigdatocannsdliAh—" It will be a roarer to-night, and if home. IN here's Toni ?" "lie said he would go over to see Melton," said my aunt, as she bit through her thread. "And if his brains are in the right place too, he'll stay there for the night." Just then a curious wail made by the wind fell upon my ear, and it was as though I had received a stab, for I knew I what it was caused by: the side door had been softly opened and closed. Then for a moment or two I sat there. as if turned to stone, feeling sure that Sage had opened hat door, and was gone.

trouble. The old folks will never hear a word from me." "But where are you going?" I panted, as a terrible sus- picion shot through my brain. "Tom Latchley is waiting for some one to come, and it's a pity he should be diappointed," he cried, and he rushed off through the howling storm.

CHAPTER Ia—COVERED BY THE SNOW. How I managed to get Sage in and up to her own room I hardly know, but I did contrive it unheard, and contrived to hide all trace of our snowy cloaks and shoes before I called up my aunt to my help; for Sage. as soon as she reached the bedroom threw herself upon her knees by her sleeping children, moaning and sobbing inco- herently, and going from one terrible hysterical fit into another. I had gone down to the dining-room at last to tell my uncle that she was a little better, to find the old man buttoned up, and, with the old horn lanthorn lit upon the table, ready to face the storm and walk six miles to fetch the doctor, when there was a sharp knocking, and John Berry arriVed. -- "I scarce had thought I'd come," he said; "but I oever thought the mare would have pulled me through. It's an awful night. I'll—My darling ill rhe cried, as we told him; "there, thank the Lord I did come." "No, no," I said; "don't go to her now," as I saw him throw off his heavy coat and cap. "Nay, but I will," he said; and I followed him up, to see Sage start at the voice, creep from the bed, and throw herself sobbing in his arms. "Jack, Jack," she cried; "take me—hold me, husband dear. lam half-mad." I left him Soothing her as she clung lovingly to his breast in an agony of remorse, and then crept down to find the outer door open, my aunt upon her knees by a chair, and Frank Romney there, coyered with snow and looking ghastly pale, while my uncle was forcing something hot to drink into his hand. Frank turned away from me as I entered, but my uncle spoke out—" She must know it, Frank, my lad, and she's as brave a girl as ever stepped. Rue' my child, there's horrible news. Frank has found Cousin Tom frozen in the snow." For a moment or two the room seemed to swim round me, but I heard my uncle give orders for the big mare to be put to the light cart, and I knew it was to fetch Toni home. Then I seemed to recover, and I crossed to Frank, and, re- gardless of his shrinking from me, I caught his wrist. "You have killed him ?" I whispered. "So help me God, no," he said, looking me full in the eyes. "I found him where I knew he was going to wait, and tried to carry him here, but I was too late." There was such an agonised, piteous look in his face, that I stooped and kissed his hand. The next moment he and my uncle were gone, while my aunt and I sat waiting for the terrible finish of that awful night. For Frank was right. Tom Latchley was dead—frozen to death on that, the coldest night of the century, while my poor heart felt frozen too. But there are other thaws besides those that melt the cruel ice and snow; and my heart was thawed by tears, by my sister's and my own, and a happier time seemed close at hand. For the next morning Frank came to me humbly,.and when I turned from him he begged me to hear him and forget his jealous folly, as he said be knew all now. I was hot and indignant the moment before, but I turned pale now, as I trembled for my sister's fame. "You know all, Frank," I said, hoarsely. "Yes, Rue," he whispered. "This letter was in the dead man's breast—her letter to him." I made a dash to snatch it from him, and he placed it in my hand. " Rue," he said, "I know your sister's secret, and I place a price upon my silence." "A price," I cried. "Oh, Frank Romney, you would not be such a coward as to betray her." He looked at me for a few moments, and then said: "My price for silence is—your forgiveness for my mad folly. Oh, Rue, Rue, my darling, teach me to be more trustful, for I love you with all my heart." Need I say that I treated him as be asked, and I have never repented it, and I never shall. For so truly was the secret kept that Sage never even suspected that my dear husband knew her trouble--one which was buried in both our hearts.

Sir,—Will you kindly afford me space to suggest to the promoters of the above object, that care should be exercised in ascertaining the mind of the greatest number as to the form it should take, lam convinced that many, with us, would wish a graceful and substantial tribute presented to the bereaved wife and little one, in preference to the one mooted, and I believe in so doing we shall bett honour his loved I memory, copying his life end exemplifying his teaching. Imagining the drain upon a ministerial stipend by such a long and peculiarly expensive illness, we would also strongly urge the knowledge of this proposal being widely spread. firmly believing there are many in former circuits and out- side the Methodist Church, who would gratefully appreciate the privilege of subscribing their names in memory of a life and ministry of such fragrance. Thanking you in I anticipation for this insertion, I am, A SUBSCRIBER.

div.p: A SEASONABLE SUGGESTION.

—a.. Sir,—With Christmas comes that awakened sense of care i for others which shows itself in many acts of neighbourly kindness. We especially remember the poor, the widow, I the sick, the homeless, the orphan. We seek to send cons- fort to every home and food to all in need, and there are at I this time so many thousands of our fellow creatures to whom actual hunger is familiar, that I trust you will per- ' mit me to make a suggestion to your readers on their be- half. It is just this, that the gifts now devoted to feeding the poor shall be this Christmas so bestowed in the choice of food, and in its preparation, as to feed at least twice as many hungry people as under the methods commonly adopted. How can this be done? I may better illustrate from an actual occurrence. Last Chrietanaenearly 500 children were fed with good soup and plum pudding at the Association Hall, Manchester, and the cost for food only was less than 21d. per child. I mention this fact that I may the better plead for just that little method in the bounty which flows at Christmas time, which will make it possible to spread its blessings ever so much wider an area, that, if possible, on next Christmay Day we may not have one, hungry child amongst us, and that, moreover, we shall have the addi- tional consciousness that in conferring this benefif _upon. them we have not been the means of destroying the life of any innocent creature which at this time of peace and good will to all God's creatures may surely claim to make itself felt among us. Much poverty, and -distrese is endured every winter. The calls on our philanthropy are excessive, and .matntyo charitablet with- out flesh meat, and that by the same diet adults may be eammpptlyy- a nldt well i s ort- import- ant in full health and strength. CHAPTER V.—Max-HIDDEN. The terrible nightmare-like feeling passed off as quickly as it had come on; and how, I hardly know now, I left the room, went straight to the side door, catching down my bat and cloak from the pegs, and passed out into the bitter night. The wind nearly snatched the cloak from me as I flung it on, and then ran along the path towards the lane, for there were fresh footprints in the newly-fallen snow ; and so quickly did I run that at the end of ten minutes I was within sight of a dark figure hurrying on before me with bended head, and the driving snow rapidly making it invisible as it hurried on. The storm was rapidly increas- ing, and the wind and drifting snow confused me; but I ran on now, and with a dispairing cry flung my arms round the figure, crying—" Sage, sister! Where are you going? Oh, for heaven's sake, stop !" "Rue!" she cried, hoarsely, and she struggled to free herself; but I clung to her tightly, and she stumbled, slip- ping on the hard ground beneath the snow, coming to her knees. I knelt beside her upon mine, and, clasping her waist, I sobbed—" Yes, yes, upon your knees, Sage—sister, pray, pray, with me—for strength. God hear our cry, and save my sister from this sin !" For a few mements, as she heard my passionate cry, she knelt there trembling, but she began to struggle again. "Don't stop me. It is too late now. I cannot help it, Bus; I must go." "You shall not go," I cried; "I know all. He has tempted you to do this wrong, and you are mad; but think, Sage—for God's sake, think. It will break John's heart." "Oh, hush, hush !" she cried, with a sbiver. "Hush, bush! I must go now !" •' You shall not," I cried ; "I will never leave you. Sage, dear, there are two little children lying there in their bed, silently calling you to come to them and avoid this sin. Sister—mother—wife, will you leave them for that cruel, reckless man?" cm, hush she cried, struggling with me fiercely. "You do not know, Rue. You cannot tell. He's waiting for me, and I must—l will go." "Never while I have breath," I panted, and then I uttered a shriek of affright. "Prank !" I said. "You here?" "Yes." he said, hoarsely, "I am here, false girl, and it is well for you that I am. -Don't struggle with her, Mrs. Berry. I have her safe. I know all, perhaps, more than " You know all," I cried. "Yea, all," he said mockingly. " How Torn Latchley is waiting for you to take you to the Mellen fly. Do you think that I'm blind? You played with me, but, do you think I'll let you throw yourself away like this? All's over between us now, but you shall not go off with him." "Frank !" I panted, as he forced me 'back before him, with Sage clinging to my arm. "Do they know at home ?" "No, but I'll tell them in a quarter of an hour's time." "No, no, Frank; dear Frank, for pity's sake no," I whispered, and I trembled with fear as I saw the mistake he had made. "I'll go down upon any knees to you here if you'll only be silent." "Why should I be silent ?" he cried, savagely. "Because you are too manly to expose a weak woman to shame." Ile caught me so fiercely by the arm that the bruise was there for weeks, as he cried— "Will you swear hero by heaven that you will not go off with that scoundrel if I hold my tongue?" " Yes," I said, eagerly. "I swear it. Ftank, dear Frank, I swear I will not go," and I tried to catch his hand. "Don't touch me, woman," he cried fiercely; and then he followed us in silence, while I clung to Sage's arm as she trembled and sobbed, and kept on mourning to herself till we reached the side door." "Now .go in," he said sternly. "I'm not good enough for you, Rue Hurst; but Tom Latchley is not. I'm too true a man, though, as you say, to trample on a woman in her
