div.p: moved an amendment to the effect that the consideration of the matter be adjourned to the 19th January, 1892. In reply to Mr. C. Houghton, Mr. GEORGE MOSS stated that in calculating the cost per annum of the Litearry Institute, an allowance had been made for a payment to the librarian. Mr. Frith had, how- ever, over-estimated the expenses. They were not more than £6O per annum. He (Mr. Moss) could show that a public reading-room could be maintained at not exceeding .£BO per year, which would leave something like MO to be expended every year in books, which was a considerable sum for a town like Runcorn. Mr. HA/miNsoN supported the resolution, because he believed it voas for the benefit of the town. He alluded to to the careers of the various institutions the town had had in the past, which had been unsuccessful because the working- classes had not been properly considered. A free library would meet their wishes, and the man who objected to pay the trifling amount of the cost was a mean man. Mr. J. W. LIGHTBURN said there seemed to be some little mist, which wanted dispersing, as to whether the library would be a free lending library or not. Dr. McDouoaLL said it was intended to be a free lending library. The proposal at first suggested was that there should be a lending library, to be opened two nights in the week. (Hear, hear.) Those who had advanced arguments against the scheme that evening had been unfortunate in their choice of words, and had stated that they could have a library if they wished, but they thought it would be a doubtful success. Now he maintainea that it would be a great success. He had not many days ago suggested that a reading-room should afterwards be added which should be self-supporting, say by 150 members, at 2s. 6d. each. He might say it at once that he could not advocate a daily library in Runcorn. It would not be possible to get the sinews of war, but what he maintained was that they could get a good library at a small cost, and could add to it 200 or 300 volumes every year. Mr. LiarrrnunN said no one would dispute the desira- bility of a free library, because beyond a certain period of life intellectual enjoyment was the only amusement left to them, but as so much doubt existed he thought if a com- mittee were appointed to look into the matter it would be an advantage, lie therefore seconded the motion for the adjournment. (Cheers.) • After some further discussion, Mr. LIGHTBURN said that on second thoughts he would withdraw from veconding Mr. Armstrong's motion, and propose an amendment to the effect that a committee consisting of the Chairman, Mr. Shaw, Dr. McDougall, Mr. Simpson, and Mr. G. S. Hazle- hurst be appointed to consider the matter, and report to a future meeting. Mr. ARMSTRONG : I will withdraw my motion and second

ApopTio 0F THE FREE LIBRA.RILS ACT AT RUNCORN. ten Monday evening, a large meeting of ratepayers, called I by Dr. Steele, chairman of the Board if Commissioners, in reply to a requisition, was held in Bethesda Congregational schoolroorn,Runcorn, for the purpose of considering the desir- ability of adopting the Free Libraries Act, 1355. Amongst those present, were the Revs. Canon Barclay, W. Preston, M.A., (Holy Trinity), J. D. Thomas, John Nowell, Drs. McDougall and Steele, Messrs. W. J. Shore, Benjamin E. Hough, J. 0. Jackson, W. Handley, Kniveton, E. 'nelson, S. C. Beckett, F. A. Lake, J. Jannion, J. Curzon, W. Tickle, T. Stringfellow, H. Sefton, G. Weedall, J. Armstrong, E. Austin, Ge Surnraerfield, L. Woodward, T. Thompson, J. Lunt, R. Whitby, T. Handley, J. Williame, P. Briseoe, R. Wright, J. J. Speakman, J. K. Digges, S. Goldsmith, J. I McQuinn, J. Northing, J. Meredith, R. Forrester, H. Cole- burn, J. Joynson, J. Simpson, R. Shaw, S. Hosworth, J. Hit- chen, D. Hughes, W. B. Brimelow, F. Adams, J. W. Light born, J. Wilson, T. Turner, W. Hankinson, F. Fairhurst, W. Dobson, G. S. Hazlehurst, A. Derbyshire, C. Johnson, T. Cooke, T. Harris, W. Mellor, T. H. Annett, P. Speakman,aC Houghton, S. Worrell, W. Brown, J. Whinyates, R. Killcross, T. Norman, D. Worthington, John GalsilJamlty, Frith, J. Le Couteur, D. Bisbrown, W. Cliff, G. Moss, R. Collier, T. Houghton, M. Barker, IW„Jvliisßoonge Roger- son, W. Sutton, H Hankinson, C. Duttotn, J. J. Craig, S. Pope, T. Simister, S. Ravenscrof take the chair. Hazlehurst, J. Bridgewater, and Thomas Sh Dr. lalcDoroau. moved that Dr Steele. a saying that the gentle- Mr.ROBERT SHAW at once objecte , t f L• • take the chair by enr ue o his post- man referred to would uthority. tion as chairman of the local a 1 'ned that Dr. Steele much preferred Dr. MCDOUGALL exp 3,1 '°TrOCPl,°,l.litt, Jos. Mr. G. S. All ZLEHURST seconded the proposition, which to have the matter submitted to the meeting. was carried unanimously. Mr. WiLmiarg BnormEs, secretary to the Commissioners, then read the notice convening the meeting. The Cuasetetele, without expressing any opinion on the matter before the meeting, said he should be glad to receive any resolution. Dr. McDornaLL, who was received with loud applause, moved "That the Public Libraries Act of 1355 be adopted fcr the district of Runcorn comprised within the limits of the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852, of the county of Chester, in pursuance of the Acts of Parliament in that behalf." He had very little to add to what he had already stated in another place about the propriety and importance of adopting the Public Libraries Act for the benefit of the people of Runcorn. He did not think that even the most Selfish or the most fastidious individual would deny that the Acts had been a great boon in towns where they had already been adopted, and he believed that in no case had the step been regretted. The speaker next quoted from a pamphlet by Mr. Mullens, Chief Librarian, at Birmingham, showing the great hunger which was manifested for books at the c pen- iag of the Free Library in that town, notpnly by the inhabi- tants of the borough, but by men and women coming from mazy miles round—from West Bromwich, Tipton, Willen- hall, and even Wolverhampton. In recommending the adoption of the act in Runcorn, he (Dr. McDougall), firmly believed that if they did so they would not be taking any leap in the dark—(bear, hear)—but a step in the right direc- tion. The great object of the Act was to provide good and useful books to be read at home by the people to promote habits of thrift, frugality, and temperance in the family circle ; in short, to encourage the man to become a better mechanic, and the mechanic a better man. (Cheers.) With respect to the rate, which seemed to be the ques- tion disturbing the minds of many people, the Acts specially provided that in no one year should they charge more, then a penny in the pound. Therefore every one who was rated to the extent of £5 per year would only be called upon to pay fivepence, and to individual owners of works who might be rated at say, £1,200, they would exactly have to pay something like 15 per annum for the immense advantage derived from the possession of a Free Public Library. (Cheers.) In his humble opinion, the adoption or rejection of the Act marked a crisis in the intellectual growth of the town, and he ventured to say that ha would be an unwise and an unjust man who woul-cl step in to oppose public opinion. He read a letter he had received from one of Runcorn's truest and noblest sons, which was as follows Dear Mr. McDougall,-1 am sorry I cannot be present at the meeting about the Free Library movement. I would have attended the ratepayers' meeting on Monday evening, but I have to be present at another meeting to be held at the same time. Ido hope the Act will be adopted. I believe it would be the best public movement that has been made in Runcorn for a long time past. Having been con- cerned in the formation of the Library at the Institute, I feel very much interested about the disposal of the books, and I think it would be a great pity for the town to lose the chance of having such a lot of books as a nucleus for a Free My unfortunate deafness renders it impossible for _should often very much like to in me to take .the ,e2f, the matters for promoting the wellar4• Runcorn people ; 'f and on this account I feel as if I could not do anY Soo I were to attend these meetings. Ido hope the owners who have to pay the rates will consider the good of the rest of the population, and will not refuse to pay the small addition to the rates which the adoption of the Act will involve. In the event of the Act being adopted, I shall be glad to give gun towerde giving the thing a good start. Believe me, yours sincerely, Simpson." (Loud applause.) The speaker said he had to urge thei ~ te-, give this movement their hearty support, as it would undoubtedly tend to the elevation of the working classes, who formed such a great proportion of the population of Runcorn •, and after all, there was a depth of meaning in that couplet of Scotland's noblest bard, in his Cotter's Saturday Night— " Prile es and lords are but the breath of kings. An honest man's the noblest work of God'" (Loud applause.) Mr. DANIEL WORTHINGTON, in seconding the motion, said they lived in the freest country under Heaven, and the very essence of their liberty lay in the fact that a com- munity was able to make its own laws and to govern itself. (Cheers.) The Imperial Legislature had passed a measure whereby they might have a Free Public Library under cer- tain conditions. One of those conditions was that the matter was optional, and thus they had real self-government. They were told that Runcorn was not a literary town, but it ap- peared to him that the best way of making it so was to adopt the Act, so that their young men could cultivate a taste for literature. There were many reasons why a free public library should be established. The cost would not be anything of so serious a nature that any workingman needed to fear it. The members of this class now obtained their intelligence under great difficulties. They had not the same chance as 'people of large towns, as in Liverpool and in Warrington, for instance. In fact they were handicapped. (Cheers.) The working-classes needed greater facilities if they would hasie them intelligent, and the present movement deserved to be crowned with success. He thought it was the greatest boon they could possibly have. Their children were grow- ing up with all the advantages of education, and if they would make them better men and possibly better Chaistians give them the means in the shape of a free public library. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT SHAW was sure no one would charge him with standing in the way of anything whicn could be for the good of the young people of Runcorn—(hear,hear)—because since he had been in the town he had done some little for them. did not care for the distinction that had been made between them and workingmen. He considered they were all workingmen' and they met there as ratepayers, whatever their other distinctions might be. The object of that meeting was to provide a public library, more especially for the young people, because they, perhaps, had most time to devote to gaining that information he was sure they were all anxious they should have. There were one or two reasons why it was might not be feaslble which had not been touched upon. They could well understand that, in a town like Birmingham, with a population of something like 500.000. a free library most certainly was a boon, and they would have fends for the replenishing ef that library when required which it was impossible th ,y could have in a town like Runcorn. They were told that the mate they could levy would secure an income of £l5O per annum. They knew that public institutions were not worked fr flotilla", and they might depend upon it that it would cost then as much for the maintenance of the library as it would for a town containing something like 80.000 or '70,000 people. Ile edenlated that it would take all they could raise to provide a place in which to place their beets, and leave them—w lice? A library that would not be worth anything to the people of Rancorn, be- cause they had no funds to replenish it with new hooks. It was usual to spend £2OO Cr £:100 in books alone. They must take into consideration whetipr they could have a library worth the trouble, or whether they would wait until the town was lar;er, or entll they could get donations. The young men of th'e town Ind now &vial facilities for an- ti-airing inform ttion as they would have were they to adopt the Libraries Act. ( Hear. hear.) They had now at the Literary !milted, a library where any young man for about one penny or twopence per week, could read the books, and no young man need be deb irred by that trifling cost. His contention was that they were not in a position to supply the library with new books from tine to tdme. In conclusion, the speaker referred to the case of St. Helene, where he alleged that linretre4a 0- pornds a year were being spent in the purchase of books. Mr. J. It FRITH was surprised at the remarks made by Mr. Shaw against the: movement. (Hear, hear). They all knew that Mr. Shaw had done something since he had been in Ituncornt - the improvement or endeavouring, to improve the ri -Mg generation. Ile, however, always considered that half a loaf was better than no bread. (Cheers). Mr. Shaw bee, ::old them that because they could not have a good library at once they should not proceed with the movement at all. Were they to make no effort in this matter until they bad a library worth £1,000? Now, he (Mr. Frith) Lappened. to know the cost per annum at some of their in- I stitutions. It appeared that, for the supply of papers and general maintenance, the cost of an institution WAS about £9O per ear. The library rate would produce about £l6O per year, which would leave a considerable balance, so that Do twenty years they might purchase something like £1,400 worth of books, even if their rateable value did not increase a halfpenny. Was not that something to seek after? If they could get other assistance similar to that offered by Mr. Elmpfmn—(zheers)—then they might hope soon to have a voluble institution. He heartily supported the motion. Mr. ARMSTRONG, of Brunswick-street, opposed the motion. In doing so he traced the history of the Workingmen's Club I end the Literary Institute, neither of which had been suc- Cestsful. Many of them had books; which It would take them more than ten years to read, and he could not see the aavantage in now establishing a free public library. He

that. Mr. John SIMPSON, who had entered the room during the discussion, said he did not expect to be able to attend that meeting, and when he did come he did not intend to say anything on the subject. It was, however, one deeply interesting to him. He had lived in Runcorn for a great number of years; in fag he was born there, and though he left it when he was a very little boy, he came back in 1828. During that time he had known a succession of at least six literary or mechanics institutes. In the case of the first estaolished, he remembered that Mr. John Thompson took the chair,and Mr. Egerton Smith, the proprietor of the Liver- pool Mercury, attended the inaugural meeting, which was a crowded one. The institution went on very successfully for a short time, but gradually the subscriptions dropped off, until it had to be closed. A person bought the fittings, and carried on a reading room a period, but that also had to be closed. A Church Institute was then started—indeed he was not sure if there was not another society started before the birth of that—but it gradually died out, and a Literary Insti- tute rose upon its ashes. This went on for some time, and he recollected that during its existence the Rev. Cannon Bar- clay, Mr. Salkeld, and other gentlemen acted as secretaries. They did all they could to keep it a going, bule in course of time it also became defunct. It really seemed as if where institutions of this kind depended upon subscriptions, there was not sufficient interest taken in them to keep them go- ing. At another time, when Mr. Ripon was agent to the Biidgewater Navigation Co., another society was commenced, and the promoters of it had the use of the Town Hall for a reading room. The movement was started with a large num- ber of subscribers and great spirit was thrown into the under- taking. They gradually came to have such small meetings that they took a little room in High-street, which was now part of Mr. Lea's shop; and in course of time this undertaking also died. He believed that about the year 1859, Mr. Philip Whiteway, junr., was the means of establishing a Free Library. A meeting was called and very great interest was •^.ken in the matter. Indeed Mr. Johnson, Mr. Whiteway, and all the principal gentlemen of the town, took an energetic part in the project. A number of books were got together and a trust deed was drawn up, but, unfortunately, it was never executed, so that no one had ever been in legal possession of the books. However, after travelling about and being in various places in the town, they found a lodgment at the Literary Institute, the committee of which took charge of them, and lent them to the subscribers. He presumed that if the in- stitute was closed the committee would want to dispose of books; but he thought it would cause them some per- plexity how -tte..y were to do so. If they adopted the Act I they would have a moderate- library to start with, as the [committee of the Literary Institute, +a -understood, were quite prepare 4 to transfer the books. Every one who con- sidered the welfare of the town must admit that something was required to be done. (Cheers.) The cost was trifling and the benefits incalculable, and no doubt to start the move- ment fairly subscriptions from the public would be forth- coming. They had not any reason to complain of high rates in Runcorn at the present time. He believed the Commis- sioners wanted to keep the rates down, and for many years ta come he did not believe that the library rate need be more than a farthing or a halfpenny in the pound. Very likely, besides subscriptions they would receive presents of books. He knew at the present time of numbers of young men in Runcorn who required books and did not know where to get them. The Literary Institute was closing, and the con- tinuatioe of the Young 'Men's Christian Association was doubtful, and he did not know what would become of many of the young men. It would be a pity if the people of Run- corn followed the bad example of Widnes. He did not think they would. (Cheers.) He sometimes 'considered they were in advance of Widnes. Then let them show them- selves better, in one respect at least. The example of Widnes in rejecting the Libraries' Act they ought not to follow, and he most sincerely hoped they would not. (Cheers.) The Rev. Wiittest Puns-role supported the resolution in an eloquent speech. He said he had had in his mind for the past two or three years whether they could not procure a freelibrary and a free reading-room, which, he thought, ought to be associated with it. Evidently Mr. Armstrong wanted to postpone that meeting to 1892, but, perhaps, he meant 1992, or to the Greek Kalends. (Laughter.) He did not see any reason why the meeting should be adjourned at all. Many men had risen from humble positions to eminence through the development of the brain-power they had given to them. But in Runcorn, although many of their young men might have the brain-power, they had not the privilege of improving themselves. Who knew but if that power re- c dyed proper attention that many an invention and wonder- ful enterprise might spring from some of them at Runcorn. (Applause.) Mr. G. S. HaztErtrusr, who was received with applause, asked whether it was not better that they should pay five- pence or tenpence per year for something that would go on permanently than they should have a number of different institutions waxing and waning, and yet not have a settled institution upon which the town could depend? He thought they should look at the question on the ground of public spirit rather than the mercenary consideration of the cost. There was not a man there who would feel the cost. He would give £5 towards the movement—(cheers)—but he entirely withdrew that offer if they did not pass the Act I that evening. (Laughter and cheers.) , Mr. JAMES Cuneox briefly dwelt upon the advantages of a free library. A RATEPAYER explained that the amendment could not I be put, as there was no provision in the Act of Parliament which provided for an adjournment. If there was an adjournment at all it must be for 12 months. Mr. Coleburn and Mr. Charles Houeliton rose to speak, but the audience declined to listen to any further oratory. The resolution as to adoptime the Act was then put, and there voted for it 101, and about half a dozen against. , The result was received with loud cheering and waving of hats. The CnetrimaN then formally declared the motion for adopting the Act carried ; and, after a vote of thanks to Dr. Steele, the proceedings terminated amidst much excitement.

I also wish to say that I consider it is very disrespectful to the Bench that the defendant is not here.—The Chairman : Of course, the case cannot be heard now—Complainant: He had the coolness to come into my house at twelve o'clock at night. —Mr. Bartlett said Mr. Code was taken to defendant's, and was there for a perfectly legitimate purpose. Having again detailed how it was that defendant got to Runcorn, the speaker proceeded to say that he, first of all, went to a cab proprietor named Peck, as he wanted a conveyance to take him to Weston Point. Mr. Peck had no horses "sharpened," , but took him to Mr. Yarwood's. He sat in the house until Mr. Yarwood should come downstairs, and the two females who were in the house gave him some bread and mirk, as he could get nothing at the hotels, owing to the late hour. While this was being done Mr. Yarwood came downstairs, and what happened he would not relate until the case was heard at a future date. The defendant had not entered his house and home to destroy the felicity and happiness of his domestic life, about which Mr. Yarwood had spoken.—Mr. Yarwood : Why, he told us that be had arrived from London, by train, within twenty minutes of the time be came to our house, and that the station master had brought him down to my place. If he attends here any morning at eleven o'clock, there is always a magistrate pre- sent to grant summonses at that time, and the matter can then be dealt with.—The proceedings in the case then ter- minated. A DISPUTE AS TO SUPPORTING AN AGED FATHER.— George Linaker and Richard Linaker, of Frodsham, were summoned to show cause why they should not contribute to the support of their father, who is an old man, and charge- able to the common fund of the Runcorn Union.—Mr. Houghton, the collector, said the father had been chargeable for many years, and the defendant Richard had been so neg- lectful in making his payments, that the Guardians had ordered him to b summoned. The other brother was em- ployed by Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co., of Widnes, and the Guardians asked that he should pay Is. 6d. per week as his share of the maintenance of 3s. 61. per week which was Riven to the father. This defendant pulled a woe begone face, and said that though he was earning about 305. per week, he could not afford to pay the amount, "as it was necessary he should look to the future."—The Chairman said the Bench had decided to call upon the defendant George to "look "to the present as well as the future, and do something to help his parent in his old age. He would have to pay is. 6d. and his other brother is. per week.—The costs in George's case were 14s. 6d., and in Richard's 10s. 6d.--Samuel Knight was summoned on a similar charge in the case of his aged father.—lt was stated that defendant received 3135. per week, and was working for Messrs. Timmins.—He was ordered to pay 25. weekly, and us. 61. costs. ASSAULTING A POLICE OrricEn. Henry Langley and David Hughes, two powerfully-built men, were charged with assaulting P.C. Hibbert. The officer said that on Saturday night, about a quarter past twelve, he was in Devonshire-square, when Longley ran against him, and hurt his shoulder. He asked him what be was about, when Langley enquired, in terms not distinguished by politeness, as to who he might be, and seized him. Hughes also melted at him and gave him a blow. He had a severe struggle with them, and only got them to the police station with the assistance of Mr. Cliffe.—Defendants were each fined 205. and costs 6s. 11d. (which included 2s. 6d. for Mr. Cliffs), or, in default, ordered to be sent to gaol one month. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. Charles Reynolds (chairman) and C. W. Hazlehurst. _

THE HAWKER'S QUESTION BEFORE THE COURT.—Mr Lake (soliciter), said he bad an application to make under the Pedlars' Act. By that measure, the granting of a cer- tificate was vested in the chief officer of the police in the place, and, in case of his refusal, there was an appeal frdm him to the magistrates. On the Bth met, Ralph Gibson, of Pool-lane, applied to Superintendent Williamson for a cer• tificate, which was refused, and he then gave notice to that officer that he should apply to the local Bench on the matter. Perhaps the simplest course would be for the Superinten- dent to acknowledge the receipt of the application, and state the reasons of his objections to granting it.—Superintendent Williamson observed that he was quite willing to admit the receipt of the notice, and he would state his grounds for re- fusing the certificate. He believed the applicant was a very respectable man, carrying on business as a greengrocer. Gibson had applied on two or three occasions for the cer- tificate, as several other people had. He refused to grant it on the ground that Gibson, when he made the application, told him he intended to sell greengrocery. On hearing this he said to him "Then if you are, you do not require a ped- lar's certificate." He believed their worships would agree with him that unless he was convinced that Gibson made the application in good faith that he was going to pursue tlfe trade of a pedlar, he was perfectly justified—and, indeed, could do no other—than refuse his application.—Mr. Lake: Then I take it that your objection is because he is selling provisions ?—Yes.—Mr. Lake said the question was whether a man whe sold provisions, or mainly provisions wee entitled to have a certificate. The Act defining a pedlar stated no- thing about what he sold, but simply mentioned a person travelling from house to house or from town to town on foot, selling commodities. The 23rd section stated that nothing in the Act should render it necessary for a certificate to be obtained by the following persons as such: commercial tra- vellers, fish, fruit, or vegetable dealers, or persons exposing goods for sale in a market; and to compel them to take out a certificate in all cases would virtually be a tax on food, which was against the general good. He called attention to sec. 6, which provided that for the purposes of the Markets and Fairs Clauses Act, a certificate under the Pedlar's Act should have the same effect as a hawker's license. Mr. Lake quoted the case of Howard v. Lupton, where a man had taken out a pedlar's certificate although he was not selling goods which absolutely required one. The authorities pro- secuted him for doing so, and they maintained that a ped- lar's certificate was not necessary, and that the defendant was not therefore protected by it. The case was taken on appeal to the Queens Bench, and it was there decided that 1 a man selling provisions was exempt from the penalties im- posed by the Markets and Fairs Clauses Act. He submitted that for the purpose of the Act he was entitled to a certificate The question came before the Bench more for direction than anything else.—The Chairman said he supposed the prose- cution arose out of the question as to the market bye-laws which had been raised in the town.—Mr. Lake: Yes.—The applicant was then called by Mr. Lake to prove having given the notice to Superiutendent Williamson. He re- marked that he intended to sell pins and hardware.—Mr. Lake: But you are going to cell vegetables, are you not ? Applicant : Yes, or hardware. The (..Thairmen : But vegetables are not hard•ware.—Mr. Lake: But if selling pins, staylaces or hardware will con- stitute him a pedlar we are perfectly willing to sell therm—Superintendent Williamson: That is original, at any rate.—Mr. Lake: We claim to be original. (Laughter.) We are perfectly agreed to sellhardw are if we can get a certificate. But, indepern' ently of that, we are entitled to a certificate to sell provisions.—The Chairman said the Bench thought Superintendent Williamson had acted rightly in refusing the certificate unless it was positively shown to him that the applicant intended, in good faith, to carry on the trade of a pedlar. As defendant had not shown the Superintendent this, Mr. Williamson was quite justified in refusing to grant the certificate.—Mr. Lake (to the Chiarman): I suppose you will have no objection to granting a Case P—The Chair- man: No; but defendant is evidently a grocer, and not a pedlar. THEFT EY AN a; Withington, aged 66, was charged with having, on the 17th inst., stolen one sovueign and a chair, the property of Mr. James Douglass, contractor, 14, Lord-street, In consequence of the illness of prosecutor's wife, the prisoner had been working at his house since the 13th inst. Ho left her there on Saturday morning, when he went to Widnes. At that time he had a sovereign in a pocket of his trousers, which were hanging behind the bedroom door. At about eight o'clock the same night, he went to put on the trousers, and found the sovereign gone. No one had-been in the room where the garment was during the day, but the prisoner would have access to it. He went out, and on returning at ten o'clock, found she had gone out. He searched for her, and found her in a house in St. John's-street. He asked her where the shawl was which his wife had lent her, but she was too far gone in liquor to make any satisfactory reply. In her apron she bad a bundle, in which was the chair cushion produced, which.: belonged to him, and bad been seen safe on the rocking chair in the kitchen on the evening of the robbery. —Elizabeth Ackers. servant to Mr. Douglass, proved that the prisoner gave her a sovereign to get changed, and she took it to the South Bank Hotel for that purpose.—P.C. Baker apprehended the woman, who acknowledged having taken the shawl, but denied knowing anything of the I cushion. She ridiculed the idea of stealing the sovereign, I as she had never seen such a coin for 16 years.—The Chair- man said that if prisoner had been younger, she would have been more severely dealt with. She would be sent to gaol • 114 days, without hard labour.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY DECEMBER 24, 1881. WARRINGTON SAYINGS BANK. ANNUAL MEETING. The annual general meeting of the trustees and managers of the Warrington Savings Bank was held on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), chairman of the trustees. There were also present—Messrs. W. Long (vice-chairman), Joseph Davies, F. Monks, truss tees; Rev. J. Yonge, S. M. Webster, J. Smethurst, S. Lees, W. Owen, junr., Thomas Whittle, D. W. Finney, J. White, T. Jolley, H. N. Houghton, J. Woolfall, managers; and J. E. Davies, actuary. The statement of the accounts having been read, The MAYOR moved that the statement of the accounts, prepared by the actuary and examined by the accountant, be approved, and one copy to be transmitted to the National Debt Commissioners, and the duplicate be pub- licly affixed in the Savings Bank. His worship said they would observe frorn the report that the bank as usual ap- peered in a flourishing condition. But he would like to ' call attention to the usefulness of the bank. During the past year there had been 14,000 transactions, and, out of a total of 8 780 accounts, there were 3,811 accounts with bal- ances under £.5. That was a very large proportion, but it was these depositors the Committee of Management wished to encourage; and they hoped parents would encourage their children to go to the bank with their savings. It was not, perhaps, generally known that a child seven years of years of age could deposit money in the bank, but such was the case. Masters and mistresses would also do well to ad- vise their servante to deposit part of their wages there, and save up for a time of need. Those depositors who could rave more than was allowed by Government to be deposited in one account, could now deposit money for investment in Government stock. That was a new feature. It was done without any more trouble to the depositors than signing a request on the bank to purchase such stock. The corn- , mittee thought that the bank in the past year had done very I well; in fact, the accounts were continually increasing, as they had done for some years, and they hoped this would continue. Mr. LONG seconded the motion, and said so far as the committee knew the business of the bank was going on in a peifectly satisfactory manner. He thought they would agree that considering the times through which they had recently gone, the bank had held its own, as well perhaps as any bank whose report he had seen, The committee were very ansions to do all they could to increase the usefulness of the bank, and if the business of the bank warranted it, be had no doubt the trustees and managers would support them in giving even greater facilities to the public for depositing their money there. In larger towns savings banks were open every day, and if in Warrington the public arrived at that pitch of saving that they could carry on the business better by having the bank open daily he thought they would agree that the bank should be opened. Without say- ing anything disparaging of the Post Office Savings Bank, the committee thought this bank had a province of its own, and that it could very well do its work in addition to the Post Office Savings Bank. The motion was carried. The following report was read:—" The Committal of Management have pleasure in submitting to the annual meeting of the trustees and managers the general statement of the funds of the bank, for the year ending 20th Novem- ber, 1881. The total funds now amount to £273,208 103. 101 The National Debt Commissioners have to the credit of the bank on general account £271,593 183. Bd., and £7OO on Separate Surplus Fund Account, as certified in the Government receipt, a copy of which is annexed. The amount due to the depositors is £271,371 ss. 3d., being an increase of £2,934 15s. 9d., after adding the interest to their accounts. The surplus beyond the £7OO in the hands of the commissioners now amounts to £1,137 ss. 7d. The number of new accounts opened during the year is 797, and 672 accounts have been closed, showing an increase of 125. The total number of depositors, including Friendly and Charitable Accounts and Penny Banks, now is 8,780. Dur- ing the year there have been 14,252 transactions ; of these 8,192 deposits and 6,060 payments, showing 2,132 more deposits than payments. Only a few transactions have taken place in investments in Government Stock, but the committee anticipate that the depositors will take more ad- vantage of the opportunity given them under the powers of the new Act. Beyond their deposits to their ordinary accounts, which is limited (at present) to £3O in one year, depositors may now deposit money for investment in Government Stock up to £lOO a year, but not to exceed £3OO in the whole. The stock dividends are entered half-yearly to the credit of the holders in their Savings' Bank Deposit Accounts as they fall due. Monthly meetings have been held by the committee, and at each meeting the general accounts of the institution have been examined and found correct. The year's working is very satisfactory, consider- ing that trade in the town has only lately begun to improve again and our country neighbours stilt complain of "bad times ;" at the same time the committee would ask the trustees and managers, and also the depositors, to recom- mend those who have hitherto neglected the advantages offered at this institution, to make a beginning. No one will ever regret having become a Savings' Bank depositor. The thrifty man is the happy man, especially if his savings are in a safe place." Mr. T. JOLLEY proposed the following resolution:— "That the report of the Committee of Management is ap- proved, ank that this meeting acknowledges the valuable services rendered to the institution by the gentlemen acting on the committee during the past year, and tenders its best thanks to them." Mr. T. WHITTLE seconded the resolution. I The ACTUARY acknowledged the assistance the com- mittee had given him daring the year in the extra work they had had. The MANOR said the committee had been assisted very much by the advice and experience of Mr. Joseph Davies— (hear,)—who was formerly an officer of the bank, and their labours had been rendered much more easy than they other- wise would have been. The resolution was carried. Mr. JOHN WHITE moved that Mr. J. R. Pickmere be elected chairman and Mr. W. Long vice-chairman for the ensuing year, and said they had every reason to believe those gentlemen had fulfilled their duties in a very satis- factory manner, and he was sure they would join in re-elec- ting them. As to increasing the facilities of the bank, he said he supposed they all concurred. in the idea that there was nothing they could better for working men than induce them to save money. They did not want to compete with the Post Office authorities, but at the same time they were in a friendly spirit competing with them, and as the Post Office Savings Bank was open every day, he thought the time had arrived, especially as trade was improving, to open the bank every day. He noticed, although the number of deposits had increased, the amount of deposits was £3,000 less than it was last year. This he thought was disappoint- ing; because the working classes had got better wages dur- ing the last year than in the previous year, and he hoped next year there would be a better state of things. Mr. F. Moxits seconded the motion, and said he thought if the institution had an object it was to give greater facili- ties than other banks for the saving of small sums. He did not think they need fear coining into competition with the Post Office Savings Banks, and he hoped some steps would be taken to afford greater facilities to promote the object for which the bank existed. The motion having been carried, The MAYOR, in replying, assured them the committee did the best in their power to promote the interests of the bank, and promised that the committee should give the question of opening the bank every day their consideration. Mr. D. W. FINNEY moved that the following gentlemen be requested to form the Committee of Management for the ensuing year :—Trustees, chairman' vice-chairman, Messrs. S. Rigby, F. Monks, J. Davies, J. White; managers, John Harrison, J. Woolfall, Wm. Owen, jour., S. Lees, John Piers, J. Smethurst, J. H. Bowes, Rev. J. Yonge, and T. Jolley. He said it gave him an opportunity of saying how much he appreciated the good that was being done by the bank. Ile,thought that Savings Bank held a position second to none in the county. He was reading a report the other day, and in making some calculations from it, found the position of the Warrington Savings Banks stood almost at the head of the provincial towns this year, as regarded the number of deposits and the number of depositors. He thought it wee gratifying to them, and it must be gratifying to the people of Warrington, to know that the bank was so well managed, and doing such a good work. Much was said in these days about thrift amongst the poor. A great deal of money amongst the poor was very unnecessarily and use- lessly spent which often might be saved if proper facilities were put in the people's way to save. He wished the com- mittee could see their way not only to open the bank daily, but to gather in small some from the large works and front the schools. He hoped next year there would be not only eight penny savings banks ,connected with the Savings Bank,but 180—(hear, hear,)L-and was sure that WhS one way in which the bank could do good. Mr. 11. N. HOUGHTON seconded the motion, which was carried. Toe ACTUARY then read the names of the treasurer and paid ()Miters of the bank, with the names of the sureties and amount of bonds, which were approved, and the certi- ficate of approval was directed to be forwarded to the National Debt Office. A vote of thanks having been accorded to the Mayor for presiding, the meeting terminated. _
FRODSTIAM.

- BENNETT AND CAMERON'S ENTERTAINMENT. -- On Thursday evening, Messrs. Bennett and Cameron gave a literary and musical entertainment (from memory) in the Town Hall, Frodsham, when an excellent programme was capitally rendered, and elicited hearty applause. Mr. fiennett's elocutionary powers are of a high older, and his clearness of enunciation and dramatic power enlists the close attention of his audience, while his humorous sketches are irresistibly funny. Mr. William Cameron is a popular favourite, and fully sustained his accutomed role, which re- sulted in encores being the order of the evenieg, to which he responded in his usual cheerful spirit. Mr. G. L. Miller gave the pianoforte overture " Zampa," and selections from "Bohemian Girl," and proved himself an efficient accom- panist.

The inquest on M. Skinner, artist, of Glover Road Sheffield, was resumed on Thursday. The coroner, in sum- ming up, directed the attention of the jury to the supposi- tion that Kate Dover herself had put the arsenic into the food by which the deceased was poisoned, but he said if she did that with the intention of doing grievous bodily harm 1 their verdict might be reduced to manslaughter. After more than an hour's consultation the jury returned avert pt "Wilful murder against Kate paver!'
OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION: SANDRINGHAM.

As the pictorial feature of our large sheet Almanac for 1882, given to each purchaser of this day's Examiner, we give a carefully-executed engraving of the principal frontage to the hall of Sandring- ham, the country seat of the Prince, of Wales. We have called the edifice a hall, because the original building on this site was the hall or manor-house of Sandringham, and also because the present struc- tures are scarcely extensive enough in size or im- posing enough in style to be dignified with the name of palace; whilst the place has become some- thing more than the shooting-box it was at first intended to be. Sandringham is a beautiful and private royal home rather than a royal palace; and when sojourning there, the Prince of Wales lives the life of the English country gentleman more than that of the grand potentate, the scion of a Royal stock, the future King of England. Sandringham Hall and estate are situate upon the Northern coast of Norfolk, and near the Eastern shore of the great bay called the Wash, which pro- jects so far from the German Ocean into the heart of England. The Prince of Wales purchased it early in the year 1862, and has therefore held it now just twenty years. The former owner was Mr. Spencer Cowper. The nearest considerable town is King's Lynn, eight miles to the south-west. The estate was well stocked with all kinds of game, excepting deer, at the time of its sale; and in the winter season wild fowl are abundant. Thus the first idea of the Prince in buying Sandringham was to secure plentiful sport. There is not much to record respecting the history of this secluded Norfolk Manor before it became the house of Royalty. The hamlet itself is so obscure that it is not even named in many dic- tionaries of English topography. The estate is named in Domesday as Sant Dersingham, and was then held by a freeman under Harold Earl Godwin. It was purchased by the Prince of Wales, as we said, in 1862, and directly afterwards works of im- provement and reconstruction in the grounds and buildings were commenced, which went on with- out intermission during nearly ten years,and which may be said to have been finished on the comple- tion of the new Mansion about 1871. The estate comprises some 7,000 acres, 2,000 of which were heaths and plantations. The improvements have extended to about 500 acres of these 2,000 acres of originally waste lands. The park is only about 2,000 acres in extent; and a portion of this park land was very inferior till it was improved by drainage and tillage. The Prince has created a model farm upon the estate, which is managed under his own personal direction. It is 480 acres in extent, and includes the original home farm at Sandringham. There are 365 acres of arable and 47 acres of grass, besides 70 acres of marsh land. About 100 acres of the Prince's arable land consists of good and productive soil; about the same quantity is a fair soil on a chalk • subsoil; and the remaining 165 acres are poor or sandy light land. The Prince's flock consists of pure South Downs and about an equal number of half-bred and Down hoggets, and Down shear- lings. The herd includes Devons, Highlanders, and a dairy of Alderney cows. The park contains several hundred deer. The model farm-buildings are erected at the rear of the Royal gardens, and face the south, being well sheltered on the north and west. The Mansion of Sandringham when it passed into Royal hands was neither large nor interesting by reason of antiquity. It was a plain building in the Elizabethan style, to which the late owner had added a porch, gables, and other minor features. Any reader who has access to a file of the Illus- trated London News will find in the number for March 29th, 1862, a pretty view of the hall as it stood at the date of its acquisition by the Prince of Wales, which he may contrast with our Engrav- ing of the hall as it stands now, after all the works of re-construction which the Prince has carried out. The new Mansion is in the same general style as the older one, but contains probably four times the accommodation, and is far more handsome archi- tecturally. The central block, it will be Been, is a bold elevation of three storeys, surmounted by gables; from the midst is an octagonal bay con- tinued on each storey, surrounded by a parapet. On either hand, on the ground level, deep porches project from the frontage. The wings at both ends of the main building are of inferior elevation, and the roofs are broken with triple gablets. The conservatories extend to the left of the hall (to the right in the picture). The terraces, rockery, shrub- beries, and ornamental water exhibited in the pic- ture will afford some conception of the artistic manner in which the grounds are laid out. The natural picturesqueness of the situation has been greatly enhanced by the successful efforts of the best landscape gardeners, working under the Prince's orders, to develop the beauty of the surroundings, by the introduction of variety in trees, shrubs, and plants. What was half a wil- derness twenty years ago has been thus trans- formed into a miniature Eden of floral splendour and leafy luxuriance. This charming seat and estate, be it remembered, have been reclaimed and embellished, and are maintained at the Prince's own cost and charge. Sandringham does not rank among the recognised Royal Palaces of the Nation, kept up at the public expense. The money spent in improving the Estate, and the residence of the Prince and his household at Sandringham during a part of each year, have been a godsend to the inhabitants of this corner of Norfolk. The main entrance to the Park is by the celebrated "Norwich Gates," from which a short drive through a straight avenue conducts to the hall. The date of the completion of the new fabric is recorded in an inscription in the vestibule of the principal entrance hall, which reads:—" This House was built by Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, and Alexandra, his wife, in the year of our Lord 1870." This delightful domicile had barely been finished when there came upon its illustrious Owner that great affliction which threatened to cut short his life. In December, 1871, just ten years ago, Sandringham was the scene of a sickness more "nigh unto death," perhaps, than was ever endured by mortal who yet survived, and of a struggle for the mastery between fell disease and the resources of curative science which will ever remain memorable. Happily, Death was worsted in the encounter, and the Prince was restored to a thankful nation. That event invests Sandringham with a solemn interest it would not else have ex- cited. It has been not only a place of pleasure, but of severest suffering and trial nobly borne, and of wifely and sisterly ministration heroically per- formed. Of the elegant interior there are but two rooms that we feel prompted to mention. One is a lovely room on the first floor, "with its pale salmon-coloured and French-gray walls; its pink and lace hangings round the deep bay of the bow- window; its medley of old china, photographs, water-colours, dwarf palms, flowers; its thousand- and-one pretty nick-nacks: its singing birds; and with the indescribable, yet felt, though unseen, presence of delicate and refined womanhood which pervades the whole of the exquisite chamber. This is the boudoir of the Princess—the room that so grew into the heart of her Royal Highness, be- I cause of early, grateful memories associated with I it, that when Sandringham was rebuilt she made it her especial stipulation that it should be reconstructed on the ' ancient lines' in the minutest particular." The other room we refer to is in the same corridor. It is a large, comfortable home-like chamber, and it is not easy now, ear- I veying its cheerful aspect and surroundings, "to saidm mduinteynotf übniudnad ion; realise the scene to which these silent walls could bear witness, what time a strong man, on this same bed, battled for breath in the very straits of the dark valley, while his dearest kinsfolk were in n whicht thhae than e honouredetlhiceiling g Prince, above b,o ne when hi the nb whileoe dn a final farewell, while in the corridor hushed re- tainers eee Bentley, obae around Yet tueeshntsoesdrt eahlf eoofdrvor eroet theb e outside in the snow-slash grief-smitted labouring folk longed, yet feared, .for tidings of their is the mark of the orifice whence projected the hfairate hook supporting the trapeze cunnieesiy devised by the slow and weary road to convalescence was wont to change his rec h t • • e um on position, or raise himself into a sitting posture That gloomy episode has passed like an evil dream. The lord of Sandringham now enjoys perfect health and vigour again , and we all wish that he and his love- able Princes d Princess an children may live, an unbroken family Circle, to keep many, many happy Christ- mas-tides under the roof of their dear country home in East Anglia.

div.head: CHARGES OF EMBEZZLEMENT AGAINST I PRESCOT TRAVELLER.
div.p: CHARGES OF EMBEZZLEMENT AGAINST I PRESCOT TRAVELLER.

At the Preseot Police Court, on Friday, before Mr. W. L. Evans, George Brownhill, of Prescot, was brought up on re mand, charged with having embezzled the moneys of his employer,Mr. Thomas Prescott, watch material manufacturer and dealer, Stanley-crescent, Present—Mi. Cross, who pro- secuted, said that the moneys taken, so far as known, were only of small amount, but in the aggregate the sum was con- siderable. Out of thirteen applications which the prosecutor had made to his customers, it transpired that all the accounts rendered by the prisoner were inaccurate, and the prosecutor did not know to what extent his loss would be in the matter. The prosecutor appointed prisoner as his traveller about the be ginning of November, last year, at a salary of £3 101. per week; and his duties were to travel through the districts pr;:viously appointed by the prosecutor, to solicit orders for goods, to collect accounts, and to remit £lO when the cash in hand exceeded £l2. At the end of each week he had to send in a statement, and to remit the balance, less his wages. It was the duty of the prisoner, when he returned to Prescot, to balance up, and hand over any balance due te prosecutor, or to receive any balance that might be due to him. When away on his journeys in June and July last, the prisoner forwarded statements which the prosecutor afterwards ascertained were incorrect, and the prisoner .did not account for various sums of money he had received After the prisoner had left the prosecutor's service, the latter, in consequence of information he received, wrote to several of his customers, and ascertained from thorn that prisoner had systematically falsified his returns. AN EARNEST APPEAL is made on behalf of JOHN HARRISON, formerly boatman at Runcorn, Ferry, now permanently disabled by bodily infirmity at the advanced age of 66. During his 45 years' public service as ferryman, he gained the respect of all who knew him by his civility, kind- ness, and steady attention to duty in all weathers, as shown by the fact that not a single accident oemrred during his time. POST OFFICE. LETTint PosTAGE-Letters not exceeding 1 oz., One Penny; not exceeding 2 oz. 11d.. not exceeding 4 oz., 23.; not exceeding 6 oz., 21d.; not exceeding 8 oz., 3d.; not exceed- ing 10 oz., 3/d.; not exceeding 12 oz., 44. A letter exceeding 12 oz. is liable to a postage of Id. for every ounce, beginning with the first ounce: thus, a letter weighing between 14 oz. and 15 oz. must be prepaid 15d. No letter may exceed the dimensions of Ift. 6in. in length, 9in. in width, and Gin. in depth. Samples sent by post are dealt with as ordinary letters, and charged as above. No money payment is taken for postage of etters, and double rates are charged if sent without stamps. NEWSPAPERS-Any Newspaper can be posted for one halfpenny, for delivery in tho United Kingdom. Newspapers for transmission abroad must be posted within eighi days from day of publication, including that day; if posted more than eight days aftei book rate of postage must be prepaid. Any newspaper found to contain an enclosure or writing of the nature of a letter, will be charged as an unpaid or insufficiently paid letter. Postage Stamps to be used in all cases of foreign directed newspapers. STAMPED NEWSPAPER WRAPPERS may be purchased singly or in any number, according to the following scale of prices :-1 for id.; 2 for Id.; 3 for ad.; 4 for 2d.; 5 for 3d.; 6 for 3id., and so on INLAND BOOK POSE-The Book Post rate is one halfpenny for every two oz., or fraction of two oz. Every book packet must beeither without a cover, or in a cover open at the ends. No book packet may exceed bibs. in weight, or 1 ft. 6 in. long, 9 in. wide, and 6 in. deep. POST CARDS, available for transmission in the United Kingdom only, may be ob- tained at all Post-offices, in packets of twelve for 7d. and 84.; or, stout cards: one, id.; two, lid.; three, 2d.; four, 21d.; five, 3id.; six, 44. Thin cards: one, id.; two, lid.; three, lid.; four, 264.; five, 3d.; six, 31d. Foreign post-cards, Id. and lid. each. POSTAL ORDERS FOR SMALL SUMS.-18., is. 6d., id.: 2s. 64.. 55., and 7s. 6d., ld. 105., 12s. 68., 155., 17s. 63., and 205., 2d. A postal order may be crossed like a cheque, by the words "sod C 0.," or specially by inserting the name of a banker. The person to whom a postal order is issued must insert the name of the person to whom it is to be paid, and that person may insert the name of the money order office at which it is desired payment should be made. GOVERNMENT INSURANCE AND ANNUITIES-The lives of persons of either sex between the ages of 16 and 60, may be insured for not less than £2O nor more than £lOO. The sums charged for deferred annuities, or deferred monthly allowances, vary with the age and sex, health, habits, and occupation of the persons. REGISTRATION -By prepayment of a fee of twopence any letter, newspaper, or other packet may be registered to any place in the United Kingdom. The registration makes transmission more secure; and the Post-office, under certain regulations, makes good the value of a lost registered letter, up to £2. Inland letters which contain coin are treated as registered, and charged on delivery a registration fee of eightpence, in addition to ordinary postage. Every letter to be registered should be presented to the clerk in the office, and a receipt obtained for it, and on no account dropped into the letter-box. Rural Post Messengers will receive letters for registration on their out- ward and inward walks. Registered-letter envelopes, bearing a 2d, stamp for the pay. ment of the registration fee, will be sold at all Post-offices and by rural messengers.

INFORMATION FOR ELECTORS. JANUARY I.—The new Register, for Counties and Boroughs, comes in force. 31. Purchasers of freehold or copyhold property must obtain complete possession on or before this day, to entitle them to be registered in July next as county voters. MARCH I.—Auditors and assessors of boroughs to be elected. 25.—Overseers to be appointed on this day, or within fourteen days. Those Surveyors of Highways whose year has expired must verify their accounts by oath before one justice within fourteen days, to be delivered to their successors after the appointment of such successors. 29. Poor Law Guardians to be elected on this day, or within fourteen days thereafter. JUNE 10.—Town Clerks to give notices to Overseers to prepare Lists of persona en titled to vote in boroughs. 20.—Overseers to publish notices that persons will not be inserted on lists of Borough or County Voters, in respect of occupation, if Poor Rates and Assessed Taxes, due previously to sth January, be not paid before the 20th July;— and to fix on church doors, for two Sundays, a copy of the County Register then in force; and notices to persons qualified to vote for counties to make claims. JULY 15.—Electoral year commences for Boroughs, for Counties it commences on the 31st; occupation of premises must therefore commence on or before these dates, In order to qualify the occupier to be on the borough or county register for next year. New occupiers of houses in boroughs and counties should see that their names are properly inserted on the first poor rate made after these dates. 20.—Assessed taxes and poor rates cue on the sth January last must be paid on or before this day, by all electors of cities and boroughs, and £l2 occupiers in counties, or they will be disqualified from voting. Last day for sending in claims for voting in counties. 22.—The List of persona in arrear of rates and taxes, and who will therefore be omitted from the next year's Register, is open for perusal, without fee, at the Overseers' office, for 14 days after this date. 25.—Persons already on the Register in respect of lodgings, and desiring to be on the next Register in respect of the same lodgings, must send in their claims. I.—Overseers to make out lists of county and borough electors. AUGUST I.—Overseers to Ix lists of voters on all church and chapel doors in their pariah, to remain there fourteen days. Overseers to keep Lists of Voters at their Offices, for sale, and also for inspection, without payment of any fee, between the hours of ten and four, for fourteen days. 20.—Last day for serving notices of objection in counties 25.—Last day for persons omitted from the list of borough voters and £l2 occupiers in counties making claims to be registered, and for serving notices of objection in boroughs. 31.—Taxes and rates, payable on March Ist, must be paid before this day. SEPTEMBER I.—Overseers to deliver lists of county voters to clerk of the peace, and to fix lists of objections to county voters and claims and objections to borough voters on church and chapel doors, to remain fourteen days. Churchwardens and overseers to make out jury lists, and publish first three Sundays. 12.—0 n or before this date, persons whose names or places of abode or the nature of whose qualifying property is not correctly stated, or in respect of whom there is any other error or omission in any List, may make a declaration and forward the same to the Town Clerk, who shall sign and deliver the same to the Revising Barrister at his first Court. From Sept. 15 to Oct 31, Revising Barrister to revise Borough Parliamentary List and Burgess List. Ocrogra 15.—Accounts of waywardens or highway surveyors to be produced at parish meeting, to be held within fifteen days before the special sessions, in the week next after the Michaelmas quarter sessions. NOVEMBER I.—The new revised Burgess List comes in force. Borough councillors to be elected. S.—Mayor and aldermen of boroughs to be elected. 15.—Day for attor- neys, proctors, notaries public, Ao., to take out certificates. DECEMBER 31.—Clerks of the peace'sign and deliver register ofcounty voters to Sheriff • and Town Clerks sign and deliver to returning officers copies of borough lists

The year 1882 is the latter part of the 5642nd and the beginning of thc ' 5643rd year since the creation of the world, according to the Jews. The year 5643 commences on Sep. 14, 1882, being the 19th year of the 297th cycle of 19 years. Tbe year 1882 answers to the 6595th of the Julian period, to the 2635th from the foundation of Rome, to the 26588 h of the Olympiads, and to the year 7890-9101 the Byzantine Era. The year 1300 of the Mohammedan Era commences on Nov. 12, 1882; and the Ramadan (month of abstinence observed by the Turks) oommencee on July 17, 1882.
